Trump hits out at Canada over retaliatory tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:31:00 UTC
16:31:00 KST

Trump hits out at Canada over retaliatory tariffs
August 23, 2026
US President Donald Trump on Sunday accused Canada of wanting "the benefits of being a [US] State, without being one" in his first remarks since trade talks between Ottawa and Washington failed.
"They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!" he wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.
What has happened in the US-Canada trade dispute?
In an ongoing trade dispute with the United States, Canada said on Saturday that it would introduce tariffs on several US products starting September 8.
The announcement comes in retaliation to the US imposing 50% tariffs earlier on Saturday on a broad range of Canadian products after the two sides failed to reach a trade deal on Friday.
"Canada will match Washington's new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa.
"In the coming days, we will release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labor Day," he said.
While the US had blamed Canada for declining to finalize the trade pact with Washington on Friday, Carney defended Ottawa's position, explaining, "We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked."
He later on Saturday met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers to discuss the suspension of the trade talks with the US.
What products are affected by the tariffs?
The US tariffs will affect a broad range of products, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods, and hockey equipment, and cover some $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of Canadian exports to its southern neighbor.
Canada's retaliatory tariffs would, in turn, target steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, Carney said.
The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff Carney explicitly described as a trade "war."
"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.
How have Canadian and US politicians reacted?
Doug Ford, the premier of Canada's most populous province Ontario and one of the most vocal opponents of US President Donald Trump's tariffs, slammed the proposed trade deal and backed Carney's decision to retaliate.
"I'm glad he didn't sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector and manufacturing sector," Ford said on Saturday.
Meanwhile, Pierre Poilievre, the leader of the official opposition Conservative Party, urged Canadians to "stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses."
In the US, Democratic lawmakers and governors have blamed Trump for the escalating trade conflict.
"Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That's Trump's economic policy in a nutshell," New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.
Michigan Congresswoman Haley Stevens also slammed "Trump's reckless and unnecessary trade war."
Friendly ties turned sour
The fresh tariffs are the culmination of long and tense trade negotiations between the two sides and mark a sharp reversal from just two days earlier, when officials from Washington and Ottawa appeared optimistic that a compromise was in the making.
According to the AP news agency, no further talks were planned to resolve the situation.
The US administration's approach to Canada is a major change from the friendly ties the two countries have traditionally had.
Trump has often said he wants tariffs on Canadian goods to encourage companies to move manufacturing back to the US.
He has also made controversial comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney said Canada understood that "America has changed" and that the two countries would "not return to their old relationship."

Mystery AI model Ox Alpha draws developers with free access

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23

16:30:00 KST

Mystery AI model Ox Alpha draws developers with free access
SAN FRANCISCO – A new artificial intelligence model called Ox Alpha is gaining traction among developers after appearing online for free, even as the identity of its creator remains a mystery.
The model appeared on AI marketplace OpenRouter last week under the label “stealth model”. Ox Alpha offers a roughly one million-token context window that can process text, image and video input, according to OpenRouter.
The unusual debut has triggered a guessing game among AI developers over who may be behind the model.
Some online speculation has pointed to China, where companies have recently rolled out increasingly capable models, including Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba Group’s latest Qwen models.
A growing number of companies from ByteDance to Sea and Alibaba have in 2026 launched models without initially claiming credit for those platforms.
By not publicising their origins from the start, tech companies may be aiming to test the waters for new-fangled services and initiatives, affording these projects more freedom to experiment.
Ox Alpha is available free with near-unlimited usage for a week, according to OpenCode, helping fuel a surge in experimentation among developers.
Stripe chief executive officer Patrick Collison described it in a post on X as “very impressive”, while users have shared reviews on YouTube and Reddit. Bloomberg

The launch would mark another step in Tesla's push into autonomous driving, with robotaxi services expected to play a key role in the company's future revenue model and artificial intelligence strategy. ■

China Focus: Humanoid robot games put real-world skills to the test
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
15:25:01 CST
16:25:01 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Inside a makeshift restaurant, a humanoid robot gripped a snack with a pair of tongs, placed it in a microwave, turned the timer dial and then moved on to deal with another order -- all under the watchful eyes of judges.
The restaurant-service contest, held earlier this week ahead of Saturday's official opening of the second World Humanoid Robot Games, offered a glimpse of a central focus of this year's event: testing robots not only in athletic competitions, but also in workplace tasks.
Running through to Wednesday, the games have attracted 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries and regions across six continents, with team participation quadrupling from the inaugural edition last year. The event features 51 competition items, up from 26 last year, while the number of matches has surged from 487 to 1,301.
Among the biggest additions are 21 scenario-based contests, covering settings such as factories, hotels, homes and logistics facilities.
Tasks ranging from industrial assembly and housekeeping to emergency rescue and library book sorting are designed around jobs that can be repetitive, physically demanding, dirty, dangerous or difficult.
At a service contest staged in a realistic hotel setting, more than 10 robot teams were given 30 minutes to tackle three tasks: moving luggage of different sizes, replenishing guest-room supplies and making beds.
"Judges look at how many tasks the robot completes, whether there are collisions and how smoothly it performs," said an organizer of the contest.
Even routine actions can pose demanding tests of robotic dexterity. In the restaurant contest, for example, robots had to turn a microwave timer to five minutes, with deviations of more than one minute costing points. They could also be penalized if too much liquid was spilled while delivering a prepared drink.
This year's games have also introduced a dedicated dexterous-hand competition, featuring eight high-precision tasks including power-tool assembly, picking up beans with tweezers, weighing powder, prying open bottle caps and connecting flexible cables.
The emphasis reflects an effort to bring competition tasks closer to actual workplace needs.
Liu Weiliang, deputy head of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said organizers had surveyed stakeholders in areas that include commercial services, landscaping inspection and emergency rescue, before designing the events.
In one case, competitive tasks reflected worker duties at supermarkets, where employees may spend long hours at night restocking shelves, packing delivery orders and returning misplaced goods -- repetitive work that can be time-consuming and physically tiring.
"Every task completed is effectively a trial run in a real-world scenario," said Liu. "There is no need to rebuild the same testing environment after the competition. Performance on the field itself provides evidence of commercial viability."
The bar for autonomy has been raised as well.
Except for the 100-meter and 400-meter hurdles, all track and other competitive events require full autonomy. In scenario-based events, fully autonomous operation carries a scoring coefficient of 1, compared with 0.5 for remote-controlled operation.
Jiang Guangzhi, head of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said that many competition rules are expected to evolve into practical technical standards, helping turn technological advances into industrial applications.
"Once robots master these 'last-meter' skills, they can turn medals into orders and move directly from the competition arena to real-world workplaces," Jiang said.
Xu Xiaolan, chairwoman of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the recently held 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing that China's humanoid robot industry had entered a critical stage of large-scale commercialization and deployment, with embodied intelligence products moving from small-batch trials toward broader adoption.
Major technical challenges, however, remain.
Wang Xingxing, founder of Unitree Robotics, said limited generalization capability is currently the biggest bottleneck facing the global humanoid robot industry.
In controlled settings, he said, AI models trained on sufficient data can achieve task success rates close to 100 percent. But performance can fall sharply once the object being handled or the surrounding environment changes.
Wang said "a ChatGPT moment in embodied intelligence" will come when a robot can be placed in an unfamiliar environment and complete about 80 percent of everyday tasks through simple voice or text instructions.
He expects such a breakthrough could come as early as within two to three years, or within five to 10 years at the latest.
For now, the games also serve as a testing ground to assess the technology's progress. Liang Hongjun, an official with Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said the World Humanoid Robot Games were designed to give companies, investors and the public a more tangible view of the development of humanoid robots.
"The industry is moving from telling technology stories to delivering real-world applications, and from pure technology development toward products and services," Liang said.
That transition, he added, will require companies to focus on technological innovation, while governments and industry organizations work on opening up application scenarios, developing standards and defining safety boundaries. ■

Chinese delegation for 48th WorldSkills Competition formed
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
15:24:59 CST
16:24:59 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has formed its national delegation for the 48th WorldSkills Competition to be held in Shanghai in September, the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security announced Sunday.
The Chinese delegation comprises 220 members, including 71 competitors who will participate in all 64 skill categories of the event. The contestants come from 21 provinces across the country, with 49 being students and 22 being working professionals. Their average age is 21, all within the age bracket from 18 to 25.
Held every two years, the WorldSkills Competition is the world's largest international gathering of skills talent. It is scheduled to take place in Shanghai from September 22 to 27 this year, with nearly 70 countries and regions expected to send about 1,400 competitors.
Since joining WorldSkills International in 2010, China has taken part in seven previous competitions, amassing a total of 93 gold medals, 41 silver medals, 28 bronze medals, and 71 medallions for excellence. The country has topped both the gold medal tally and the overall team standings for four consecutive editions.
The competition covers a wide range of professional skills divided into six major categories, including manufacturing and engineering technology, information and communication technology, construction and building technology, transportation and logistics, creative arts and fashion as well as social and personal services.
It will feature 64 skills, including seven new skills, such as software testing and unmanned aerial systems. The competition focuses primarily on practical work and generally does not include theoretical exams, with competitors instead completing hands-on tasks.
A spokesperson for the Chinese delegation said the team will strictly abide by event regulations, compete fairly and with sportsmanship, and strive to demonstrate both skill excellence and a positive image, showcasing the craftsmanship and professionalism of China's young skilled workers.
The delegation's official awards ceremony attire and competition uniforms have also been unveiled. Both outfits draw inspiration from the wooden structural craftsmanship widely found in ancient Chinese architecture, reflecting a heritage of artisanship and cultural confidence. ■

HONG KONG, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Paul Chan, financial secretary of China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government, said on Sunday that funds raised from AI-related IPOs in Hong Kong reached nearly 100 billion HK dollars (about 12.75 billion U.S. dollars) between last December and this May, accounting for about 55 percent of the total IPO funds raised during the period.
Chan wrote on his blog that the country's rapid development in AI has provided a significant boost to Hong Kong's economy and financial markets. Partly driven by robust global demand for advanced electronics and AI-related products, Hong Kong's exports recorded high double-digit growth for several consecutive quarters, helping the city's economic growth in the first half of this year exceed original expectations.
Citing a multinational tech firm's report, Chan added that if local small- and medium-sized enterprises can catch up with large firms in using AI by 2035, it could bring up to 65 billion HK dollars in economic benefits to Hong Kong.
Meanwhile, Chan emphasized that Hong Kong must step up efforts to prepare for and address the challenges that evolving frontier technologies may bring to the job market. (1 U.S. dollar equals 7.84 Hong Kong dollars) ■

French triathlete wins Tallinn Ironman, Estonian 10th in record field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:23:00 UTC
16:23:00 KST

French triathlete wins Tallinn Ironman, Estonian 10th in record field
French triathlete Remi Conte won the full-distance Tallinn Ironman on Saturday. The first Estonian finisher placed 10th.
The event went ahead despite the windy conditions and Level 2 storm warning, with Conte completing the course in a time of eight hours and eight minutes.
"It's now been three years since I last finished an Ironman. It's all emotional, but I'm very happy," he told ERR after the race. Kristofer Kamberg was the top Estonian competitor, finishing 10th.
The race is the largest triathlon in the Baltic states and attracted a record 4,300 entrants this year, for the full triathlon on Saturday and the 70.3 half-distance on Sunday. Around 1,500 people were involved in staffing the event, whose headquarters was the Unibet Arena.
Chief organizer Ain-Alar Juhanson told ERR a total of 97 nations are represented in the event across all categories, with 1,900 people due to start the full race, almost as many competing in the 70.3 race, as well as 150 teams. "Those are numbers we have never seen here before," Juhanson added.
Lake Raku, just south of Tallinn, was used for the swimming stage for the first time.
The toughest part of the 226-kilometer race for the winner turned out to be the final discipline, the run. "The start of the swim was delayed a little because of fog. We started later. The bike was okay, a bit of wind, and I didn't get any rain at first. But it started raining at the beginning of the second lap of the run," Conte noted.
Kamberg completed the course in eight hours and 37 minutes, 29 minutes behind the winner, giving him 10th place. "It wasn't easy. In fact, it was hard the whole time. The weather was probably in our favor, even though it's raining, because it didn't get hot, and my first reaction is: damn, this really is hard," Kamberg said.
This was only his second Ironman, and he called himself a "below-average Estonian amateur" who had not put a massive emphasis on training in the run-up to the event. In a triathlon context, his level of modest training would take up about 10–12 hours a week. "I was actually a little worried about that coming here," he continued, and, as with Conte, found the run the hardest part.
"My leg muscles started giving out midway through the run, and that was really the main reason my pace dropped off as it did," Kamberg added.
The Baltics' largest triathlon festival culminates in Tallinn on Sunday with a half-distance race, where Estonians Kaidi Kivioja and Henry Räppo defend their titles. The event is already underway at the time of writing.
In the women's race, Kaidi Kivioja is looking to repeat last year's win, and her Estonian record over the full distance at the European Championships in Germany in June bodes well for that.
"You can't just look at past results and assume that anything is guaranteed this Sunday. But I'm going to go out there and give it my best," Kivioja said, noting she took on a new coach and new training regime this year.
Some of the traffic restrictions in place Saturday will remain in place on Sunday. The 70.3 race got underway at 9.00 a.m. today.

====================================================================================================

Israel’s battle for global consciousness: Why the Sparta doctrine harms national security - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:22:58 UTC
16:22:58 KST

Israel’s national security doctrine, formulated by David Ben-Gurion in the 1950s, rests on three pillars: deterrence, early warning, and decisive victory.
Deterrence is meant to persuade the enemy that it cannot defeat Israel and therefore, rationally, should refrain from attacking. If deterrence fails, intelligence must provide sufficient warning to mobilize the reserves, allowing Israel to maintain a relatively small standing army in peacetime.
And decisive victory means seeking unequivocal wins as quickly as possible while shifting the fighting onto enemy territory. Victory restores deterrence, postpones the next war, and gives Israel time to grow stronger between conflicts.
Is this doctrine still valid after October 7?
Some say no. Hamas was not deterred, intelligence failed to provide warning, and Israel did not achieve a swift, decisive victory. This, they argue, was no accident but the result of a changed reality: many of our enemies are now terrorist organizations rather than state actors; their motivations are ideological and religious and do not necessarily conform to conventional calculations of deterrence; the arena itself has changed – our enemies are no longer only those massed along our borders. The doctrine, therefore, must be rethought.
Others argue that the classical doctrine remains sound, but that Israel, lulled by overconfidence, failed to follow it. We did not create deterrence – we simply assumed it existed, and we were wrong. We dismissed warning signs that were, in fact, there. And for years, we abandoned the pursuit of decisive victory in favor of “managing the conflict” and “quiet in return for quiet.” On this view, Israel must return to Ben-Gurion’s principles and apply them with resolve.
A third approach would preserve the classical doctrine while adding two further elements: defense – the ability to withstand a surprise attack if deterrence and advance warning fail – and preemption – taking the initiative to eliminate emerging threats before they fully ripen.
But this debate is taking place on too narrow a field. National security doctrine must address not only how we confront enemies waging physical war against us, but also those waging a battle to shape global consciousness – the perceptions and narratives through which Israel is understood. National security is measured not only by our ability to defend our borders, but also by Israel’s standing in the international arena.
Until recently, Israel’s relations with the United States and several leading European countries constituted a formidable diplomatic Iron Dome, protecting us in critical arenas – security, economics, diplomacy, law, and culture. In recent years, and especially since October 7, we have been losing ground in the battle over global consciousness. Negative views of Israel are becoming increasingly entrenched. Challenges to the legitimacy of the Jewish nation-state are finding traction. The demonization of Israel is gaining ground both in the European Union, Israel’s largest trading partner, and in the United States, our most important security and diplomatic ally.
The evidence is mounting not only in public opinion polls but also in concrete actions. Our adversaries could achieve their own “total victory” in this struggle if a future American president decided to impose an arms embargo on Israel. Is that really inconceivable? The consequences could be devastating.
Not everything is within our control. Deep currents of antisemitism, polarizing identity politics, social media platforms that traffic in hatred, social inequality, and other forces are poisoning the international arena. But much does depend on us – both through what we fail to do and through what we actually do.
Our failure to act has been profound. Israel has largely been absent from this battlefield – if by presence we mean the formulation and implementation of a coherent strategy. For too many years, our national investment in this arena was negligible – less than the cost of a single Israeli Air Force squadron.
And some of our own actions hand our enemies ammunition. We alienate the world – including our friends – when we tolerate Jewish terrorism, use disproportionate force, engage in racist rhetoric, and erode confidence in our own democratic institutions.
The bottom line is clear: if we lose the battle over global consciousness, Israel’s national security will be gravely weakened. Israel will not be able to flourish as it once did if it comes to be regarded as a “Sparta” – an embattled fortress-state living by the sword behind high walls.
We need to change course.
First, Israel must establish an authoritative institutional framework for this mission. Alongside the three organizations responsible for our physical security – the IDF at our borders, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) at home, and the Mossad abroad – we need a fourth national body of comparable authority and stature charged with conducting the battle over global consciousness.
Second, Israeli policy across the board, including the use of military force, must be shaped by a national security doctrine that recognizes this battle as critical to securing our future.
Yedidia Stern is president of JPPI – the Jewish People Policy Institute – and a professor (emeritus) of law at Bar-Ilan University.

India's Coast Guard and Navy continued search-and-rescue operations off the eastern coast on Sunday after a Panama-flagged cargo vessel carrying 24 crew sank, with two Chinese nationals rescued, a senior official said.
The two rescued Chinese seafarers said the vessel developed a list on Friday and sank within eight minutes, forcing crew to abandon ship, Shyam Jagannathan, director general of India's Maritime Administration, told Reuters.
Jagannathan said the chances of finding survivors generally fall sharply after 12 hours, but rescuers were continuing the search.
Twenty-two crew members remain missing from the Ocean Winner, including 18 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals, and one Bangladeshi, according to the Indian Coast Guard.
The Indian Navy is closely coordinating with the Coast Guard to locate the remaining crew, the Navy said in a post on X.
The Coast Guard has sent two vessels from Sri Vijaya Puram, formerly known as Port Blair, for the search-and-rescue operation, a Coast Guard spokesperson said.
Ship sinks over 200 miles from port for unknown reasons
The Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore bound for China after departing from India's eastern Paradip port on Friday, according to an initial report prepared by India's Maritime Administration.
The cargo ship sank about 240 nautical miles from the port, according to government sources.
The cause of the sinking was not immediately known.

2026-08-23
07:22:40 UTC
16:22:40 KST

Iran has made billions of dollars despite sanctions and amid the United States blockade, Supreme National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaee claimed in an interview with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) station on Saturday.
He also stated that Iran had sold millions of barrels of oil, bypassing the US naval blockade.
"In the past month or two, we sold seventy million barrels of oil," he said. "Now every day we sell oil to American ships on that side, as much as we produce."
He also warned that other countries should not join the US "economic war" against Iran, threatening to strike any that participated.
"Of course, we negotiate with him first," he said. "We hold a meeting, we say, 'go and separate your ranks from America,' and if they don't act, we will strike. We will strike the interests of the country."
In addition, Rezaee threatened the US, claiming that Iran had not attacked American bases unprovoked before. Now that the US had declared economic warfare, he explained, Iran would strike "a few oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere."
Iran would also attack bases if the US added forces to it, he said.
"They will not make any movements in the southern direction," he added. "We will find out if they have met with the counter-revolutionary groups. We will attack them there."
US, Israel aiming to promote war to sell more weapons, Iran claims
During the interview, Rezaee accused the US and Israel of intentionally fostering the regional conflicts in order to sell weaponry, saying that Iran had no interest in the war.
"If we were warmongers, would we have gone to three negotiations with the Americans?" he defended. "How many ceasefires would we have accepted? Of course, we are not warmongers, but we will not surrender under any circumstances. We will defend our nation wholeheartedly."
The Strait of Hormuz is currently closed, he also claimed, and will reopen only if the US "fulfills its obligations."
Discussing the Mecca defense pact between Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia, Rezaee claimed that the Gulf countries had been spurred by the US abandoning them.
"America told them, 'Goodbye, we are leaving.' They want to fill America's void."
Iran would also be evolving its defenses in the wake of the war with Israel and the US, he said, saying that "Iran today will no longer be the Iran it was before the war.
"Of course, the pretentious and arrogant America will not be the America it was before the war," he added.
US President Donald Trump's "stupidity," he said, came in creating a huge debt for Americans and their allies.
"He wanted to make America great again with his election slogan, but what did he make great?" he said. "He made the debts greater. The debt on the 30-year US bond rate has become greater."
In order to finance itself now, Razaee claimed, the US "must borrow at a rate of three and seven tenths of 2020, meaning that for every hundred billion dollars in debt, it must spend three and seven tenths of a billion dollars more annually than in the past. If you multiply this by the thirty-year US bonds in those 40 trillion bonds, perhaps several times our annual budget is imposed on the American people and American companies."
US endangered world by attacking Iran over nuclear weapon, Razaee accuses
The Supreme National Security Council head also addressed the US claims that it had begun the war with Iran in order to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons, accusing America that by doing so it had actually put the world in greater danger.
"The United States said it came to prevent the atomic bomb," he explained. "Now the whole world is saying, 'Wow, neither the NPT [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons] nor membership in the Atomic Energy Organization is effective. And it turned out that this atomic issue is very important. The United States has started a war. Why shouldn't we go after the atomic bomb?'"
Iran, Razaee claimed, had accepted the presence of IAEA inspectors, numerous checks and forms of supervision, and other concessions for its nuclear energy projects.
"Well, now the world says that if Iran, which has been so obedient, is attacked, and its nuclear facilities are attacked, why don't we go and make a bomb so that no one can attack us?"

Katz orders IDF to accelerate destruction of Hezbollah infrastructure in southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:22:34 UTC
16:22:34 KST

The IDF is increasing its pace of destroying Hezbollah's terror infrastructure in southern Lebanon, following instructions given by Defense Minister Israel Katz.
The focus is on Hezbollah strongholds, most of which are Shi'ite villages that the organization built with Iranian funding over more than two decades.
According to officers in the IDF's Northern Command, Hezbollah, with Iranian guidance, built a strategic plan centered around military infrastructure.
The plan focused on villages including Kafr Kila, Al Khiam, Bint Jbeil, and Taibe, which sit along strategic routes and ridges whose control prevents Israeli ground maneuvers deep into Lebanon while simultaneously granting Hezbollah the ability to quickly reach the Israeli border should it want to attack the Galilee.
During searches conducted in these areas, the IDF uncovered countless facilities used by thousands of terrorists as shelters for extended periods, allowing them to also emerge from hidden positions and surprise the IDF.
Israeli troops also located weapons depots, command centers, observation posts, and launch sites.
The IDF is not only destroying Hezbollah infrastructure during these operations, but is also working to open new routes that will provide easier access to operational areas, improve force security, and enable faster supply deliveries.
The routes will also allow maintenance teams to enter the Lebanese territory and repair engineering and armored combat vehicles operating in the area.
Villages built as military 'fortresses'
Some villages were built as military “fortresses” designed to provide Hezbollah terrorists with a high level of engineering protection, primarily from IDF airstrikes. IDF searches located infrastructure in the heart of villages and towns, beneath civilian homes, including in areas such as Zawtar al Sharqiya.
The IDF noted that the continued engineering activity in these areas also prevents Hezbollah from carrying out guerrilla operations.
Officers currently operating in the field also emphasized that, with intelligence support, searches are being carried out in smaller villages such as Beit al Sayyad, located south of Tyre, where Hezbollah invested heavily in infrastructure. The IDF is using its engineering capabilities to destroy these sites.
Meanwhile, security officials claim that the Lebanese army has so far failed to achieve the expected engineering results based on understandings mediated by the US. They claim the Lebanese army fears Hezbollah and is therefore not moving quickly to locate and destroy terrorist infrastructure.
The officials added that the IDF will need to continue its engineering activity in southern Lebanon in order to collapse Hezbollah’s strategic infrastructure. They said that, taken together, these efforts would deliver a severe blow to the Shiite organization.

Russia Uses Air Shadow Fleet to Supply Forces in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:21:00 UTC
16:21:00 KST

Russia is using a network of military and private aircraft, similar to its maritime “shadow fleet”, to sustain its forces in Africa’s Sahel.
At least 75 flights linked to Russian state-aligned military forces travelled to Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger between January 2025 and July 2026, according to an analysis by the Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The network resembles the logic of Russia’s better-known maritime “shadow fleet” of tankers used to export sanctioned Russian oil: rather than relying exclusively on clearly identifiable state assets, Moscow uses a mix of military operators, government agencies and private carriers to keep its supply lines running.
The most active operator was Flight Unit 224, a Russian defence ministry-controlled carrier already under US sanctions, the study found. But the study also identified Sapsan Airlines, Liz Aviation and Russia’s ‘Ministry for Emergency Situations’ among operators not sanctioned by the EU, US or UK.
The flights point to a broader logistics system rather than isolated movements. State aircraft regularly travelled through Russian-controlled bases in Syria and Libya, while private carriers tended to use commercial hubs in Turkey, Algeria and the UAE.
Tomáš Zdechovský, Czech EPP MEP and First Lieutenant in the Czech Army said the findings should trigger an urgent assessment by the EU institutions and member states.
Ukraine Destroys Su-24M at Saky, Hits Primorsko-Akhtarsk Airfield
“If these aircraft and companies are knowingly transporting Russian military personnel or military-related cargo to support the Africa Corps, they should face targeted sanctions, regardless of where the aircraft are registered,” he told Euractiv.
Brussels has progressively expanded its targeting of Russia’s maritime shadow fleet, including companies and other enablers based in third countries. Its latest sanctions package added 41 vessels and entities supporting the network.
Libya is becoming particularly important to this network as Moscow expands its military infrastructure there.
The Washington-based, offcial “Africa Defense Forum” , citing data from the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency’s Tearline project, reported that Russia plans to fund infrastructure projects and deploy personnel at six Libyan air bases.
The sites, stretching across central, eastern and southern Libya, are being equipped or refurbished to support Russian aircraft, air defence systems, drones and personnel.

Major tech firms to help upskill Hong Kong workers under ‘AI for All’: Paul Chan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Major tech firms to help upskill Hong Kong workers under ‘AI for All’: Paul Chan
Finance chief warns frontier tech will challenge the job market, urging faster action to equip young people with AI skills and workplace opportunities
Hong Kong’s employees retraining board will partner with major tech firms to launch an artificial intelligence (AI) training programme for the working population in November, the city’s finance chief has said.
In his Sunday blog, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the HK$50 million (US$6.4 million) “AI for All” inclusive programme, announced in the February budget, would feature more than 200 activities and was expected to benefit 50,000 people within two years.
“The development and application of frontier technology will pose challenges to the job market. We must speed up our response, helping young people master the skills and giving them opportunities to apply them in the workplace,” he said.
“Hong Kong is home to many small and medium-sized enterprises whose agility, adaptability, and innovative spirit have seen them through past tech shifts and economic cycles. As we navigate this current paradigm shift, we will fully support them in adapting, preparing, and continuing to grow.”
Chan cited a survey finding that almost 70 per cent of Hong Kong residents were proficient in using AI, while about 20 per cent were highly proficient and leveraged AI agents to automate daily tasks.
He said the report further estimated that if Hong Kong’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) could catch up to large corporations in AI adoption by 2035, it could unlock up to HK$65 billion in economic value for the city.

NCSIST releases information on Strong Bow missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:17:48 UTC
16:17:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Chung Shan Institute of Science and Technology has released information about its new Strong Bow missile on its website.
The Strong Bow is a land-based, mid-tier system designed to counter tactical ballistic missiles, according to the institute. It can intercept incoming tactical ballistic missiles at medium altitude and form a layered interception network with lower-tier missile defense systems, it added.
The missile uses thrust-vector control during its terminal phase, maintaining excellent maneuverability even in the thin atmosphere, the institute said.
It is equipped with precision guidance and a directional warhead, along with an integrated composite rocket motor that improves manufacturability. Its active electronically scanned array radar supports target classification and identification, engagement of multiple tactical ballistic missile targets, electronic counter-countermeasures, and high-precision tracking.
Each mobile launcher contains four missile canisters.
The military plans to build at least 128 Strong Bow missiles. The system will be deployed alongside Sky Bow III and Patriot Advanced Capability-3 interceptors as part of the layered T-Dome air defense network.

WASHINGTON, August 23. /TASS/. An expected visit of US lawmakers to Russia would contribute to the fight against Russophobia spread by American mainstream media, independent candidate for US President Diane Sare told TASS.
"Dialogue is always better than silence. American lawmakers absolutely should visit Russia and speak with their Russian counterparts," she said in an interview with TASS.
"They should also visit Russian cities and get a sense of the thinking of the Russian people, which is hard to know from the United States given the Russophobia being peddled in most of the American mainstream news media," Sare continued.
According to her, "American lawmakers are also aware during the midterm election season that their constituents are very unhappy."
"Their constituents are suffering from high inflation in the costs of energy and food and would be appreciative if their federal representatives would do something to alleviate the pain. Collaborating with Russia on projects of mutual interest, such as the Bering Strait Tunnel or space exploration, could be very beneficial," the US presidential candidate noted.
"If our lawmakers would speak with their Russian counterparts, they would also learn that Russia could help the United States to extricate itself from the Iran war, which we are losing and which nobody wants," Sare added.
A delegation of the Russian parliament’s lower chamber, the State Duma, held working meetings in Washington on March 26-27. Luna has repeatedly stressed that she supports maintaining contacts and developing trade relations between Russia and the United States.

Congress MP Jairam Ramesh questions delay in formal closure of Monsoon Session
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Sunday questioned the “abnormal” delay in proroguing the Monsoon Session of Parliament, noting that the time gap between adjournment and prorogation is generally two to four days, but the Monsoon Session is yet to be prorogued after being adjourned on August 13.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh questioned whether the delay was because Union Home Minister Amit Shah was still looking for a two-thirds majority to get the delimitation-linked Constitutional amendment bill passed in a special session.The government, for its part, has denied any plans to convene a special session."The time gap between the adjournment of the Lok Sabha sine die and its prorogation is generally two to four days - although there are many instances when adjournment and prorogation have taken place on the very same day. Australia records 1st case of bird flu in mammal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:10:22 UTC
16:10:22 KST

Aamir Latif
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Australia on Sunday confirmed its first case of bird flu in a mammal after a long-nosed fur seal found in South Australia tested positive for the virus, local media reported.
Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins told reporters that the seal was found at Beachport, 300 kilometers south of the state capital Adelaide, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.
"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds," Collins said.
The infection was likely caused by exposure to infected wild birds or their shared environment, she said, adding that the detection did not appear to be associated with any other sick or dead marine mammals.
There have now been 298 positive H5 bird flu cases recorded in Australia since the outbreak, with 194 of those in South Australia.
"At this stage there is no evidence of infection in our poultry or agriculture systems," Collins said.
South Australia Environment Minister Emily Bourke said there were "devastating numbers" of detections in the state, with the fur seal case "something we always knew would be coming."
She said there is "no cure" or ability to stop bird flu, but the government is working very closely with the federal government on its national vaccination program.
She urged pet owners to keep their dogs on leads and cats indoors.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said in comments published on Saturday that Kyiv had opened “Pandora's box” with its strikes on Russian economic targets, saying that Russia would hit back at Ukraine's “most sensitive economic sectors.”
Ukraine has this summer escalated a campaign of drone strikes targeting Russian economic infrastructure, including oil refineries and online retailers' warehouses, seeking to destroy infrastructure it says is central to Russia's war effort.
Russia has responded with strikes against Ukrainian economic infrastructure, including Ukrainian grain exports via the Black Sea.
“The Kyiv regime set out to damage our economy. What did it do? It opened this Pandora’s box itself. Well then, expect a response targeting your most sensitive economic sectors,” Putin said in comments to a Russian state television journalist.

Russia and Ukraine had previously adhered to a Turkish-brokered deal to protect grain exports on the Black Sea. But Russia exited the deal in 2023.

Why Trump’s economic pain could spark more Iranian attacks on Gulf nations
The plan is likely to prompt Tehran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf in a bid to push up oil prices and force Trump to retreat
President Donald Trump is betting new sanctions, a naval blockade and ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can accomplish what thousands of bombs and missiles could not: force Tehran to accept a deal to end the war on US terms.
But like other US efforts to force Iran into capitulation, there is one main problem: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has claimed control of the vital Strait of Hormuz and sent volleys of attack drones across the Gulf, may be impervious to such pressure – and has plenty of ways to retaliate.
A major part of the US effort will come on Monday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised to unveil details of a plan designed to shift the conflict from tit-for-tat strikes across the Middle East to full-blown economic isolation – a campaign that could touch nations ranging from China and India to Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
Yet significant new economic pressure is likely to prompt Iran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf, including against energy infrastructure, in an attempt to push up oil prices and raise the cost of the US effort, forcing Trump to shift his approach once again.
“If this is actually effective, at some point, Iran will lash out again – they just will have no alternative,” said Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who worked on Iran issues at the State Department and White House National Security Council until last year. “Trump may see this as a different phase of the war, but I don’t think Iran does.”
Since the US and Israel first attacked Iran on February 28, Iran has repeatedly shown the ability to endure air strikes on thousands of targets, layers of sanctions and a US navy blockade – yet still retain the ability to hit back.

‘Pretty shambolic’: new EU border checks cause stress for UK travellers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

On top of fears about extreme heat and possible jet fuel shortages, Britons planning summer holidays in the EU this year had another thing to worry about – long queues and waiting times caused by the bloc’s new border checks.
The EU digital entry and exit system (EES), which requires non-EU citizens to register and be photographed and fingerprinted on arrival and departure from the Schengen zone, has been technically in full force since April after launching last autumn, but has been beset by teething problems.
Despite reports of passengers facing three-hour delays and missed connections, Brussels rejected calls by airports and airlines to suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period. However, border police have been allowed to relax requirements if queues become unmanageable under an opt-out that expires next month.
Those who shared with the Guardian their experiences of the system since its introduction highlighted a range of problems and snags.
‘We checked in to Europe, but the EES says we haven’t checked out’
One of the main purposes of the system is to track whether non-EU citizens have spent more than their permitted 90 days in the bloc in a rolling 180-day period.
However, Martin Farrall, a retired university professor, says his EES record failed to record his exit from the Schengen zone and he had to chase the authorities to update it.
In May, the 67-year-old and his wife arrived by ferry at Hoek van Holland at the start of their camping trip in Denmark, both with a full residency allowance.
Martin says the Dutch border police enrolled them into EES “But no entry stamp was made on our passports,” he adds.
“On 30 June, 55 days after entry, we returned to the UK on the Dunkerque-Dover ferry. The French border police asked us where and when we entered Schengen, and we were handed back our passports without an exit stamp.”
Once home, Martin checked his residency tally and found that instead of having 35 days left it was rapidly diminishing.
“It appeared that EES had not been updated to show I’d left the Schengen area,” says Martin, who lives in Warwickshire. He was concerned that he would be registered as an “overstayer” at risk of refusal of entry in future.
He reported the error to the Directorate General for Foreign Nationals in France on 13 July but says he has not received a response..
When Martin checked on his day allowance again on 7 August, the EES website said he had zero days left, but when he looked on 17 August it had updated.
“The EES website now claims I have 34 days left to travel in the 180 window! When I checked my wife’s passport she apparently has 90 days left despite us both having the same travel to Schengen history. So God only knows what’s going on.
“I wonder how many other people who were waved through because of the hold-ups may also be in the same position.”
‘The system obviously wasn’t ready – it’s pretty shambolic’
Nadia, from Greater Manchester, thinks the system is not “communicating with other member states”. She made two trips to Schengen areas this summer with very contrasting experiences.
A trip to Tenerife in June was “quite straightforward”, but her experience in July at Frankfurt airport where she was picking up a connecting flight home, was much less so.
“The queue there was ridiculously long, and there was very limited information,” she says. “People were wandering around trying to work out where they needed to go.
“I’m very well travelled and pretty confident, but even I was slightly unsure and was thinking, is there some other queue I should be joining? There was no one nearby to check with without losing your place.”
Eventually, her passport was checked. “He didn’t actually take fingerprints then,” says Nadia, who is a solicitor. “I think the queue was so long they decided to dispense with that.
“It’s the efficiency of the system I question and the fact that individual member states’ systems do not talk to one another. They shouldn’t need to get information again if you have already gone through.
“It’s pretty shambolic, and I think people missing their flights because of it is just not acceptable, especially when there’s no recourse; it’s not your fault.”
Nadia is also unhappy about having to give her fingerprints repeatedly. “I’ve done it in a few countries now, but it’s something I feel very strongly opposed to,” she says.
“This is not in keeping with the intention of the scheme, which suggests that once registered, you should not have to keep re-entering your biometric data. You also wonder where the information is going – who’s seeing it, who else has access to it?”
‘There should be clearer signage about exemptions’
Evie, originally from Manchester but studying in Munich, says her student visa has caused EES confusion.
“In Munich airport, there are TV screens which explain the function of EES as a system to register ‘visitors’. As I hold an extended-stay visa for the purpose of studying, I would not describe myself as a ‘visitor’ as I can stay in Germany for up to 12 months,” the 23-year-old says.
She says that upon seeing she had a British passport, she was often directed toward the EES queue and had to explain her visa situation, after which she “was normally allowed to stand in the queue with everyone else”.
Evie says this has happened “virtually every time” she has flown in and out of Germany – in December, January, February and April – and believes there should be better signposting to avoid mix-ups, especially given unreliable airport wifi makes accessing online information difficult.
‘You could see people getting anxious’
Kevin and his wife, Christine, travelled to Lanzarote in June but struggled to get the machine to register their details.
“The arrivals hall was packed, but there were loads of machines,” the 75-year-old says. “Some were not working. I noticed people getting angry when their fingerprints would not enter. People started holding their fingers in different positions, and when that didn’t work, they would hit the glass harder.”
He says there was “not much assistance to be found” and when all attempts failed, people queued up to “have it done manually at the kiosk”.
“You could see people getting anxious,” says Kevin, who lives with Christine, 73, in Merseyside. He says the machines eventually registered them both.
The couple’s next trip is to Palma for a cruise, and they are bracing themselves for there to be issues. “We’ll be visiting different countries on the cruise,” Kevin says. “What happens then?”
‘The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me’
Martin, 68, a retired IT worker, said he and his wife struggled to operate the screen to register at Schiphol airport in the Netherlands.
“The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me,” says Martin of their trip at the end of April. “My wife had similar issues with her 71-year-old hands. Older people with drier fingers have trouble with touch screens.”
Eventually, Martin, who lives in Stockport, was sent to manual entry “where they forgot to stamp my passport”.
“When exiting Dusseldorf, the Germans got a bit excited about that and asked how we got into Europe,” he adds. “I just said the Dutch didn’t stamp our passports, and they accepted that.
“The interface is poorly laid out and will confuse the less technical I have an IT background, and it feels like the system was not walked through enough times. It’s a mess. It also hasn’t been properly tested for older people.”
‘My wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look’
Ed Griffiths, 67, a retired IT specialist, says his wife has impaired vision and could not work the machine at Prague airport as they passed through last September as she was unable to read the instructions.
“The photo/fingerprint machine failed for both of us, and we spent one hour 15 minutes standing in a slow queue of confused people waiting for staff to retry it, but my wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look, so they skipped the photo and she was waved through,” says Ed, who lives in Buckinghamshire. The delay meant their prebooked taxi nearly left without them.
Then the couple were in Milan in March and Ed had to re-register despite already having done so in Prague.
“The machine ignored my previous registration, my fingerprint was asked for and failed, I waited an hour in a queue for manual assistance retry,” he says. His wife, also 67, however, did manage registration and was waved through.
More recently, in Vienna in May an officer supervised the booths for photos and fingerprints. Again, the system ignored his previous registration, but the couple got through in five minutes.
“Twice we have been registered already, and it made no discernible difference,” Ed says. “We have not found assistance at machines, but at booths there has been some help.”

====================================================================================================

London’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

Ten years ago, Alastair Harper was an advocate for young people’s health sitting in a stuffy meeting room in London planning an air pollution campaign. “My phone started buzzing,” he said. “I took the call, and then told the room I needed to leave immediately.
“I had to get to UCLH [one of London’s major hospitals]. My own child was headed there in a blue-lit ambulance because she was struggling to breathe London’s toxic air.”
Hundreds of thousands of parents across the UK capital had similar experiences in those years. Between about 6,000 and 8,000 people were dying prematurely each year in London in the late 2010s. In 2020, an inquest found that the death of Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah in 2013 had been a direct result of air pollution, the first time it had been listed as a cause of death in the UK.
This week, a study from Queen Mary University London (QMUL) showed a significant reversal. Children’s lungs had grown bigger and stronger since the most polluting vehicles have been restricted on the capital’s roads, scientists found. The ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) – introduced by London’s mayor Sadiq Khan in 2019 and expanded in 2021 and 2023 – charges £12.50 a day for more polluting vehicles that do not meet stringent standards. It has drastically cut levels of nitrogen dioxide, a harmful pollutant.
To Harper, who later worked for Khan as an environmental adviser, and now works independently, relief at his own child’s recovery has been supplemented by the satisfaction of knowing that far fewer parents will experience such dread. “To know now that same air is so much safer for the kids that breathe it because of the political choice of one man makes me feel proud of this city,” he said.
Nick Hopkinson, a professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London, said the QMUL study was not a surprise. “There is an absolute wealth of evidence that air pollution is a major cause of ill health and premature death across the planet,” he said. Air pollution kills 7 million people a year globally, according to the World Health Organization.
Poor air not only causes respiratory difficulties and the stunting of children’s lungs, but also heart disease and stroke. It is associated with some forms of cancer, dementia, autism and cognitive difficulties in children too. New studies are adding to our knowledge, but we have known for decades of the basic dangers of dirty air. So why is there so much opposition to curbs on air pollution, which are clearly sound public health measures?
This opposition, culture war even, is central for all cities hoping to follow Khan’s lead. The leading causes of air pollution vary around the world – coal use in power stations in China and India, agricultural burning in south-east Asia, waste burning in many of the poorest countries and dust and local industry in others – but road traffic is a constant.
The technology to cut all of these types of air pollution already exists, says a former social development minister of Ecuador and now executive director of the Breathe Cities initiative, whose supporters include the Clean Air Fund and C40, a global coalition of mayors and leaders of nearly 100 major cities. “We know that we have the means to make a difference, and we are sharing knowledge and success stories so they can be replicated with impactful policies,” she said.
In the case of coal, the alternatives are renewable energy. Halting the burning of forests and peatlands would also combat the climate crisis. The alternatives to polluting traffic are public transport, electric vehicles, the redesign of cities and encouragement of active transport – walking and cycling. Trees are also important everywhere.
Paris and Barcelona have shown what is possible within a few years when mayors embrace the joys of cycling, following the lead long ago taken in Denmark and the Netherlands. New York’s Zohran Mamdani, now wearing a cycle helmet, hopes to do the same. But elsewhere in car-dominated America, infamously poor public transport provision, an intractable SUV culture and a president in Donald Trump intent on rolling back environmental protections mean widespread change is unlikely.
Other cities are working to make a difference. Bogotá is about to embark on its second Zuma, a clean air zone that involves expanding cycle lanes and footpaths, paving roads to suppress dust and planting trees. The Colombian capital won last year’s global Earthshot prize for its first Zuma. The city’s environment secretary, Adriana Soto, said: “Residents helped shape the design, particularly how the works would maintain access to their homes and respond to local mobility needs.” Hundreds of cities around the world now have clean air zones of varying sizes.
Another is Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, which passed an air quality act in 2022 that requires harmful emissions to be halved by 2035 and has installed a network of 50 low-cost monitoring stations as a first step. Imports of vehicles more than eight years old are banned, and the city is consulting on establishing clean air zones. The lead for the C40 Breathe Cities project in Nairobi, Victor Indasi, said: “More remains to be done, but Nairobi is firmly on the right trajectory.”
Bulgaria’s capital, Sofia, is saddled with old-fashioned heating systems dependent on coal and wood burning. These are being phased out and replaced with cleaner heat pumps, subsidised for those on low incomes, as part of a city-wide introduction – the first in south-east Europe – of low-emissions zones for transport and heating. Recent results show a 22% reduction in the average concentration of PM10 particulate matter, and a halving of days that exceed air quality guidance levels. Poland is also cutting its reliance on solid fuels.
In Australia, Melbourne’s mayor was inspired by a speech Khan gave last year before Brazil’s Cop30 climate summit. The first step was discovering that state-level monitoring was telling the city little about the real quality of its air at a neighbourhood level. “It was surprising to us that this wasn’t being measured,” a spokesperson said. With the new monitoring data coming in, the mayor has yet to decide what actions will be taken, whether a clean air zone or other restrictions, or carrots in the form of scrappage schemes and improved public transport. “We are still at the beginning of this journey,” the spokesperson said.
London’s low emission zone might not have happened if Khan had not staked his reputation on it. When he launched the scheme in 2019, he faced fierce opposition from political opponents and large groups of voters, and even his own party. The plan was challenged in the courts, businesses complained of the supposedly crippling costs, and Khan received personal threats and shouts of “Nazi” at public appearances. One survey found 60% of Londoners who replied to a consultation were against it.
In 2023, the resurgent Labour party under its new leader Keir Starmer faced an important byelection in Uxbridge, on the outer edge of London. The Ulez was a key issue for voters and Labour lost by a small margin, leading Starmer’s advisers to blame the zone and demand row-backs in London and elsewhere. Andy Burnham, then the mayor of Greater Manchester, who took over from Starmer as prime minister this autumn, abandoned plans for a Ulez after Uxbridge.
In all of these cities there is a sense of caution, even hesitancy, and none are moving fast enough. In London, the successes of the Ulez are threatened by the ballooning number of wood-burning stoves, a fashion accessory rather than a necessity for most of their urban owners. These are now a bigger source of particle pollution than traffic. More than 110,000 children were admitted to hospital with breathing difficulties in London in 2024.
Monitoring is a vital first step, but what is done with the data is what counts. That will involve tough measures. “There is always a price. You have to change people’s behaviour, you have to change the transport, the heating, the energy generation,” said Hopkinson. “The way things are in cities is the way they have developed over long periods, and changing all that is difficult.”
The pollution is often invisible. As Vaca Jones put it: “Air is not a tangible public good that people can feel and see. That means it is not a priority on the political agenda.”
Vested interests also intervene. Though studies show that air pollution takes an economic as well as a physical toll, businesses often complain – with little evidence – that curbs on driving will hurt them.
There is also the fact that the people driving the cars and operating the polluting factories are often not the same people whose children are being admitted to hospital. “Those who are suffering are those who have done least to cause the pollution,” said Chris Griffiths, a professor of primary care at Oxford University.
When Khan embarked on London’s Ulez, hysterical misinformation quickly spread online, suggesting the mayor intended to shut down London for his own ends. His deputy, Mete Coban, recalls the shock. “The personal abuse Sadiq got on the back of it was incredible,” he said. “I think it’s this, the misinformation, that is the number one thing that puts off other countries from doing this.”
Hopkinson said: “There is a kind of madness about it. “Disinformation, which is lying to people, is confusing them. They are trying to persuade people that air pollution is not bad for them, and climate change is not real.
“They are spreading wild conspiracy theories [for instance that 15-minute cities, where all amenities can be accessed within a small area, are devices of government control] and the far right are exploiting this and generating grievance.”
With the latest study adding to a growing pool of evidence of the Ulez’s success, proponents of cleaner urban air hope to be able to cut through the madness with facts that speak loudly to parents and responsible people everywhere.
As Hopkinson put it: “The question for pro-pollution campaigners is ‘why do you hate children?’”

‘So much still needs to be done’: Italian town marks 10 years since devastating earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

As people gather in Amatrice on Monday for a mass to mark the 10th anniversary of the earthquake that struck the hilltop town and several neighbouring communities, killing 303 and leaving thousands homeless, politicians and other public figures will pay tribute.
But for many, their words will offer little comfort: 10 years on, much of Amatrice, whose historic centre was wiped out by the 6.0 magnitude quake, is still being rebuilt and more than half of its roughly 2,100 residents continue to live in temporary housing.
“They will make a good show of it, bow their heads and say: ‘We did a lot,’” said Sonia Santarelli, the president of Comitato Civico 3e36, a grassroots initiative established soon after the disaster. “But nobody will put their neck on the line. They will say the reconstruction is going well … but how can that be when so many are in homes that are uninhabitable?”
A report published last week by ActionAid Italy highlighted severe delays in rebuilding Amatrice and other areas damaged by the earthquake. According to the findings, as of April 2026, construction on roughly two-thirds of the planned public projects had yet to begin, rising to seven in 10 in the hardest-hit areas. Some €4.85bn (£4.15bn) has been earmarked for the works, the report said.
The earthquake struck in the early hours on 24 August 2016, its tremors felt as far as Rome. Santarelli, who owns an agriturismo, or farm stay, in the hamlet of Torrita close to Amatrice, recalled being woken by a loud blast and the sound of buildings collapsing. There was virtually nothing left of the hamlet, she said, but fortunately nobody there died.
Santarelli counts her blessings that she was not made homeless either. Comitato Civico 3e36, whose name references the precise time – 3.36am – the earthquake hit, was founded to defend the communities affected and to ensure citizens have a voice in the reconstruction process.
Prefabricated housing villages were set up in 41 sites across the affected areas. The wooden homes are cramped and especially stifling in the heat. “The heat and humidity squelch you,” said Santarelli.
Furthermore, they are undignified places in which to die, she claimed, owing to limited space restricting the easy movement of coffins. Residents have also complained that the rooms are too small for traditional wakes.
Some of those displaced are still paying mortgages on homes that don’t exist any more. “You cannot make people live in these conditions for so long,” said Santarelli. “So much work still needs to be done.”
Projects that have been completed in Amatrice include a school and a handful of buildings in the historic centre. Construction of a new hospital is nearing completion and could open in 2027, provided it is fully equipped and staffed.
There are many explanations for the sluggish reconstruction. Matteo Renzi, the prime minister at the time of the quake, had pledged to rebuild the towns as they were. Renzi resigned at the end of 2016 after a referendum defeat and since then Italy has had five different governments, each appointing commissioners for the rebuild.
As with previous major earthquakes, such as the one that hit L’Aquila in 2009, reconstruction has been mired by bureaucracy, legal disputes and the general complexity of rebuilding historic centres in mountainous areas.
Much of the pressure falls on the mayor. Elected in 2021, Giorgio Cortellesi said reconstruction efforts were hampered by the Covid pandemic and then by a government eco-renovation scheme, which was intended to revive the post-pandemic economy but instead pushed up the cost of building materials and lured construction workers away to more profitable jobs in other parts of Italy.
Cortellesi, an engineer who was determined to contribute to Amatrice’s revival after miraculously finding his two sons alive during a desperate search through the rubble in the dark, said the reconstruction has gathered pace over the past couple of years.
However, there is “a significant housing emergency”, he acknowledged, exacerbated by construction firms renting out homes for their staff, in turn driving up rents for people who live there. He said the council is working to reclaim some of those properties.
As for the prefabricated villages, which are nearing the end of their 10-year warranty, they will need to be dismantled and their residents moved into their rebuilt homes. “They will return to their homes, which will be the safest in Italy and the most energy efficient,” Cortellesi said, but without offering a timeline for completion.
Amatrice’s population has declined over the past decade, with many choosing to move elsewhere for better prospects. But there is also a resilience among those who have stayed.
Sergio Pirozzi, who was mayor at the time of the calamity, is one of them. Within minutes of the earthquake striking, he captured the devastation in a few stark words: “Half of the town is gone.”
A football coach, Pirozzi had been at a dinner marking the 50th anniversary of the local team a few hours before. “Of those who I was with that night, 36 died and there were others who lost their wives and children. It is not something I will ever overcome,” he said.
And yet, despite also having to live with the delays and frustrations of rebuilding, Pirozzi’s attachment to Amatrice is undiminished: “For me, even today, this is the most beautiful place in the world.”

First Bus bans under-16s in Stoke-on-Trent travelling alone after 6pm after disorder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

For some, it is a quotidian nuisance that inevitably occurs when you are in the vicinity of teenagers. For others, it is an expression of modern-day lawlessness among young people.
Whatever view you take, antisocial behaviour on public transport has become a hot debate – and with the introduction of free bus travel for kids aged 5 to 15 across England during August, matters have come to a head in Staffordshire.
On Friday, the bus company First Bus banned all passengers aged 15 and under travelling without an adult after 6pm in Stoke-on-Trent until further notice.
The company said multiple incidents of antisocial behaviour had occurred since the government’s “cost of living-busting” flagship free travel scheme was introduced on 1 August, including one involving more than 100 young people acting in an “intimidating and aggressive way” at Hanley bus station in the city centre.
“Police had to be called,” local First Bus regional director Simon Mathieson told a journalist on BBC Radio Stoke. “Lots of my drivers, who want to do a good job, [were] feeling very unsafe; lots of passengers, trying to get home, [were] feeling very unsafe.”
He revealed the company had seen a large uptake of the free travel offer by children in the area, describing it as a brilliant scheme to get people using buses. But he added that one driver had since reported children had been swinging on strap handles on the handrails of his bus and running up and down the vehicle while it was in motion.
“That’s not really helping people feel like they can travel in safety and comfort,” Mathieson said. “Unfortunately – and very regretfully – because of the antisocial behaviour … We’ve made the decision to protect staff and other customers on the buses.”
Last year, the Liberal Democrats called for tougher action to be taken to tackle “headphone dodgers” who play loud music on buses and trains, including fines of up to £1,000.
The Scottish government is planning to bring in legislation that will allow it to force people who benefit from its free bus travel scheme – including young people aged 5 to 21 – to abide by a forthcoming code of conduct, or have their right to concessionary travel withdrawn or suspended.
But others say policies to prevent antisocial behaviour in public places are already disproportionate and can result in hefty fines.
For example, one passenger at Waterloo station who put a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a “completely full” bin was recently fined £500 by a Lambeth council enforcement officer who had been standing at a distance, watching the bin.
An 86-year-old pensioner was fined £250 in Skegness, Lincolnshire, last year for spitting out a leaf after it blew into his mouth.
Cllr Finlay Gordon-McCusker, the cabinet minister for transport at Stoke-on-Trent council, said it was disappointing that First Bus had decided to ban all unaccompanied under-16s in the evenings. “Sadly, the children paying the price are overwhelmingly the ones who did nothing wrong.”
He said that during his discussions with the company, he had questioned why more transport safety officers could not have been deployed to monitor the routes that were affected instead. “It’s a real shame that First Bus felt that this was their only option … It’s certainly not the option I would have liked to see put in place.”
He and his fellow councillors had welcomed the government’s free bus travel scheme in August, he said. “But clearly it’s presented an opportunity for some kids to travel across the city and cause trouble, which is what they’ve done in this situation.”
That doesn’t mean there is anything wrong with the policy, he added. “Teenagers with nothing to do in August isn’t a new phenomenon. The scheme didn’t create the behaviour. It changed its geography.”
He added: “What the free travel did, possibly, was move it [the antisocial behaviour] from the estates where it’s dispersed and largely unreported to the bus station where it’s concentrated, it’s visible and it lands in an incident log.”
He disagrees that banning unaccompanied children from buses in evenings is the right way to tackle antisocial behaviour in Stoke-on-Trent. A better solution might have been greater police presence at the bus station, he said, so that young people could have continued to benefit from the freedom of having unlimited free bus travel during the summer holidays.
“It’s certainly not fair,” he said. “I think it’s a crying shame that that freedom [to travel] has been taken away because of the unacceptable behaviour of a very small minority of young people.”
First Bus declined to be interviewed by the Guardian but said in a statement the decision had been approved by the Department for Transport (DfT) and has the full support of the council.
Drivers will continue to be able to exercise their discretion to provide free travel for unaccompanied children and young people if they are vulnerable or to ensure their safety.
A government spokesperson said: “Our Great British Summer Savings scheme allows kids under 15 to travel for free on participating services, to give families room to breathe and enjoy days out throughout August.
 
 “The scheme rightly offers all local operators flexibilities to deal with issues like anti-social behaviour, such as the right to refuse travel or localised time restrictions.”
