UK orders reviews of franchising sector after Vodafone allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Ministers have commissioned a pair of in-depth reports into how franchising businesses are policed in the UK, as the government considers introducing new laws after high-profile allegations about conduct in the sector.
The action follows a Guardian investigation last December, which revealed claims that Adrian Howe, a former Vodafone employee who had agreed to start a franchise in 2018, had taken his own life after pressure from the FTSE 100 telecoms group.
The Department for Business and Trade is understood to be working with the British Franchise Association on a study of the domestic market, while it has also engaged the Centre for Economic Policy Research to analyse different models in operation internationally.
Both studies will feed into the government’s assessment of the legal framework required to “ensure franchisees are properly protected, while avoiding unnecessary burdens on small businesses”.
The developments come as the department said that Lord Leong, who was named in July as minister for small business and enterprise, has been handed franchising as part of his portfolio.
His appointment follows a pledge in January by Keir Starmer to review laws governing franchising agreements, as part of the official response to the Howe case. The former Vodafone store manager was found drowned days before his new franchise was due to open its doors when his relatives said he had become convinced his deal with the multinational company would prove financially disastrous.
December’s Guardian investigation also spoke to two former Vodafone franchisees who recounted that commission cuts by the company in 2020 had caused their franchising companies to run up huge debts, which they each said contributed to them making attempts on their own lives.
They were among a group of 62 former Vodafone franchisees who brought a high court claim in 2024, alleging the company “unjustly enriched” itself and which MPs have compared to the Post Office Horizon IT scandal.
In July, Vodafone settled the 19-month-old court claim via a confidential agreement “without any admission of liability”. Howe was not included in that claim, which was launched after his death, but his family has since said they will continue to press the government to introduce an “Adrian’s law” to incorporate new regulations to govern the franchising sector.
Campaigners have argued that franchisees are uniquely exposed under the current UK system as the law treats their small companies as equals to huge corporations – even though there are often large imbalances in power formalised within the franchise agreements that govern the relationship between both parties.
During an adjournment debate on franchising in July 2025, the former Conservative minister John Hayes told MPs: “Franchising can be used as a method to exaggerate the power of the business at the heart of the franchise and to weaken the position of franchisees. My assertion is that is common and is particular in the case of Vodafone.”
A Vodafone UK spokesperson said: “While we are sorry if any partners have had a difficult experience, we reject any suggestion that our franchisees were put under undue pressure.
“We continue to run a successful franchise operation of over 350 stores, and many of our existing franchisees have expanded their business with us by taking on additional stores. We encourage everyone to raise issues, and we will always seek to resolve them.”
The company said last year it “wholly rejects” any suggestion that it had “knowingly or recklessly or negligently” put anybody involved with its franchise stores under unreasonable pressure.
Mental health experts emphasise that suicide is usually complex and can often involve many triggers.
The company has added that comparisons to the Post Office scandal are “wholly inappropriate”.

The South Asian cricketers bringing their sport to Lithuania one park meadow at a time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

On weekend mornings in Vingis Park, Vilnius' largest green space, walkers and joggers sometimes stop to watch something they've never seen before: cricket.
It takes a group of men about an hour just to set the pitch up – stretching a mat across the grass and pinning it down – and even then, the uneven ground sends the ball bouncing at odd angles. But for the South Asians who gather here a few times a month, it's worth it.
Cricket is one of the world's most widely followed sports, with a particular grip on the Indian subcontinent. The 2025 Champions Trophy final between India and New Zealand drew around 230 million viewers in India alone.
In countries like India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, it is less a game than a piece of national identity – something most people grow up playing before they can properly explain the rules.
Lithuania, a country of fewer than three million people in northeastern Europe, is not among them. But a small and growing community of South Asian expats is trying to change that.
Finding something familiar
Taufeeq Shaik moved from India to Lithuania four years ago for work. Shortly after arriving in Vilnius, he found a Facebook group of people playing cricket in the city and went along.
"I realised people were playing seriously. That increased my interest – not just to play cricket, but to grow the community, to bring this game to Lithuania," he said.
Playing in an open public space means fielding a lot of curious questions. Passers-by stop to ask what's going on, and the players have learned to explain the basics – and sometimes to hand someone a bat and let them try. A few have come back.
The rules, admittedly, take some explaining. Cricket evolved in England over four centuries and spread worldwide during the British Empire; today it is sometimes described as a cross between baseball and chess, owing to the tactical complexity that sits beneath its unhurried surface.
The basic idea is simple enough: one team bats, scoring runs by hitting the ball and running between two sets of stumps; the other bowls and fields, trying to get the batters out. Matches range from three-hour Twenty20 games to traditional five-day Test matches.
A community of 60
Lithuania currently has four cricket clubs: Vilnius Cricket Club, Aquila Cricket Club, Kaunas Cricket Club, and Falcon Cricket Club, with around 60 active players – most of them South Asian expats working or studying in Lithuania.
Matches between the Vilnius and Kaunas clubs, players say, carry a competitive edge not unlike the fierce basketball rivalry between Vilnius' Rytas and Kaunas' Žalgiris clubs – though the tension evaporates the moment the game ends.
"I'm from one region of India, my teammates are from other regions. When we come together to play, we become like a family. Most of the people I play cricket with here are close friends," said Shaik.
The pitch problem
The community's biggest obstacle is practical: there are no proper cricket pitches in Lithuania.
Professional cricket requires a specially prepared surface, and the makeshift mat laid out in Vingis Park is a poor substitute – audibly so, as the ball skids unpredictably off the uneven ground beneath it.
As a result, official competitive matches are usually played across the border in Latvia or Estonia, which both have proper facilities.
"The first challenge is the playing surface," Shaik said. "If we want the player base to grow, if we want to host matches against clubs from other countries, this pitch isn't suitable for that."
The community has been in contact with the Lithuanian sports ministry, trying to make the case for investment in proper facilities – though cricket remains far enough from the mainstream that progress is slow. "We're happy with what we have for now. But we know it's not enough."
ICC-certified coaches and school visits
There are grounds for optimism, though. Several Lithuanian schools have begun showing interest in introducing cricket to pupils, and the community has a handful of coaches certified by the International Cricket Council – the sport's global governing body – who are able to visit classrooms and sports lessons.
One of them is Vinayagasundaram Subramani, who goes by Vinay, and who has lived in Lithuania for eight years, learning Lithuanian while working in a supermarket.
"Cricket has given me so much here. I got my ICC certificate, I can travel to schools to teach children. It's given me friendships I wouldn't otherwise have," he said.
When he and his teammates tell curious Lithuanians that they compete in matches representing Lithuania, he says, the reaction is invariably warm. "I've never seen anyone come and shout at us that we're taking their space. That simply doesn't happen here. Lithuanians are very welcoming, very kind. We feel like we belong."
What he misses most, playing cricket in a park far from home, is simple: "The only thing missing is friends and family cheering for you from the boundary. That's the only thing. But here we have teammates who support each other. Sometimes we even livestream matches when we travel to play in other European countries."

Australia confirms H5N1 bird flu case in local mammal
August 23, 2026
Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal on Sunday, after it found the deadly virus in a long-nosed fur seal.
Authorities in the state of South Australia said they found the virus in the seal in the coastal town of Beachport, about 310 kilometers (192 miles) from the state capital, Adelaide.
Austrialia has been combating the highly pathogenic influenza after it arrived in the country in June. Earlier this month it reported its first mass seabird deaths, marking an escalation.
What did authorities have to say?
There are an estimated 100,000 long-nosed fur seals in the state's waters. The infected individual was found dead with no signs of injury, authorities said.
Its death "does not appear to be associated with other sick or dead marine mammals," Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said in televised remarks.
"Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in the natural environment it is not possible to avoid significant losses," Collins added.
"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds," Collins was quoted by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation as saying.
The virus has not spread to Australia's poultry or agriculture, according to the government, which counted 297 confirmed cases as of Friday.
Earlier in August, the government said it would begin a bird vaccination program based on the species' vulnerability to the virus and conservation impact.

Kazakhstan votes in parliamentary election expected to strengthen president’s grip on power
TALLINN, Estonia (AP) — Polls opened Sunday in Kazakhstan’s parliamentary elections, a vote expected to further to strengthen President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s power in Central Asia’s largest nation.
The ruling pro-presidential Adilet party is widely predicted to win an overwhelming majority, with several smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also anticipated to enter parliament.
Tokayev, 73 — a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who previously worked at the United Nations — has been in office since 2019.
It is the country’s first elections to a new, single-chamber parliament called the Kurultai.
Sunday’s vote is the culmination of a constitutional overhaul Tokayev initiated in March, when 87% of voters supported a referendum to merge the two chambers of parliament into one and grant the president authority to appoint key officials, subject to parliamentary approval, including reestablishing the vice presidency.
Tokayev, who has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over the war in Ukraine, has justified the changes by citing the need for rapid decision-making in a fast-changing world.
Last month, Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Court ruled that the amendments effectively reset the clock on Tokayev’s previous terms in office, opening the door for him to run for another seven-year term.
The election comes at a difficult economic moment for Kazakhstan: inflation hit 10.2% in February, and tax hikes have fueled public discontent.
Analysts say the economic strain has made authorities wary of a repeat of the unrest of January 2022, when fuel price protests spiraled into violence that left dozens of protesters and police officers dead — a scenario Tokayev is seeking to guard against by concentrating power in his own hands.
Tokayev said the vote promises to be a “truly historic event.”
“Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country’s history,” Tokayev said Friday. “Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state.”
The vote is also taking place against a backdrop of intensifying crackdowns on press freedom. Media organizations have urged Tokayev to drop criminal charges against several journalists currently under house arrest and to revise the country’s legislation to ensure press freedom. Authorities have opened roughly 10 criminal cases against independent journalists and popular bloggers.
The most recent case involves Lukpan Akhmedyarov, an independent journalist who hosts the YouTube project “Prosto Zhurnalistika”, or Simply Journalism. He told The Associated Press that a criminal case was opened against him in August on charges of “disseminating false information” after he published a list of Kazakhstani citizens fighting in Ukraine. He faces up to seven years in prison.
“In the run-up to these parliamentary elections, repression has intensified sharply, with attacks on independent media, cyberattacks, and criminal cases launched against independent journalists and popular bloggers,” Akhmedyarov told the AP from Almaty. “It feels like the authorities want to silence all media outlets they don’t control — everyone they couldn’t reach an agreement with or couldn’t buy off.”
Akhmedyarov said the streets of Kazakhstan’s major cities are “flooded with advertisements and posters for the pro-presidential Adilet party.”
“It is not very difficult to predict the outcome of these elections,” he said.

Ukrainian drone hits Ozon logistics complex in Orenburg, causing fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:49:57 UTC
15:49:57 KST

Elena Teslova
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
A Ukrainian drone attack on the Russian city of Orenburg damaged a logistics complex operated by online retailer Ozon early Sunday, causing a fire but no casualties, local authorities said.
Several drones were shot down over the city's special economic zone, where industrial enterprises are located, Orenburg Mayor Albert Yumadilov said on the Russian social media platform Max.
Debris from the downed drones fell on the territory of Ozon's logistics complex, causing a fire that was quickly extinguished by emergency crews, he said.
More than 300 employees were evacuated from the facility following the incident. No injuries were reported, and operations at the warehouse were temporarily suspended.
Ozon said it was temporarily not accepting deliveries to the Orenburg warehouse.
Goods stored at the facility would be removed from the marketplace's listings while the warehouse's operations remain suspended, the company said.
The Orenburg airport had earlier imposed temporary restrictions on aircraft takeoffs and landings amid the drone attack.
The incident marked the second Ozon warehouse to be affected by a drone attack in two days. A company facility in Russia's Samara region caught fire following a drone attack on Saturday.
Meanwhile, firefighters continued battling a large warehouse fire in St. Petersburg's Pushkinsky District at 135 Kolpinskoye Highway.
The blaze, which broke out overnight, had spread to 82,000 square meters and was assigned a Level 4 fire severity rating, according to the St. Petersburg branch of Russia's Emergencies Ministry.
A total of 217 firefighters and 65 pieces of equipment were deployed to fight the blaze, including 132 personnel and 42 fire engines from the federal Emergencies Ministry.
No casualties have been reported, according to preliminary information.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defense systems shot down 328 Ukrainian drones overnight.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,476,580 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:46:18 UTC
15:46:18 KST

Russia has lost around 1,476,580 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 22.
The figure includes 1,310 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,292 tanks, 25,202 armored combat vehicles, 138,219 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,451 artillery systems, 2,054 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,584 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 474,641 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,352 unmanned ground systems, 5,052 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, and 4,569 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces shelled 23 settlements in the Sumy region nearly 70 times. Two people were killed, and six sustained injuries and trauma.
Two civilians were killed in Sumy region, while six more people sustained injuries and trauma as a result of enemy attacks. This was reported by UNN, citing the morning report on the security situation in the region.
Details
Russian troops shelled the region nearly 70 times, with 23 settlements coming under fire.
In the Seredyna-Buda community, a 61-year-old man was killed after riding his bicycle over an explosive object. In the same community, a 50-year-old woman was killed in an explosion involving another unidentified object, while a 71-year-old woman was injured.
In addition, a 52-year-old woman and a 24-year-old man were injured as a result of mortar shelling in this community.
In the Krasnopillia community, a Russian drone struck a car. A 51-year-old man was injured.
In the Esman community, a 60-year-old man sustained injuries and trauma after an enemy UAV struck a residential building.
There was another casualty in the Shostka community: a 73-year-old man was injured as a result of an airstrike.
Overall, from the morning of August 22 to the morning of August 23, 2026, Russian troops carried out nearly 70 attacks on 23 settlements in 15 territorial communities of Sumy region. The greatest number of attacks was recorded in Sumy, Shostka and Konotop districts.
The Khotin, Mykolaivka rural, Yunakivka, Krasnopillia, Bereza, Hlukhiv, Esman, Znob-Novhorodske, Shostka, Putyvl, Buryn, Bochechkiv, Krolevets and Velyka Pysarivka communities came under enemy attack.
Russian troops used mortars, artillery, FPV drones, unmanned aerial vehicles and guided aerial bombs for the attacks.
Numerous instances of destruction and damage to civilian infrastructure were recorded as a result of the shelling. In the Bereza community, private residential buildings and civilian infrastructure facilities were damaged; in the Znob-Novhorodske community, a private house was damaged.
In the Romny community, non-residential premises and a bus were damaged. In the Shostka community, apartment buildings, a civilian infrastructure facility, an outbuilding, non-residential premises, a car and a bus were damaged.
A private house in the Mykolaivka rural community, a car in the Krasnopillia community and a civilian infrastructure facility in the Krolevets community were also damaged. In the Seredyna-Buda community, private residential buildings were damaged and destroyed.

There were 254 combat engagements at the front, Russia carried out 98 airstrikes and launched 11,859 drones. The Armed Forces of Ukraine eliminated 1,310 occupiers.

Voting Begins In Kazakh Elections Marred By Exclusion Of Opposition, Attacks On Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:44:01 UTC
15:44:01 KST

Voting has begun in elections for Kazakhstan's new, unicameral parliament -- but opposition groups have been excluded from the vote in a tightly-controlled process that follows changes to the country's constitution.
Seven state-vetted parties are contesting the election while opposition groups were denied the status of political parties under legislation used to exclude them.
The political field is also restricted outside the ballot.
Under the election-monitoring rules, domestic nongovernmental groups receiving direct or indirect foreign funding cannot observe inside polling stations.
This has left independent Kazakh watchdogs outside the official monitoring process.
The authorities say 777 foreign observers are accredited, many representing regional organizations including the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), whose interim report noted the absence of genuine opposition parties and independent candidates and concerns over restrictions on political expression, is also observing the vote.
More than 70 parliamentarians and staff from around 30 countries are deploying as part of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly observation mission, its 13th election observation mission in Kazakhstan since 1994.
The OSCE has criticized all of the elections held in this period, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor as head of state, Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev.
The vote is also taking place amid pressure on independent media.
According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism.
The CEC is expected to release preliminary results on August 24, with final results due within seven days. Separately, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) will present its preliminary findings on August 24.
The vote follows constitutional changes approved in a March referendum that replaced the previous bicameral parliament with a single chamber, the Kurultai.
The Adilet party, which absorbed the former ruling party’s political structures as a new vehicle for the post-Nazarbaev era, is expected to dominate the first Kurultai.
A nationwide poll by the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development put the party at 70.2 percent support, positioning it to further cement Toqaev's grip on power.

The enemy launched two missile strikes using six missiles and 98 airstrikes, dropping 329 guided glide bombs. In addition, Russian forces used 11,859 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,318 attacks on settlements and Ukrainian troop positions.
Artillery fire hit Korenok, Ulanove, Bachivsk, Volfyne, Yastrubshchyna, and Luzhky in Sumy region. An airstrike targeted the area around Potapivka.
The Defense Forces’ aviation, missile forces, and artillery struck three areas where Russian personnel were concentrated, four UAV control posts, and one Russian command-and-observation post.
On the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk axes, Ukrainian forces repelled 13 Russian assaults. At the same time, Russian troops conducted one airstrike using three guided aerial bombs and carried out 67 attacks on Ukrainian positions and settlements, including five using multiple-launch rocket systems.
On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Ukrainian units repelled 21 Russian attacks. The invaders attempted to advance near Izbytske and toward Okhrimivka and Volokhivka.
On the Kupiansk axis, the enemy attacked twice toward Zahryzove.
Attempts to penetrate Ukrainian defenses were repelled on the Lyman axis, where Russian forces launched nine attacks near Lyman and toward Stepove, Shyikivka, Kopanky, Novoselivka, and Drobysheve.
On the Sloviansk axis, Russian forces carried out seven assault actions near Kryva Luka, Zakitne, and Ozerne, as well as toward Mykolaivka and Rai-Oleksandrivka.
On the Kramatorsk axis, Russian forces attacked three times toward Minkivka, Yurkivka, and Tykhonivka.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, 25 Russian attacks were recorded. The invaders conducted assault operations near Kostiantynivka, Illinivka, and Mykolaipillia, as well as toward Novoselivka and Stepanivka.
On the Pokrovsk axis, Ukrainian forces repelled 24 Russian attacks. The enemy was active near Bilytske, Serhiivka, Molodetske, and Kotlyne, and also launched assaults toward Novopavlivka, Shakhove, Kucheriv Yar, Novyi Donbas, Shevchenko, Myrne, and Udachne.

Magnitude 5.9 earthquake jolts eastern Japan, injuring over 20 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:41:50 UTC
15:41:50 KST

Aamir Latif
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
A magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck eastern Japan early Sunday, injuring more than 20 people and disrupting transportation, local media reported, citing the country’s weather agency and local authorities.
No tsunami alert was issued after the quake, which originated in the southern part of Ibaraki prefecture at a depth of 68 kilometers (42 miles), Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported, quoting the Japan Meteorological Agency.
The tremor registered lower 5 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale of 7 in parts of the prefecture as well as in central Tokyo.
More than 20 people were injured, including a young man and a woman in her 70s in Saitama, north of Tokyo, as well as nine people in Kanagawa and four in Chiba prefectures.
Several train services were delayed following the quake, while some trains ran at reduced speeds.
Some express services operated by Tobu Railway remained halted.
An intensity of lower 5 was also recorded in parts of Saitama and Chiba prefectures and central Tokyo.
No abnormalities were detected at the Tokai No. 2 nuclear power plant in Ibaraki prefecture or the disaster-stricken Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant and the nearby Fukushima Daini plant in northeastern Japan.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi instructed officials to ascertain the extent of the damage from the quake and provide timely information to the public.
The weather agency urged the public to remain alert for an earthquake registering lower 5 on the seismic intensity scale over the next week, especially during the next two to three days.
The latest quake was felt across a wide swath of the country, including northeastern and central Japan.

Interview: China's global initiatives offer new opportunities for cooperation, says Italian business leader
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:37:38 CST
15:37:38 KST

ROME, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The China-proposed four global initiatives offer a new perspective on international governance and new opportunities for international cooperation amid geopolitical fragmentation and global instability, said an Italian business leader.
The initiatives represent China's efforts to provide coordinated responses to challenges that transcend national borders, Mario Boselli, chairman of the Italy China Council Foundation, said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
They also represent a deepening of China's international vision following more than a decade of the Belt and Road Initiative, extending the focus from economic and infrastructure cooperation to development, security, dialogue among civilizations and global governance, he said.
He believes that the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI) could offer opportunities to deepen cooperation between China and Europe, including Italy.
The GDI's focus on climate change, the UN Sustainable Development Goals, digitalization and technological innovation could create opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy, photovoltaics and energy storage, among others, said Boselli.
Italy and China can also strengthen cooperation among universities and research institutions in biotechnology, healthcare, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, he added.
Noting that the GCI could promote cooperation in culture, heritage conservation, universities and youth exchanges, he said Italy, with its rich cultural heritage and the strong appeal of "Made in Italy" in China, is "one of the most natural European partners" for such initiatives.
Taken together, the four initiatives outline a vision of a multipolar world with greater participation by emerging economies and countries of the Global South, Boselli said.
With its tradition of dialogue with China and complementary economic strengths, Italy can play a bridging role between China and Europe, promoting practical cooperation in sustainable development, innovation, culture and global governance, he said.
China's initiatives may not provide an immediate solution to current international tensions, but can offer "a space for reflection and dialogue" to identify more inclusive, practical and long-term forms of cooperation, he added. ■

37 injured after 5.9-magnitude earthquake hits eastern Japan's Ibaraki
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:37:23 CST
15:37:23 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- At least 37 people were injured after a 5.9-magnitude earthquake struck Ibaraki Prefecture, northeast of Tokyo, early Sunday. The earthquake also caused burst water pipes and disruptions to transportation in some areas, local media reported.
Japan's Fuji News Network, citing the Fire and Disaster Management Agency, reported that as of 10 a.m. local time, at least 37 people were injured in Tokyo, Ibaraki Prefecture, Kanagawa Prefecture and other areas.
The earthquake temporarily disrupted some train services in the Kanto region, although operations are gradually being restored. Multiple water pipes burst in Tokyo and other areas, causing temporary flooding on some roads.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, the temblor occurred at around 2 a.m. local time on Sunday at a depth of about 70 km, measuring lower 5 on Japan's seismic intensity scale of 7 in parts of Ibaraki, Saitama and Chiba prefectures as well as Tokyo's Adachi Ward.
A lower 5 quake is defined by the agency as shaking that causes most people to be frightened and to hold on to something stable, while objects may fall from shelves.
The quake was clearly felt in Tokyo, with some people living in the city posting on social media that it was the strongest shaking they had experienced in recent years. The tremor was also felt across a wide swath of the country, including northeastern and central Japan.
The weather agency urged the public to remain alert for an earthquake registering lower 5 over the next week, especially during the next two to three days.
No abnormalities were detected at the Tokai No. 2 nuclear power plant in Ibaraki Prefecture or the disaster-stricken Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant and the nearby Fukushima Daini plant in northeastern Japan, according to their operators. ■

Day of the State Flag of Ukraine: the history of the blue-and-yellow banner
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:36:04 EEST
15:36:04 KST

Day of the State Flag of Ukraine: the history of the blue-and-yellow banner
Kyiv • UNN
The blue-and-yellow flag has come a long way from medieval heraldry to becoming Ukraine’s national symbol. Its official proportions are 2:3.
Every year on August 23, Ukraine celebrates State Flag Day. The blue-and-yellow flag is one of Ukraine’s three main state symbols, along with the State Coat of Arms and the State Anthem. Today, it is associated throughout the world with Ukrainian statehood, the struggle for independence, resistance to Russian aggression, and international support for Ukraine.
At the same time, the history of the blue and yellow colors in Ukrainian lands began long before the proclamation of independence in 1991. They were used in heraldry as early as the Middle Ages; in the 19th century, they became symbols of the Ukrainian national movement, and during the Ukrainian Revolution of 1917–1921, they were ultimately established as the colors of Ukrainian statehood.
How this happened, what one needs to know about the Ukrainian flag, and what may surprise people about it is explained by UNN.
History of the State Flag of Ukraine
The blue and yellow colors have deep roots in Ukrainian heraldry. The most famous example is the coat of arms of the Principality of Galicia–Volhynia and the later Ruthenian land, which depicted a golden lion on a blue background. A similar color scheme was also used in the symbolism of cities and lands that are part of modern Ukraine. In particular, the blue and gold colors can be traced in the heraldic emblems of Lviv and Galicia.
However, medieval banners cannot be directly equated with the modern Ukrainian state flag. At that time, flags were predominantly associated with specific princes, cities, lands, or military units. The blue and yellow colors became national much later—in the 19th century, when national movements were actively forming in Europe.
Origins of the Ukrainian Flag
An important stage in the history of the Ukrainian flag was the 1848 revolution in the Austrian Empire, known as the "Spring of Nations." At that time, the Main Ruthenian Council was established in Lviv—the first Ukrainian political organization in Galicia. It was this council that began using the blue and yellow colors as national symbols.
In June 1848, the blue-and-yellow flag appeared above Lviv City Hall. Historians often call this period one of the key moments in the formation of modern Ukrainian national symbols.
In the second half of the 19th century, blue-and-yellow flags were increasingly used by Ukrainian cultural, sports, educational, and civic organizations in Galicia and Bukovyna. They appeared during folk festivals, anniversaries of Ukrainian figures, student events, sporting competitions, and other mass gatherings. Gradually, blue and yellow ceased to be merely regional heraldic colors and began to be perceived as symbols of the entire Ukrainian national movement.
The Flag of Ukraine Before 1917
In the Ukrainian lands that were part of the Russian Empire, the development of national symbols was more complicated. For a long time, the Ukrainian cultural and political movement was subject to restrictions, so blue-and-yellow flags could not be used there as openly as in Galicia.
The situation began to change at the beginning of the 20th century. After the Revolution of 1905, Ukrainian organizations had more opportunities to operate. Blue-and-yellow colors were used during Shevchenko celebrations, demonstrations, student gatherings, and other public events. By the beginning of the First World War, the blue-and-yellow combination was already a well-known symbol of the Ukrainian national movement on both sides of the border between the Russian and Austro-Hungarian Empires.
At the same time, there was no single state standard for the flag at that point. Different arrangements of the colors could be seen, as well as flags bearing coats of arms or other symbols.
The Flag of Ukraine in 1917–1918
After the February Revolution of 1917 and the fall of the Russian autocracy, the Ukrainian national movement intensified sharply. In March 1917, the Ukrainian Central Rada was established in Kyiv. Blue-and-yellow banners were increasingly used at mass Ukrainian demonstrations, military congresses, and rallies.
After the proclamation of the Ukrainian People's Republic, these colors effectively became state colors. In 1918, blue-and-yellow symbols were used by Ukrainian military units, diplomatic missions, and state institutions.
Blue and yellow remained the state colors after Hetman Pavlo Skoropadskyi came to power and the Ukrainian State was established. Later, the Directory of the Ukrainian People's Republic continued to use them.
A version can still be heard in society claiming that the UNR's flag was originally yellow-and-blue and that the order of the colors was later deliberately changed. However, historians point out that various versions of the flags were used during the Ukrainian Revolution, and there is no documentary evidence confirming the legend of an official "turning over" of the flag.
Over time, the version with the blue stripe on top and the yellow one below became generally accepted.
What happened to the flag under Soviet rule
After the defeat of the Ukrainian state formations of the early 20th century, most of Ukraine's territory became part of the USSR. Blue-and-yellow symbols were banned there. Their use was interpreted by the Soviet authorities as a manifestation of Ukrainian nationalism and anti-Soviet activity.
The official flag of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic was a red banner. Its design changed repeatedly. In 1949, the Ukrainian SSR flag received two horizontal stripes - red and light blue - with a sickle, hammer, and star. Meanwhile, the blue-and-yellow flag continued to be used by representatives of the Ukrainian political émigré community and participants in the liberation and dissident movements.
The Flag of Ukraine in 1991
The revival of Ukrainian national symbols began in the late 1980s, when political censorship weakened in the USSR and mass democratic and national movements emerged. Blue-and-yellow flags increasingly appeared at rallies and demonstrations.
On July 24, 1990, the blue-and-yellow flag was ceremonially raised near the building of the Kyiv City Council. For a long time afterward, this date was unofficially regarded in the capital as Ukrainian Flag Day.
On August 24, 1991, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine. That same day, the blue-and-yellow flag was brought into the parliament's session hall.
On September 4, 1991, the national flag was raised over the building of the Verkhovna Rada. Its status as a state symbol was finally закреплено after the All-Ukrainian referendum in support of independence.
On January 28, 1992, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the resolution "On the State Flag of Ukraine." It approved a rectangular flag consisting of two equal-width horizontal stripes: the upper one blue and the lower one yellow. The ratio of the flag's width to its length is 2:3.
In 1996, the flag's status was also enshrined in the Constitution of Ukraine. Article 20 of the Basic Law stipulates that the State Flag of Ukraine is a banner of two equal horizontal stripes of blue and yellow.
What the Flag of Ukraine symbolizes
The best-known interpretation of the Ukrainian flag's colors is blue sky over a golden wheat field. This is how it is most often interpreted today, especially in popular culture. Yellow is associated with grain fields, prosperity, and labor, while blue is associated with the sky, freedom, and peace.
However, it is worth remembering , that this is a symbolic, rather than an officially established by the state, interpretation. The Constitution and other regulatory documents define the flag's colors and proportions but do not establish their specific meaning. From a historical perspective, blue and gold primarily have heraldic origins. Therefore, the image of "the sky over a wheat field" should be viewed as a modern popular interpretation that has become firmly established in public consciousness.
After the restoration of independence, the flag became one of the main symbols of Ukrainian statehood. During the Revolution of Dignity, blue-and-yellow banners were among the main symbols of the protests.
After the beginning of Russian aggression against Ukraine in 2014, and especially after the full-scale invasion in 2022, the Ukrainian flag acquired another powerful symbolic dimension.
The raising of the blue-and-yellow flag in cities and villages liberated from Russian occupation has become a symbol of the restoration of Ukrainian statehood. In other countries around the world, Ukrainian flags are used during solidarity rallies and displayed near government institutions and diplomatic missions.
Facts about the Ukrainian flag
Ukraine’s National Flag Day was officially established by a presidential decree in 2004. The holiday is observed on August 23, the eve of Ukraine’s Independence Day.
In 2009, an annual official ceremony to raise the National Flag on August 23 was introduced throughout Ukraine.
The official proportions of the Ukrainian flag are 2:3, and the blue and yellow horizontal stripes are of equal width.
The Ukrainian flag has also been to space. In 1997, it was taken there by Leonid Kadenyuk, the first astronaut of independent Ukraine, who flew aboard the American space shuttle Columbia.
The blue-and-yellow banner holds a special place in military tradition. Ukrainian troops raise flags in liberated territories, and photographs of the flag being raised often become symbolic confirmation that a settlement has returned to Ukrainian control.
During the years of the full-scale war, the blue-and-yellow flag has become one of the world’s most recognizable Ukrainian symbols.
Over several centuries, blue and yellow evolved from the heraldic colors of individual Ukrainian lands into national symbols, a banner banned by the Soviet authorities, and the official flag of an independent state. Today, it represents not only Ukraine as a state but also the historical continuity of Ukrainians’ struggle for the right to their own independence.

Red faces as Sydney Marathon medal shows German stadium

Red faces as Sydney Marathon medal shows German stadium
August 23, 2026
Organizers of the 2026 Sydney Marathon are making the best of the situation after minting tens of thousands of medals engraved with depictions of landmarks from the eastern Australian city along with one that doesn't belong — the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany.
The medal should have instead shown the Allianz Stadium in Sydney, which is one of the sights that participants in the upcoming race will pass while running the the 42.2-kilometer (26.2-mile) course.
More than 40,000 participants are expected to earn the medal as a "badge of honor" for completing the race on August 30.
Other landmarks shown include the famous Opera House and the Sydney Harbour Bridge.
What have organizers said about the medal mix-up?
"A little too much international flavor has found its way onto the back of the finishers medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.
"We're not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error; though it's certainly given everyone somehing to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humor," the spokesperson said.
"With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive."
"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget," the spokesperson added.
"It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."
Good-humored reaction from Munich
Munich's Allianz Arena has responded in light-hearted manner.
"Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!" it posted on Instagram.
"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena — Sydney Opera — Unique Architecture — Both are worth a visit!"
The daily Sydney Morning Herald also came up with a gleefully teasing headline: "The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map."
The other side of the medal shows shows a gold-and-indigo pattern by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian that has been widely commended.
Killian has said he was not involved in the design of the side showing the landmarks.

Could NATO go to war with Israel over Turkey? | Explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:31:46 UTC
15:31:46 KST

The increasingly open confrontation between Israel and Turkey has raised a question that until recently belonged largely to hypothetical war games: What happens if two of the Middle East’s strongest militaries begin shooting at each other, given that Turkey is a member of NATO?
The answer is less dramatic than the phrase “NATO versus Israel” suggests. A direct Israeli attack on Turkish territory could give Ankara a strong basis to seek collective defense under NATO’s Article 5. But a clash between Israeli and Turkish forces in Syria would be considerably more complicated, and would not automatically oblige NATO’s other members to attack Israel.
The question has become more relevant as Israel and Turkey increasingly collide over Syria. Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur air base in northwestern Syria on August 18 after a Turkish delegation visited the facility, saying it was acting to prevent a Turkish military deployment there. Turkey condemned the strike, while the Syrian government denied that a permanent Turkish base was planned.
The dispute reflects a broader struggle over Syria’s future. Turkey is one of President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s most important regional backers and is helping rebuild Syrian military capabilities, while Israel is determined to prevent military infrastructure it considers threatening from taking shape near its borders. That creates an obvious danger: Israeli aircraft could eventually strike a site where Turkish soldiers, equipment or aircraft are present.
What Article 5 actually covers
Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty says an armed attack against one NATO member is considered an attack against them all. Turkey, which joined the alliance in 1952, is explicitly protected.
But geography is crucial. Article 6 specifies that the collective-defense guarantee covers Turkish territory, as well as allied forces, vessels and aircraft in defined areas that include the Mediterranean. Turkish ground forces deployed inside Syria do not fit as neatly within that geographical framework because Syria itself is outside NATO territory.
An Israeli strike in Syria that killed Turkish soldiers could therefore cause an enormous crisis without automatically being treated in the same way as an attack on Ankara, Istanbul or a Turkish military base inside Turkey.
A confrontation at sea or in the air could present a different legal question. The treaty expressly refers to allied vessels and aircraft in the Mediterranean, meaning an attack on a Turkish warship or military aircraft there could provide Ankara with a stronger argument for seeking Article 5 protection.
Article 5 does not mean NATO automatically attacks Israel
Even if Article 5 were invoked, NATO would not simply declare war on Israel.
Each member is required to assist the ally that has been attacked, but the treaty allows every country to decide what action it considers necessary. That assistance can include military force, but does not have to. NATO members could instead provide intelligence, air defenses, surveillance, logistics or forces to protect Turkish territory.
That distinction becomes especially important in the case of Israel because NATO decisions are political as well as military, and the United States would sit at the center of any response.
The US would be caught between two crucial partners
Washington has exceptionally important relationships with both sides.
Turkey is a treaty ally, one of NATO’s most militarily significant members and an increasingly important U.S. partner in shaping the future of Syria. President Donald Trump has also maintained a close working relationship with Erdoğan, whose government has become an important regional interlocutor for Washington.
Israel, however, remains one of the United States’ closest strategic and military partners outside NATO. Trump has maintained close ties with Netanyahu even as disagreements over Syria, Iran and other regional issues have become increasingly visible.
The contradiction is already affecting U.S. policy. In July, Netanyahu asked Trump to rein in Erdoğan’s increasingly hostile rhetoric toward Israel and urged him not to approve weapons sales that could help modernize the Turkish air force. Trump, meanwhile, has cultivated ties with both leaders.
Washington is also directly involved in trying to prevent Syria from becoming the arena for an Israeli-Turkish confrontation. The Trump administration has brokered arrangements involving Israel and Syria and has repeatedly pressed for de-escalation. U.S. officials reacted sharply to the latest Israeli strike in Syria precisely because they feared that an incident involving Turkish forces could spiral into something much larger.
This makes an American-backed NATO attack on Israel one of the least likely outcomes of an initial confrontation. Washington would have strong reasons to defend Turkish territory if it came under attack, but equally strong reasons to prevent a situation in which U.S. forces or other NATO militaries were ordered to fight Israel.
The much more likely American response would be intense pressure on both governments to stop the escalation, combined with defensive support for Turkey if necessary.
Turkey would probably turn first to Article 4
Before Article 5, Ankara would have another NATO mechanism available: Article 4.
It allows a member to request consultations whenever it believes its territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened. Turkey has used it repeatedly during crises involving Syria.
That history offers a useful guide to how an Israel-Turkey crisis might unfold. Rather than immediately entering a war, NATO could reinforce Turkish air defenses, increase intelligence and surveillance operations, deploy additional aircraft or naval forces and send a political warning that attacks on Turkish territory would cross a much more serious threshold.
Such measures could give Ankara meaningful alliance backing without requiring NATO aircraft to attack Israel.
Where the real danger begins
The greatest risk is therefore not that an Israeli strike in Syria suddenly triggers a NATO war. It is that a limited incident starts an escalation neither side originally intended.
Israeli aircraft could hit Turkish personnel or equipment in Syria. Ankara could retaliate against Israeli military assets. Israel could respond again. Turkey could seek NATO consultations, while Washington attempts to impose a ceasefire before the confrontation moves beyond Syrian territory.
The calculation changes dramatically if Israel strikes Turkey itself. Turkish territory is explicitly covered by NATO’s collective-defense guarantee, giving Ankara a much clearer basis for invoking Article 5. NATO members would then have to decide what assistance they were prepared to provide.
How the confrontation began would matter as well. NATO is a defensive alliance. Turkey could not necessarily initiate hostilities elsewhere and assume that every Israeli response would automatically amount to an Article 5 attack. Allies would examine where the fighting occurred, who initiated it and whether the incident fell within the treaty.
Could NATO actually fight Israel?
In theory, yes. If Israel carried out an armed attack covered by the treaty, NATO members could decide that military force was necessary to help defend Turkey.
In practice, a full NATO war against Israel would remain an extraordinary scenario, not least because the United States would have powerful strategic interests on both sides.
That may ultimately be the most important safeguard. Washington would be caught between a formal treaty commitment to Turkey and a decades-old strategic relationship with Israel, giving it an overwhelming incentive to stop a confrontation before either side forced it to choose.
The real danger is therefore not an automatic NATO attack after the first exchange of fire. It is an escalation that gradually removes the diplomatic exits: from a clash in Syria, to Turkish retaliation, to an Israeli counterstrike, and eventually to an attack on Turkish territory that places NATO’s collective-defense commitment directly on the table.
At that point, what began as another confrontation over Syria would no longer be only an Israeli-Turkish crisis.

Ahmad Adil
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
A Panama-flagged cargo vessel sank off the coast of Odisha in eastern India, with two people rescued, as authorities launched a major search and rescue operation, an official statement said Sunday.
The vessel MV Ocean Winner was carrying 24 crew members, including 20 Chinese nationals, three from Myanmar and one Bangladeshi, the Indian Coast Guard said in a statement on US social media company X.
Officials said the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Sri Vijaya Puram, the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, launched a rescue operation Saturday after receiving a distress alert from the Ocean Winner and subsequently losing contact with the vessel.
The Indian Coast Guard said two survivors were rescued from life rafts during the operation.
Three ships have also been deployed to conduct surface searches for the remaining crew members, it added.

As always, came away impressed by their energy and ambition. PM Modi, Shah greet citizens on National Space Day

Union home minister Amit Shah also extended his greetings, noting that the day commemorates India's Chandrayaan-3 landing on the Moon's south polar region.“Warm greetings to every citizen on #NationalSpaceDay. It is a momentous day that marks the occasion when India's Chandrayaan-3 touched down on the Moon's South Pole, and celebrates our scientists at Isro for making an indelible imprint of their genius on the sands of time,” Shah said in a post on X.

Chandrayaan-3 achievement at centre of celebrations
The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 made a controlled soft landing on the lunar surface on August 23, 2023, making India the first country to achieve a soft landing near the Moon's south polar region.The Pragyan rover was subsequently deployed to conduct scientific experiments and collect data.The third National Space Day celebrations were held in Ahmedabad on Sunday, with Union Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Gujarat Cabinet Minister Arjun Modhwadia, Isro Chairman V Narayanan and IN-SPACe Chairman Pawan Goenka among those attending, according to ANI.Narayanan recalled the early years of India's space programme while highlighting the country's progress in the sector.“When we started the country's space programme, we moved rocket parts using old bicycles. From that humble beginning, today we have reached the number one position in nine areas,” he said.The Isro chairman also said Chandrayaan-3 had generated scientific data that was made available to researchers globally.
“Chandrayaan-3 achieved a soft landing near the south pole of the Moon. Today, it is not only about the soft landing; we have also obtained a wealth of scientific data,” Narayanan said.He described the mission's ability to inspire Indians as another major achievement, saying, “One of the major achievements of Chandrayaan-3 was that it inspired 140 crore Indians across the globe.”National Space Day celebrations are aimed at highlighting India's achievements in space exploration and encouraging greater interest in science, technology, research and innovation.

New museum exhibition in Lovech draws strong interest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:27:02 UTC

Sunday 23 August 2026 08:10
Sunday, 23 August 2026, 08:10
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Lovech’s rich history is attracting an increasing number of young visitors thanks to the new permanent exhibition at the city’s Regional History Museum. Opened at the beginning of July, it has already become the museum’s second most visited attraction, with particularly strong interest among students, families, and local residents, said Silvia Vuteva, curator and ethnographer at the Regional History Museum-Lovech, during a special press conference.
Silvia Vuteva
PHOTO BTA
Located along the Osam River in northern Bulgaria, the city holds an important place in Bulgarian history. During the 19th century, Lovech was a major center of trade and craftsmanship and was associated with the activities of Vasil Levski, who established one of the most important centers of the Internal Revolutionary Organization here in the period before Bulgaria’s Liberation in 1878.
PHOTO BTA
The Regional History Museum’s newest exhibition is spread across seven themed halls and traces the development of Lovech and the surrounding region from antiquity to the present day. Among the nearly 5,000 exhibits on display are archaeological finds, everyday objects, documents and materials related to the city’s cultural, spiritual and economic life.
PHOTO BTA
The history is presented through digital technologies, multimedia and educational materials. Some of the halls also feature reconstructions, including a Neolithic dwelling, a military trench, and the interior of a home from Bulgaria’s socialist period.
Visitors spend an average of between one and one and a half hours exploring the exhibition. Since the beginning of August, it has welcomed 17 groups, including 43 university students.
PHOTO BTA
One of the exhibition’s main objectives is to present local history in the context of the nation’s broader history and to show how the past has shaped the identity of Lovech and its residents.

Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia

Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia
The Level 2 storm which hit Estonia on Saturday has started to subside, though strong winds and rain are still forecast for Sunday.
Heavy rain — with some locations receiving the average monthly rainfall in the space of 24 hours — and strong winds swept across Estonia over the weekend, bringing down trees, causing power outages and disrupting ferry services.
The weather warning has been downgraded to Level 1 (yellow) in western and southern Estonia as of Sunday morning. Eastern Estonia – Ida-Viru, Lääne-Viru, Järva, Jõgeva and Tartu counties – are now not subject to the warning and the weather map is showing green as of the time of writing.
Heavy rain is to continue over Estonia on Sunday morning, with 24-hour totals of 50–70 millimeters and up to 90 millimeters in some areas. These higher figures are roughly the same as the overall average rainfall for August, usually the wettest month, in Estonia.
Wind gusts reached as high as 30 meters per second on Saturday and the Rescue Board (Päästeamet) has been notified of fallen trees on roads and power lines.
The storm also left households without power: On Saturday evening, 3,410 households were without power according to Elektrilevi. As of 9 a.m. Sunday, that figure had fallen to around 2,600, though around half the outages were in southeastern Estonia.
Heavy rainfall of 50–100 millimeters overnight threatened Tallinn's sewage and drainage system, and Tallinna Vesi issued flood prevention advice, including clearing gutters, avoiding parking in flood-prone areas, and reducing water use during the rain.
Urmas Kütt, head of pipeline operations at Tallinna Vesi, noted that during and immediately after heavy rain, the public should avoid using large amounts of water to avoid placing additional strain on the wastewater system. Stormwater should not be directed into the sewer network to avoid overloading the system, and Kütt stressed people should avoid flooded basements and manholes due to electrocution and other hazards.
Ferry services were subject to cancellation during the storm but are back online as of Sunday morning. The 8.30 a.m. sailing from Rohuküla to Heltermaa (Hiiumaa) went ahead, and the 10 a.m. service in the other direction is also on schedule. No changes to the Virtsu to Kuivastu (Muhu/Saaremaa) route timetable are currently expected.
The storm also hit Latvia and Lithuania. Latvia's weather service issued a storm warning, outdoor events were canceled and roads were flooded in several places. In Riga, water accumulated beneath viaducts, disrupting traffic. According to Lithuanian media, at least one person was killed after being struck by a falling tree and over 150,000 households were left without power.

blue portals and brick vaults shape DKA’s apartment renovation in rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:14:46 UTC
15:14:46 KST

In Rome, DKA – Diele Kerciku Architetture renovates A12 Apartment, a 100-square-meter home where the existing architecture becomes the basis for a more open domestic layout. Brick vaults, generous ceiling heights and a sequence of enclosed rooms defined the original apartment, and instead of concealing these features, the studio used them as a framework for the intervention.
The clients asked for a larger and more convivial living area capable of connecting the kitchen, living room and everyday spaces. DKA responded through a process of subtraction, opening portions of the load-bearing walls to create new visual and spatial connections while preserving the rhythm of the original openings. The brick vaults remain clearly legible throughout, allowing the historic structure to run continuously through the updated plan.
the bespoke bookcase acts as an architectural element | images courtesy of DKA
BLUE JOINERY TURNS THRESHOLDS INTO ARCHITECTURE
The entrance works as a central distributive axis between the apartment’s two wings. Along it, a long pale-blue bespoke joinery element integrates wardrobes, storage and access to service spaces into one continuous volume. Deeper blue portals mark the transitions between rooms, framing views and giving the thresholds a stronger architectural presence.
In the living area, a large custom-designed bookcase extends beyond the role of furniture and begins to operate almost as part of the room itself. The kitchen, designed by Poliform, introduces a more technical palette of etched glass and steel, set against light oak parquet and the apartment’s existing finishes. These reflective surfaces sharpen the contrast between the new intervention and the heavier material character of the historic shell.
deep-blue portals frame views between rooms and emphasize the transition between domestic spaces
COLOR ORGANIZES THE HOME
The same strategy continues into the private spaces. In the children’s bedroom, a suspended net creates an additional level for play, rest and movement, turning the room into a more flexible domestic landscape. Elsewhere, shades of blue, pale blue and red identify volumes, emphasize passages and connect architecture with bespoke furniture, rather than operating simply as decorative accents.
Lighting by Flos and Artemide further reinforces these relationships, adding depth to the contrast between old and new materials. Through selective structural changes, custom-made elements and a tightly controlled chromatic palette, DKA preserves the legibility of A12 Apartment’s historic fabric while making its spaces work for contemporary life. The result does not attempt to smooth away the difference between periods; it lets the brick vaults and the blue joinery share the room, each very much aware of the other.

Quick hits: A Shoriful stunner amid more left-arm carnage in the 29th two-day Test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:08:39 UTC
15:08:39 KST

Australia vs Bangladesh quick hits: Shoriful Islam's ball of the series, more Mitchell Starc carnage in the 29th two-day Test
Mitchell Starc delivers once more but it's another left-arm seamer who delivers the ball of the series, as Test cricket is blessed with its 29th two-day match.
Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.
1. Shoriful's ball of the series
It wouldn't have taken a rocket scientist to determine that Cam Green held the key for Australia at the start of day two.
The towering all-rounder, buoyed by his drought-breaking ton in Darwin, was once again looking precisely the player he had for so long promised to be.
With Green well set on 67 and clattering boundaries to either side of the wicket, it was going to take something special to remove the big man.
And Shoriful Islam, having already ripped through Australia's middle order late on day two, delivered something very, very special.
The left-armer's pinpoint yorker swung in late and dramatically, with Green falling over himself in a futile attempt to keep it out.
The ball thudded into the Australian's big toe on its way past the stumps and, after a brief consultation with DRS, was given out LBW to what was surely the ball of the series.
And that wasn't the end of the story for left-arm seamers on day two …
2. Starc continues the left-arm carnage
Shoriful, who was almost inconceivably yanked from the bowling attack after that stunner against Green, ended the innings with figures of 7-48, the best-ever return for a Bangladeshi bowler while playing away from home.
Combine that with the 6-12 Mitchell Starc plundered early on day one, and left-arm seam had returned overall figures of 13-60, while accounting for 13 of the 20 wickets to fall in the match.
And it wasn't long before those numbers were improved even further.
He couldn't manage a wicket in his first set, but Starc struck with his eighth delivery of the innings, extracting some extra bounce to have Shadman Islam caught off a leading edge at point.
And the very next ball, Starc had his eighth of the match, having kissed the top of Mominul Haque's off stump with the Bangladeshi attempting an ill-advised leave.
An almost-customary double strike from Australia's supreme new-ball destroyer.
Starc eventually finished with figures of 4-39 for the innings and, with 10-51, the second-best match figures of his career.
3. Smith takes a screamer after tea
Tailender Taskin Ahmed had set himself well in the lead-up to the tea break, but he fell at the very first hurdle in the evening session.
Lyon's first delivery was a beauty, pitching and turning away from the leftie, who swung hard and found a healthy outside edge.
And Steve Smith, in place at his familiar position at slip, had to have his wits about him to complete a very good one-handed grab.
He's Test cricket's most prolific catcher for a reason, after all.
Taskin, who had provided perhaps Bangladesh's brightest spot in an otherwise pitch-black innings in swatting a massive six over long on in the shadows of tea, was out for 7.
4. The shortest session ever?
With Shoriful in at No. 11, the end was very clearly nigh in Mackay.
However, Shoriful showed in the first innings that he had at least some ability with the bat, top scoring with a rather frenetic 14 from 19 deliveries.
He survived the first ball of his second dig, defending Lyon out into the off side.
But it was all over with the very next ball.
Shoriful had a big swing at one, caught a thick outside edge and ballooned a dolly out to Starc at point, with Australia's superlative spearhead fittingly bringing the match to an end.
With two wickets falling in just three balls, it had to be close to the shortest non-weather-affected session in Test history.
5. The 29th two-day Test
There have been 2,632 Test matches played in cricket's lengthy red-ball history, with 457 of them held in Australia.
As of today, there have been just 29 finish inside two days.
Only five of those have happened in Australia.
And yet, in the last 20 Tests that have been played on these shores, it has happened four times.
Australia thumped South Africa on a Gabba green top in 2022, and then there were two, two-day Tests during last summer's Ashes, one in Perth and the other at the MCG.
The only Australia-hosted Test to finish inside two days before that game in Brisbane four years ago took place in Melbourne against the West Indies, in February 1931.
Eleven of the two-day Tests in history took place before World War I (between 1882 and 1912), a further three either side of World War II (1931-1946) but then none between 1946 and 1999.
Then, since 2000, there have been 13 two-day Tests. The cost of a fast-paced world, perhaps.

in brief
- The race medal depicts Allianz Arena in Munich rather than Sydney's Allianz Stadium.

Organisers of the 2026 Sydney Marathon have been left red-faced after unveiling a finishers’ medal featuring a stadium in Germany — thousands of kilometres from the race finish line.
The two-sided medal features Sydney landmarks, including the Opera House and Sydney Harbour Bridge, but also depicts the distinctive Allianz Arena in Munich.
Marathon organisers have acknowledged the "unfortunate error", with the medal showing the German stadium’s distinctive diamond-patterned exterior rather than the flatter design of Sydney’s Allianz Stadium.
"A little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finishers' medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.
"We're not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error, though it's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour."

"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget," the spokesperson added.
"It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

Nine out of 10 unsolved murders in London linked to minority ethnic victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

Killers who take the lives of black people have a greater chance of getting away with their crimes than those who target white people, new research shows.
Analysis of unsolved homicides in London between 2019 and 2023 found minority ethnic British people made up 61% of victims. When researchers assessed unsolved murders, 92.9% of cases in the capital were connected with a victim who was a person of colour.
Also between 2019 and 2023, black people were victims in 40% of all homicides and represented 73% of all unsolved murder cases during that period. Black victims made up 83.7%, 36 victims, of unsolved shootings and 73.5%, 39 victims, of unsolved stabbings.
The Metropolitan police say the racial disparity is due in part to black people having lower trust in the police, which they say they are trying to improve.
The Met’s head of homicide, commander Paul Brogden, told the Guardian: “We know serious violence disproportionately affects certain communities, particularly young black men, who have the lowest trust in policing. This means sadly victims or witnesses are less likely to come forward and trust us.”
The study, conducted by Action on Armed Violence, also found that deaths by shooting were more likely to be unsolved than those by stabbing. Between 2019 and 2023, London averaged 124.6 homicides a year, with stabbings accounting for 65.3% of all killings and shootings 8.7%.
Yet among the 41 murders from this period that remain unsolved, shootings made up 38%, more than four times their share of overall homicide total.
Brogden said: “As this report outlines, that is an added complexity following shootings or stabbings on the streets, where identifying suspects requires more detailed investigative work, particularly when compared to domestic murders.
“While we use every tool at our disposal such as CCTV and forensics, often it’s witness evidence which can prove vital in securing convictions.”
DCI Alex Gammampila, a senior Scotland Yard homicide detective, said: “There tends to be more planning and thought to it [a shooting], rather than a spontaneous pick up of a knife and stabbing thrust.
“All this makes firearms offences more challenging to solve.”
The average age of homicide victims in London is about 36. However, for unsolved cases, the average victim’s age drops significantly to 28, indicating a notable skew toward younger victims.
Iain Overton, of Action on Armed Violence, said of the findings: “Our data suggest that London’s unsolved murders are not evenly distributed. Instead, they are concentrated among young Black men and in cases involving firearm violence.
“While there are many reasons for why such murder investigations are especially difficult, the result must seem often clear to the victims’ families: those communities most affected by deadly violence are often the least likely to see those responsible brought to justice. This in itself risks deepening existing mistrust and creating the perception of unequal protection under the law. And that can’t be a good thing.”
The Met has a high clear-up rate for homicides, running at nine out of 10 killings resulting in justice. Last year the Met recorded 97 homicides in London, down from 153 in 2019, and the lowest in a decade.
The study says between 2015 and 2024 there were 110 unsolved homicides, 9%, of 1,222 killings in that period.

New licensing for game shoots could stop poisoning of birds of prey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

From the end of August, Land Rovers load up with tweed-clad shooters, who go off to large estates and compete to fill the biggest “bag” of game birds, often shooting dozens at a time – a practice which has long appalled bird conservationists.
Soon, the years-long campaign to stop the poisoning of birds of prey, as well as the release of tens of millions of pheasants into the countryside, could be victorious as a result of government plans for a new licensing scheme for shoots.
The scheme could end the centuries-long tradition, or at least severely curtail it. Currently, about 30 million pheasants are set loose each year by shooting estates for people to pay to shoot.
This number could be reduced if shoots are given licences to release only a certain number of birds. The introduction of licences would also mean estates that are linked to the poisoning or shooting of birds of prey could lose their ability to host shoots.
Beccy Speight, the chief executive of the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), has been campaigning on this issue for many years and is preparing documents to send in an “evidence sprint” to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which has committed to consider only allowing estates to shoot under licence.
“We think this is a totally reasonable step to take. It is not to ban shooting in any sense; it is about saying we need shooting to be in a sustainable form, and it needs to be licensed so this wildlife crime can’t continue,” Speight says.
There is currently a licensing scheme for grouse in Scotland. Estates are given five-year licences to host shoots as long as they follow a code of practice, including protecting habitat for other birds such as waders. Shoots that are linked to the poisoning of birds of prey can lose their licence. Speight thinks a similar scheme could work in England.
Deaths of raptors such as buzzards, eagles and hen harriers are often linked to shooting estates because of fears from gamekeepers that they will prey on birds including grouse, partridge and pheasant.
Magnificent white-tailed eagles can now be found swooping in the skies of south-west England thanks to a reintroduction programme. But raptors have faced persecution. Natural England recently found five white eagles in Dorset that had died from the same brand of rat poison. The Health and Safety Executive is investigating whether the poison was used in accordance with legal requirements designed to protect wildlife.
“It makes me feel sick,” Speight says. “All that work, these eagles are amazing birds. It is why we need licensing.”
Seven satellite-tagged hen harriers were found poisoned or shot on or near grouse moors last year. Speight adds: “We find the satellite-tagged bodies and that is probably just the tip of the iceberg- buzzards, for example, aren’t satellite tagged so we can never find or test their bodies. It’s a serious problem that is going on in our natural world.”
Many people shoot sustainably, killing what they can eat or give to friends and family, and keep estates in a wilder condition, promoting biodiversity beyond just the birds which are kept to shoot.
Under a licensing system, this would be preserved. Speight explains: “Shooting is a continuum, from small walk-up shoots up to very intensive bag-driven shoots, and it would probably result in more shooting at the start and middle rather than at that extreme end.”
The shooting industry has been furious at Speight’s campaigning. Roger Seddon, of the Countryside Alliance, recently described her as a “pied piper” and a “puppeteer controlling the environment secretary like a marionette”.
Asked about this, Speight was exasperated: “It’s absolutely not true. It’s the job of the RSPB to drive its cause, which is a world where people and nature thrive side by side.”
Speight is exhausted after dealing with the fallout from three devastating wildfires on RSPB reserves this summer. “They still have people putting hotspots of fire out,” she says.
This is relevant to the shooting debate, too. For example, large intensive grouse moors are made up of dry heather habitat, which involves draining wet peatland and creating a monoculture of one plant. “Heather is incredibly flammable. Dried out peat is releasing carbon into the atmosphere but also becomes very susceptible to fire,” Speight says.
Speight says recent claims that wildfires are caused by rewilding are “nonsense”. “There is no evidence to back that up,” she said. “With rewilding, you get these more broken, natural mosaics with water in the landscape, which creates breaks and holds water in the landscape more. That has to be good from a wildfire perspective.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “Sustainable shooting has an important place in our rural communities, and we want to make sure high environmental and animal welfare standards are in place so that the practice succeeds and we’re protecting our ecosystems.
“We will work with key groups to explore other moves, such as licensing or other conditions for recreational game bird shooting and release. This will begin with evidence gathering and any changes will be subject to public consultation.”
