Israel, Turkiye and the new regional reordering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:35:48 UTC
03:35:48 KST

Israel, Turkiye and the new regional reordering
In Syria, Israel is not only at odds with Turkiye but also with the regional and international consensus.
On Tuesday, Israeli fighter jets attacked Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria, drawing condemnations from the United States, the United Kingdom, the United Nations, as well as regional countries. The Israeli government claimed that it had intelligence of Turkish military movement to the site.
In a subsequent interview, US Ambassador to Turkiye and Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said the US had received this intelligence from the Israelis six days before the attack. However, US intelligence conducted its own due diligence and found no basis for the claim.
The incident not only reflects a shift in the dynamics between Turkiye and Israel, but also signals a regional reordering that the latter is no longer at the centre of.
The Turkish response
Seeing the Israeli attack on the Syrian base as a provocation, Ankara refrained from escalating and instead provided an off-ramp out of the crisis. It framed the issue not in bilateral terms but as one between Israel and the US, and between Israel and the regional and international consensus.
Normally, there is a deconfliction mechanism between Turkiye and Israel. However, as Barrack indicated in the interview, Israel did not warn Turkiye about the attack, which could have triggered a military response.
The US envoy called for a deconfliction mechanism, but such an initiative can be effective only if the sides involved want it to be. In this case, there is no evidence that Israel sought de-escalation. In fact, it appears escalation was the intended outcome, as Israel notified neither Turkiye nor the US about the attack and acted on a pretext that the US intelligence found no basis for – a ploy to boost Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s electoral campaign.
After the US-imposed lull on the Iran front, Netanyahu is likely seeking escalation on other fronts, be it Syria, Lebanon or Gaza, in the run-up to the Israeli election. The challenge for Turkiye would be to avoid taking Netanyahu’s bait while also preventing the normalisation of such aggression.
That would require direct intervention by US President Donald Trump to rein in Netanyahu. Indeed, a trilateral deconfliction mechanism can work and be credible only if the US throws real weight behind it.
But even if a mechanism is in place, it would not change the fact that Syria has altered the lens through which Turkiye and Israel view each other. For a long time, the core of Turkiye’s discontent with Israel was the Palestinian issue. Hence, it was more humanitarian-, identity- and solidarity-based in nature.
Today, Ankara views Israeli attempts to undermine the Syrian transition as having direct repercussions for its national security. Therefore, Turkiye is no longer seeing Israel solely through the prism of the Palestinian question. Rather, it increasingly sees it as a national security challenge, with Israeli regional revisionism threatening its interests.
The international consensus on Syria
From the Eastern Mediterranean to the Horn of Africa and the wider Middle East, Turkiye and Israel have conflicting policies, priorities and threat perceptions. Despite this, Syria serves as a microcosm of Turkiye and Israel’s visions of the regional order.
Ankara wants its southern neighbour to be centralised, stable and capable militarily. In contrast, Israel wants a Syria that is weak, fragmented and bereft of serious military might.
Yet this is not merely a conflict between Turkish and Israeli visions. Israel is at odds with the regional and international consensus on Syria. The US, the UK, Europe and regional states have all supported a centralised and stable government in Damascus. In an ironic way, the only other regional state that probably wants a weak or failed Syria is Iran.
Like any other sovereign state, Syria will have an army. If Israel believes that the only way to ensure its own security is by keeping its neighbouring or regional states weak, fragmented and bereft of military capability, this is a recipe for perpetual wars and for regional and international isolation.
The undermining of the Syrian state and the failure of its transition would pave the way for non-state actors and radicalism, which would bode ill for the entire region, including Israel. Indeed, neighbouring Lebanon should serve as a cautionary tale. The Israeli occupation and the weakness of the Lebanese state gave birth to and empowered Hezbollah.
Post-Abrahamic Middle East
Israel and Turkiye’s ideas of regional order are also at odds. The recent Mecca Pact, which brought together Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, is not inherently anti-Israel. However, it represents a regional shift that signals the failure of the order envisioned by the Abraham Accords, or similar initiatives such as India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) or the strategic partnership between India, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, and the US known as I2U2.
The Abrahamic vision of the regional order was premised on Arab-Israeli normalisation and cooperation under the US security umbrella. Hard containment of Iran, soft containment of Turkiye, and de-emphasising the Palestinian issue were also part of the same vision.
Inherently, this Abrahamic vision had more to do with Israel and its regional normalisation than the Arab states and their needs and priorities.
However, with its aggressive and revisionist policies, Israel has deepened the prospect of its regional isolation, increased the cost of any normalisation, and doomed this Abrahamic – or Israeli-centric – vision of regional order.
Israeli revisionism is not only driving a wedge between Israel and other major regional states, but it is also revealing the gap between Israel and the US on the question of regional reordering.
While Israel opposes the Mecca Pact, Trump has hailed it, likely seeing it as aligned with his strategy of burden-sharing and burden-shifting with regional allies, and as enjoying more regional legitimacy and acceptance. The US position might also reflect a recalibration of Washington’s regional vision.
Over the last decade, the US invested heavily in creating a regional order premised on Israel and the Arab-Gulf states. But this was essentially an Israeli-centric project for the regional order.
This vision is no longer tenable, and no one is more responsible for its demise than Israel itself.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Swedish police identify 17-year-old girl as victim in school sword attack
Brinell School’s principal says the 18-year-old suspected of carrying out Friday’s deadly sword attack was a student there.
Swedish police have identified the victim of Friday’s deadly sword attack at a Fagersta high school as a 17-year-old girl, as her classmates and the country’s political leaders gather to mourn her.
“The person killed in this incident is a young 17-year-old female. Her family has been informed,” police said on Saturday, declining to release further details.

Local newspaper Fagersta-Posten reported that her parents confirmed the death.
The Brinell School’s principal told local media the 18-year-old suspect was a student there. He entered the building on Friday afternoon, just days after classes resumed from summer break, and was arrested at the scene of the attack.
Two boys, aged 12 and 17, were seriously wounded in the attack, one requiring emergency surgery. A third victim was treated for light injuries and has since gone home.
By Saturday morning, the scene outside Brinell had transformed into a memorial of candles, flowers and a steady stream of visitors, including Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson, who travelled to Fagersta to pay their respects.
Political parties across the country paused campaigning ahead of September’s election.
An unnamed police source told the Reuters news agency that investigators are looking into whether the suspect had ties to online communities that promote school violence.
Police are examining a TikTok account, taken down hours after the attack, that posted an image of a sword 20 minutes before it began and had previously featured videos referencing past school attacks in Sweden and Norwegian mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik.
“The investigators are looking into various online communities which might have egged on the suspect to carry out the attack,” the Reuters source said.
Prosecutors have ordered the person held on suspicion of murder and multiple counts of attempted murder.
Police say they have carried out about 80 interviews so far, with plans to question nearly all of the school’s roughly 450 staff members and students.
The attack adds to a grim pattern. Sweden endured its deadliest school shooting last year, when a gunman killed 10 people in Orebro, and a 2015 sword attack in Trollhattan that killed three people in what authorities called a racially motivated hate crime.

A moderate earthquake of magnitude 5.9 shakes eastern Japan. No tsunami alert is issued
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:23:02 UTC
03:23:02 KST

A moderate earthquake shakes Japan, injuring more than 30 people in the Tokyo region
TOKYO (AP) — A moderate earthquake rattled eastern Japan, including the Tokyo area, early Sunday, injuring more than 30 people, most of them lightly, officials said. There was no danger of a tsunami.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, the quake had a preliminary magnitude of 5.9 and its epicenter was in the southern Ibaraki prefecture with a depth of 70 kilometers (42 miles). The U.S. Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 5.8.
At least 37 people were injured in five prefectures in the region — 15 in Tokyo, nine in Saitama, eight in Kanagawa, four in Chiba and one in Ibaraki — according to prefectural officials and the Fire and Disaster Management Agency.
Most of the injured were hurt when they fell down or hit themselves against furniture or doors as they were caught off guard by the quake while sleeping and got out of bed in a panic, officials said. Among them was a woman in her 80s who fell off the bed and suffered a serious hip injury in Yokohama, in the Kanagawa prefecture, the Yomiuri newspaper reported.
A 23-year-old man told the Asahi newspaper that he felt a vertical jolt seconds after his earthquake alert went off when he was shopping in Tokyo’s eastern district of Taito. He said he feared getting hit by merchandise that fell from shelves as the building shook.
The quake caused delays to express trains serving Tokyo and Narita Airport and other local trains serving northeastern regions, but Shinkansen bullet trains were running normally, their operator East Japan Raiway Co. said.
The government set up a task force to assess the extent of possible damage, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on X.
The Japan Meteorological Agency urged the residents in the area to use caution against another possible moderate earthquake for about a week.
The temblor set off emergency quake alerts on mobile phones and also significantly shook Tokyo. NHK public television showed traffic on roads in nearby cities, including Mito and Saitama, seemingly normal.
An underground water pipe ruptured in Tokyo’s eastern ward of Koto, with water pouring onto the road, NHK footage showed. The pipe has been repaired and the leak stopped.
There were no reports of anomalies from about a dozen nuclear power plants and other facilities that handle nuclear materials, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.
Last month, a magnitude 7.1 quake struck the Kumamoto area on Japan’s southernmost island of Kyushu, killing 38 people and injuring 364.

Scores of people kidnapped from a mosque as armed groups attacked multiple villages in Nigeria
A number of people were kidnapped from a mosque in a spree of abductions at several villages in Nigeria ‘s north-central Niger state, police said Saturday.
The assailants attacked a mosque in Kpenya village after attacks in a string of villages in the remote Borgu Local Government Area of Niger state Friday, police spokesperson Wasiu Abiodun said.
Such attacks are common in Nigeria, where multiple armed groups operate, killing and kidnapping people for ransom. The groups sometimes clash in competition with each other. No group has claimed responsibility for the Friday attacks.
Abiodun did not provide figures but said no lives were lost in the Friday attacks, and said the military was deployed to the area. Residents said scores of people were abducted, with some estimating between 60 and 80 people were kidnapped. A search for survivors was underway Saturday.
Borgu area council chairman Abdullahi Mohammed Nasir said at least 60 people were kidnapped and an unspecified number of people sustained gunshot injuries while trying to escape the gunmen.
“People were abducted while praying at a Juma’at mosque on Friday,” Nasir said. “That was when the bad people came and surrounded the mosque and took them away.”
Zubairu Umar Talba, a youth leader in the Dekara area in Borgu, told The Associated Press that his 85-year-old father was among those who were taken. “Nobody can tell you the exact number of people abducted because, so far, about 80 of our people have been abducted and many have fled the area,” he said.

This specific type of positive emotion predicts life satisfaction better than the rest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:00:51 UTC
03:00:51 KST

An analysis of data from two longitudinal studies conducted in Germany and the Netherlands found that both energized and pleasant positive emotions are associated with life satisfaction, but that this association was much stronger with pleasant positive emotions. The paper was published in the Journal of Positive Psychology.
Subjective well-being is a person’s overall evaluation of how well their life is going. It is typically described as a combination of how satisfied people are with their lives and how frequently they experience positive and negative emotions. Yet researchers still disagree about exactly how these components fit together and whether they reflect a single underlying form of well-being.
One particularly important source of confusion concerns positive affect, which is often treated as if it were one simple psychological state. In reality, the term can refer to very different experiences, ranging from calm pleasure and happiness to excitement, enthusiasm, interest, and energetic engagement.
This means that two studies can both claim to measure positive affect while actually assessing rather different emotional experiences. The distinction matters because pleasant and energized positive emotions may play different roles in well-being. Pleasant feelings may be especially closely connected to satisfaction because they signal that things are going well or that important goals have been achieved. More energized states such as interest, engagement, and enthusiasm may instead be especially useful for motivating activity, exploration, and personal growth.
Study author Jinrui Liu and her colleagues conducted a study in which they explored whether positive emotions and life satisfaction are associated with each other over time. They also wanted to know whether energized and pleasant positive emotions have associations of similar strength with life satisfaction. Finally, they wanted to know whether personality traits that predict energized positive emotions are the same ones that predict pleasant positive emotions.
Study authors analyzed data from the Panel Analysis of Intimate Relationships and Family Dynamics from Germany (PAIRFAM) and the Longitudinal Internet Studies for the Social Sciences (LISS) from the Netherlands. PAIRFAM is a longitudinal study of more than 12,000 individuals from three different birth groups (those born between 1971 and 1973, between 1981 and 1983, and between 1991 and 1993). Study authors analyzed data collected between 2014 and 2021.
The LISS data used in this analysis was collected between 2013 and 2024. The LISS conducted monthly internet surveys of a sample of Dutch individuals aged 16 and older from 5,000 households in each data collection wave. They were recruited randomly from the Dutch population. The sample analyzed in this study included 17,532 participants. 53.3% of them were women.
The measure of pleasant positive emotions used in this analysis was derived from an assessment of depression in PAIRFAM, using items initially meant to capture a lack of depressive symptoms, which actually describe the presence of pleasant feelings (e.g., “I am happy”, “I feel good”).
The assessment of energized positive emotions came from the LISS dataset where the Positive and Negative Affect Scale was used. Both datasets contained a measure of life satisfaction. Additionally, both datasets contained assessments of participants’ personalities in line with the Big Five model (the BFI-20 in the PAIRFAM, and IPIP-50 in the LISS).
Results showed that both pleasant and energized positive emotions were associated with life satisfaction, but that the association with pleasant positive emotions was much stronger. The associations ran in both temporal directions, meaning that earlier life satisfaction was associated with later positive emotions and vice versa.
The associations of the two types of positive emotions with personality traits of extraversion and neuroticism also differed. Neuroticism showed a stronger negative association with pleasant positive emotions, while energized positive emotions were more strongly associated with extraversion.
“In sum, our results indicate that pleasant and energized PA [positive affect] are not interchangeable in longitudinal SWB [subjective well-being] dynamics. Both PA types showed bidirectional within-person associations with LS [life satisfaction] beyond their shared trait-like SWB factor, supporting the view that these SWB elements are further causally related beyond a common underlying construct. However, these associations were consistently stronger for pleasant PA with LS than energized PA,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the theoretical conceptualization of subjective well-being. However, it should be noted that the study authors’ measurements of energized and pleasant positive emotions were driven by the data that were available in the datasets they used. It is possible that different ways of measuring these two categories of positive emotions would yield different results.
The paper, “Jingle all the way? Pleasant and energized positive affect show differential longitudinal relationships with life satisfaction and personality,” was authored by Jinrui Liu, Joar Vittersø, Irene J. E. Teulings, Ragnhild Bang Nes, Lilian Mayerhofer, and Espen Røysamb.

Armed men kidnap dozens in attacks on Nigerian villages
Police say three villages and a mosque were attacked, and worshippers kidnapped in central Niger State.
Armed men have kidnapped dozens of people during an attack on a mosque and surrounding villages in Nigeria’s central Niger State, survivors and police officials say.
The raiders stormed Kpenya Mosque in the Dekara district of Borgu Local Government Area at around 2pm (13:00 GMT) on Friday, after first attacking the villages of Gidan-Zana and Kpenya, police spokesperson Wasiu Abiodun said on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Nigeria’s election campaign begins with Tinubu facing a reform test
- list 2 of 3Death toll from Nigeria boat accident rises to at least 52
- list 3 of 3Nigeria and the Sahel: A growing security divide
Abiodun told the Reuters news agency that police were aware of the kidnappings but had not received reports of anyone being killed, and that a “joint security detachment has been deployed to the area for assessment and rescue operations”.
He said police could not yet confirm the number of people who were taken.
Local residents told Reuters that more than 60 worshippers were kidnapped, but the figure could not be independently verified.
Separately, residents told the AFP news agency that people were also killed, another claim that could not immediately be confirmed.
Jibril Ahmad, a survivor of the assault on Dekara, blamed members of the Lakurawa armed group.
“Soon after finishing the normal Friday prayer, the armed group of Lakurawa, in their hundreds, wielding guns, knives and machetes, began to attack us,” Ahmad told AFP, claiming that people were “slaughtered”.
During the attack, a third group, Mahmuda, intervened and clashed with the kidnappers, allowing some abductees to escape, he said.
Federal lawmaker Jafaru Mohammed told AFP that several nearby villages were also struck.
“Some members of the Mahmuda group were against the doctrine of the Lakurawa, and when they heard of what the Lakurawa were doing, they fought them,” Mohammed said.
The attack unfolded in a region near Nigeria’s western border with Benin that has seen growing activity from local armed groups and fighters from the neighbouring region, even as the country’s 17-year armed rebellion remains concentrated in the northeast.
The violence in Niger State continued into Saturday. Resident Abdullahi Ahmad said the group returned to the area to seize more people as a “bargaining chip” in advance of an expected troop deployment, and planted landmines on the road out of Dekara.
“A man and his family who were fleeing the town yesterday were killed when their car hit a landmine planted by the terrorists. Everyone is living in fear,” he said.
Mass abductions have been a hallmark tactic of the country’s armed groups and have evolved into a lucrative, multimillion-dollar industry involving networks of both ideological and nonideological gangs across Nigeria’s northwest and central regions.

Breanna Stewart wants a safe space as transgender debate sparks rallies at Fever games
NEW YORK (AP) — New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart has always seen the WNBA as an inclusive place that has served as a safe space for both its fans and the players. That’s been challenged lately.
The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA. Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
There have been small rallies and protests outside Indiana Fever games after the issue came to a head when Sophie Cunningham of the Fever said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. There were a pair of peaceful rallies representing both sides of the transgender issue that took place before the Fever faced the New York Liberty on Saturday night.
“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” Stewart told a small group of reporters Saturday morning. “I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space.”
Cunningham felt that all the attention that her comments have garnered has been positive by bringing more fans to the game.
“You have a lot of new fans, not only just watching, but coming to games and seeing the environment and seeing the talent,” she said before the game. “I think anytime you can get more eyes on the W, that’s an awesome thing, because then that inspires other young kids that maybe have never seen the game or heard about the game or been to a game, they get that experience. So I definitely think that it’s been a very positive thing.”
At least three fans were asked by WNBA security personnel to cover shirts that had messages about transgender women participating in women’s sports during last Sunday’s game at Atlanta between the Dream and the Fever. The league later said the fans should have been free to wear those shirts.
Stewart said Liberty fans specifically, but WNBA fans in general, come to games because “they can feel like they can be themselves in whatever capacity that is and we don’t want to lose sight of that.”
The Liberty forward said everyone is entitled to their own opinion and if that stops being allowed there are much bigger issues. However, she said, trying to divide teams and players shouldn’t be tolerated.
“If we don’t allow (free speech), we need to like really kind of go back and look at more things. I think the bigger thing is people are trying to divide us as teams, but also as teammates or as opponents,” she said. “This league is incredibly inclusive and what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So, we don’t want to take that platform away.”
Stewart has been an ally for the transgender community during her career. She faced some online backlash last year when one of her signature shoes had a Harry Potter theme to it. Stewart is a huge fan of the Harry Potter books and subsequent movies by author J.K. Rowlings, who has drawn criticism for her anti-trans stance.
Stewart has donated royalties from that shoe to The Trevor Project, a suicide prevention and crisis intervention nonprofit organization for LGBTQ+ youth.

Ex-IAF vice-chief Kapoor says India’s 4.5-gen Tejas may not have relevance in 2030s, country must partner with global consortiums like FCAS or GCAP for 6th-gen programme

NEW DELHI: Less than two months after retirement as the IAF's vice chief, Air Marshal Nagesh Kapoor (Retd) has slammed the delay in the delivery of Tejas (LCA) fighter jet by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited to the air force, saying, “why must it be that a machine that was promised to us so many years back with a certain set of capabilities continues to be denied to us on one pretext or the other”.In an interview to NDTV, the IAF veteran said, “Why must we be hamstrung because someone somewhere has not been able to keep their promises?”The delivery of the indigenous LCA Tejas Mk1A jets by HAL to the IAF has faced multi-year delays, primarily caused by late supplies of F404-IN20 engines by American GE company, complex mission software validation, and stringent operational requirements set by the IAF.When asked if advanced Tejas Mk-2 may be operationally relevant when it starts entering service in big numbers in mid 2030s at a time when China is already raising its fleet of its 5th-generation fighter jet, the former vice-chief said, “No, operationally, definitely no.”With China on its way to deploying 500 5th-generation J-20 fighters by 2030, India is still struggling to get the delivery of the first squadron by 4.5-generation Tejas Mk1A. But they must come at a much faster speed,” he said.When asked about Russia’s 5th-gen fighter jet Su-57, the former vice-chief said when the Russian fighter is compared to western jets like American F-35, western jets have an edge over the Su-57 as they have better avionics and stealth.Air Marshal Kapoor (Retd) suggested that India should partner with an European consortium working on state-of-the-art sixth generation platforms. “There are other things that are happening — why not join FCAS (Future Combat Air System is the European programme for 6th generation jet under development by French Dassault Aviation, Airbus and Indra Sistemas) Why not GCAP (Global Combat Air Programme is a multinational initiative led by Italy, Japan, and UK to jointly develop a sixth-generation jet).
”“'You are probably going with a consortium which has got a good record of delivery, of development. Why go through this Gen 4, Gen 4.5 steps when you know the next best thing is already being thought of and why not just join up there?,” the IAF veteran said.
His comments underline the difficult choices facing India’s air power planners: meeting immediate squadron requirements while ensuring that indigenous programmes do not fall behind the rapid evolution of military aviation technology.

Trump seeks to block the BBC’s attempt to subpoena Ivanka Trump, Trump Jr

Trump seeks to block the BBC’s attempt to subpoena Ivanka Trump, Trump Jr
While lawyers for the US president argue the subpoenas are ‘cynical’, the BBC says they could help shine light on a $10bn defamation case.
United States President Donald Trump has called on a federal court to deny a motion by the BBC to subpoena members of his immediate family, as part of a $10bn lawsuit over a documentary the broadcaster aired.
On Friday, lawyers for Trump argued that the BBC had embarked on a “politically charged discovery campaign” by seeking to compel testimony from Trump’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr, his first daughter Ivanka Trump and his son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Editor of US newspaper Stars and Stripes reportedly fired under Trump
- list 2 of 3Trump administration subpoenas New York Times reporters over coverage
- list 3 of 3ABC News says FCC is carrying out intimidation campaign to shape coverage
Trump’s team appealed to the court to reject the BBC’s motion, comparing it to a fishing expedition that goes beyond the scope of the case.
“This case concerns a narrow wrong — the BBC’s deliberate splicing together of two passages of President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech spoken nearly fifty-five minutes apart,” Friday’s court filing said.
“Rather than litigate that narrow claim, the BBC has attempted to pursue a sweeping investigation disguised as discovery.”
The case began in December, when Trump announced he would sue the BBC over an episode of the documentary series Panorama, which chronicled the Republican leader’s path to a second term as president.
Part of the documentary focuses on the events of January 6, 2021, the day the results of the 2020 election were to be certified. Trump had lost that election but falsely claimed his defeat was the result of fraud.
At a speech in front of the White House on that day, he repeated the unfounded accusation that the election had been “rigged” to a rally of his supporters, some of whom participated in an attack on the US Capitol in the hours afterwards.
The Panorama episode included snippets from Trump’s speech, and critics argued that two sentences from his address had been edited together to sound like one continuous quote.
The first line was: “After this, we’re going to walk down, and I’ll be there with you, we’re going to walk down.” The second came from later in the speech: “And we fight. We fight like hell.”
Though the BBC apologised for the editing and took the Panorama episode down from its platforms, Trump nevertheless filed a multibillion-dollar lawsuit accusing the broadcaster of defamation.
The BBC has denied that charge and pledged to fight the lawsuit in court. The case is currently being heard before the US district court in southern Florida.
As part of its defence, the BBC has sought testimony from figures close to Trump, to establish his thoughts and actions on the day of the January 6 attack.
It pointed out that both Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump were present at their father’s speech, and that they spoke to the president and his inner circle as the violence erupted at the Capitol.
Text messages released by the US Congress show Donald Trump Jr urged his father’s chief of staff to “condemn this sh**”, a fact cited in the BBC’s motion.
While Kushner was not present at the White House, the BBC maintains that his role as Trump’s adviser would also help establish the facts of that day.
Lawyers for the broadcaster say that, after speaking with congressional leaders, Kushner drafted “a proposed statement” for Trump to present, “which would have condemned the use of violence”.
The testimony of Trump Jr, Ivanka Trump and Kushner can help illustrate the president’s “burden to prove that it would be materially false to imply that he incited violence on January 6”, according to the BBC’s motion.
But, the motion added, the BBC has been unable to serve the three family members with subpoenas due to the presence of their US Secret Service protection.
The BBC reportedly attempted to deliver subpoenas to Ivanka Trump and Kushner at their residence in May, only to face Secret Service agents who said they were not authorised to accept the documents.
Likewise, that same month, the BBC was unable to hand Trump Jr a subpoena at Trump Tower in New York. It has therefore asked the court for permission to use certified mail to deliver the documents instead.
But in Friday’s court filing, Trump’s lawyers accused the BBC of carrying out a “cynical” campaign that involved the “harassment of the President’s family, associates, staff, officials, and others”.
It also called the BBC’s efforts “a boundless re-investigation of the events that occurred on January 6, 2021”.
The filing suggests that any interactions involving Ivanka Trump and Kushner are “subject to the executive privilege” of the presidency, since the husband-wife duo served as adviser and senior adviser to Trump, respectively.
Trump has made sweeping claims to executive privilege throughout his two terms in office.
Just this month, the US Department of Justice issued a memo saying such privilege shielded communication even with private advisers who worked outside the executive branch, effectively declaring interactions with companies and private individuals off-limits for subpoenas.
Critics fear the memo will be a hurdle to government transparency under Trump — and may even prevent Congress from accessing investigative materials.
Senator Adam Schiff of California framed the memo as an insurance policy against congressional oversight, should the Republican Party lose its majorities in Congress during November’s midterm elections.
“This latest opinion should be seen as a partisan measure to insulate the president and his corrupt activities from Congressional subpoenas when the majority flips,” he wrote in a statement on August 11.
The federal court in southern Florida has yet to rule on the BBC’s subpoena requests.
The BBC, meanwhile, has sought to have the entire case tossed, on the basis that Trump is attempting to dampen free speech.

‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:47:02 UTC
02:47:02 KST

‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
The Liberian government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. But politicians say they were not consulted.
Monrovia, Liberia – Samwar Fallah began receiving calls this week from people in the United States seeking information about 20 relatives sent to Liberia, a country none of them is a citizen of.
The families asked the Monrovia-based lawyer to find out where their relatives were taken and what would happen to them. He could not tell them much.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4First group of US deportees, out of an expected 1,200, arrive in Liberia
- list 2 of 4Liberia to take 1,200 deportees from the US
- list 3 of 4Liberia’s kush crisis: The hidden trade behind a generation at risk
- list 4 of 4From palava huts to TikTok: How Liberians are preserving their past
He knows the group landed at Roberts International Airport near capital Monrovia on Thursday and was driven away in a bus by Liberian officials. He does not know where they were taken, whether they are free to leave, or what legal status they now hold.
Fallah avoids calling them deportees because the government has not defined their status under Liberian law.
“You cannot relocate a citizen from one country to another without clear information as to why that person has been relocated,” Fallah told Al Jazeera. “Imagine you coming from maybe El Salvador and then you find out you are on a plane to Liberia.”
The group is the first transferred under an arrangement allowing Liberia to receive up to 1,200 people deported from the US over the next 12 months.
The Liberian government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. Politicians say they were not consulted.
Fallah, assisting the families without charge alongside two US immigration lawyers, said they want to know whether their relatives may settle in Liberia, choose where they can go, or eventually return to the US.
He has no answers.
The arrangement involves third-country deportation: sending people to a country other than their country of citizenship. It has raised questions about executive power, sovereignty and the rights of those transferred.
‘Guests of the Republic’
The government said the deportees have not been detained and described the arrangement with the US as humanitarian.
Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah said those transferred would be received as “guests of the Republic”. They are free to leave and may seek asylum, he added.
Piah linked the decision to Liberia’s history as a settlement for free and formerly enslaved Black people from the US and a country whose citizens sought protection abroad during 14 years of civil war.
“Liberia’s gesture is entirely humanitarian and in keeping with the country’s longstanding traditions,” he said.
Piah insisted Liberia would not bear the cost. Accommodation, food and eventual onward travel would be covered by the US government and an international partner organisation, he said.
However, the government has not provided further information about the people who arrived on Thursday. It has not disclosed their full nationalities, where they are being housed, the legal documents under which they entered Liberia, or the identity of the international organisation paying for and managing their stay.
The Reuters news agency on Friday reported that five of those people refused to leave the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea. Al Jazeera has not verified the report independently.
Justice Minister Natu Oswald Tweh said Liberia reviews each passenger list and may reject anyone. “Most of them are people who had immigration violations and offences,” he said.
But the government has not published its screening criteria or said whether any arrivals had US protection orders preventing their return to their countries.
Al Jazeera found out that most of those deported were nationals of Latin American countries, including Venezuela and Cuba.
But “guests” does not establish a legal status under Liberian law. It remains unclear whether those people entered on temporary permits, whether they can work, or whether they must apply for asylum or residency.
Although Piah said the group was free to leave, officials did not allow journalists to speak with them at the airport. They walked down the aircraft steps, boarded a bus and were driven away under official supervision.
Was legislative approval required?
Some of the strongest objections came from politicians who say the arrangement may require legislative approval.
Nimba County Senator Samuel Kogar cited Article 57 of Liberia’s constitution, which empowers the president to conduct foreign affairs and conclude treaties, conventions and similar agreements “with the concurrence of a majority of each House of the Legislature”.
“Was this arrangement brought before both Houses of the Legislature and approved by the required majority?” Kogar asked. “If not, then under what legal authority was this agreement made?”
The government said the arrangement rests on diplomatic notes exchanged on September 4 and September 10 last year.
Third Country Deportation Watch, a project operated by Refugees International and Human Rights First, said the text appeared on the US State Department’s website in March. Most Liberians heard about it only in August.
Representative Anthony F Williams, a member of House committees covering national security, human rights and foreign affairs, rejected the idea that the executive could act alone.
“No agreement that borders on the national security of this country, the sovereignty of the country, can just be entered into by the executive branch alone,” he told Al Jazeera.
The legislature is on a break until October. Williams said he would seek answers on housing, healthcare, screening and Liberia’s authority to detain or remove anyone.
His concerns, he said, were about state capacity, not the arrivals.
Liberia lacks the biometric systems and trained personnel to document as many as 1,200 people moving across counties or porous borders, he said, adding that those fleeing persecution could also be traced by the governments they escaped.
Eddie Jarwolo, executive director of NAYMOTE Partners for Democratic Development, said no published plan showed how Liberia would accommodate the arrivals without further straining public services.
Civil society groups were not consulted, he said. He called for independent monitoring of living conditions, spending and legal compliance.
Was there a diplomatic tradeoff?
The government insists Liberia received no payment or diplomatic reward for accepting the transfers. Critics have called for disclosure of the negotiations.
The arrangement emerged amid several US decisions affecting Liberia. On December 9, 2025, the countries signed a five-year, $124m health memorandum. Washington also extended B1/B2 visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months.
Al Jazeera previously reported that those measures followed Liberia’s agreement to accept Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose mistaken removal from the US to a Salvadoran prison became a political and legal flashpoint.
The US later sought court permission to send him to Liberia.
Meanwhile, migrant visas for Liberians were halted in January, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, and the US awarded Liberia $5m this year for migration management.
Neither government has publicly established a direct link between the deportation arrangement and the visa move. Jarwolo of NAYMOTE said the two nations should disclose whether visa extension was linked to accepting third-country deportees.
“If they were linked, it would raise serious concerns about Liberia’s negotiating position, national sovereignty and public safety,” he said. “Development assistance should not require Liberia to accept individuals whose backgrounds and legal status have not been transparently disclosed and properly assessed.”
University of Liberia Student Union president William Sando said he learned of the arrangement through Facebook before Piah confirmed it.
“They have not adequately informed the Liberian people,” he said, rejecting the minister’s argument as “disconnected from the current reality”.
Sando wanted the government to disclose where the arrivals will live and whether those who remain may work.
Kogar, the senator, said the questions went beyond an opposition to migration.
“This is not a small issue,” he said. “We are talking about our sovereignty, our laws, our national security, and the responsibility we have to the Liberian people. Where are we, the Liberians?”

Iranian artist showcases “Constitutional Revolution of Iran” at US exhibition

Iranian artist showcases “Constitutional Revolution of Iran” at US exhibition
TEHRAN- Iranian photographer and filmmaker Armin Amirian is participating in the 13th International FL3TCH3R Exhibition in the US with his artwork “Constitutional Revolution of Iran.”
The exhibition is being held from August 7 to September 27, at the Fishman Gallery in Johnson City, Tennessee, bringing together works by international artists selected by this year’s juror and curator, Jessica Burke.
“Constitutional Revolution of Iran” is part of Amirian’s “Until History Freezes” series, which he created in 2020 as a continuation of his narrative approach to art.
In the series, figures associated with Iran’s Constitutional Revolution emerge beneath a layer of ice, creating a visual interpretation of a pivotal chapter in the country’s modern history.
The Constitutional Revolution, which began in 1905 and culminated in the establishment of a constitutional system in Iran, marked a major turning point in the country’s political and social development. The movement sought to establish the rule of law and limit absolute royal authority through the creation of a parliament and a constitutional framework.
Amirian’s participation in the Fletcher exhibition marks another step in an international artistic career that includes more than 100 exhibitions and festivals around the world. He has previously received several honors, including the Distinguished Artist Award from the Fletcher Foundation.
Works from the “Until History Freezes” series have previously been presented in solo exhibitions in Iran, Italy and France, as well as in international exhibitions at venues including the Saatchi Gallery in London and exhibitions in the United States, Germany and Spain.
The Fletcher exhibitions were established in memory of Fletcher Dyer, with the aim of continuing his legacy of addressing social and political issues through art. The annual exhibition provides an international platform for artists whose works engage with contemporary social and political themes.
This year’s exhibition features works selected by Burke, who serves as the juror and curator of the 13th edition. The Fletcher Exhibition awards ceremony is scheduled to take place on September 4 at Fishman Gallery.

Duncan Macmillan’s “People, Places and Things” on stage at Art Palace
TEHRAN – The play “People, Places and Things” by the British playwright Duncan Macmillan is currently on stage at Art Palace in Tehran.
Masoumeh Beygi has translated and directed the 75-minute play. She also performs in the play along with Hamidreza Bodaghi, Sara Sajadi, Iman Sayad Borhani, Reza Karimi, Navid Askari, Shayan Mohammadi, and Pouria Nikkhah.
Duncan Macmillan’s intoxicating hit play is about Emma, a struggling actress whose life is spinning recklessly out of control.
Emma, a talented theatre actress, collapses during rehearsals for a staging of “The Seagull” by Chekhov, due to the abuse of alcohol and drugs; the company she works for dismisses her and requires her to detox in order to return to acting. Unwillingly, Emma checks in a rehabilitation clinic, initially determined to stay there only for the time necessary to be declared clean and return to work, but she ends up staying there for several months.
Emma was having the time of her life. Now she’s in rehab. Her first step is to admit that she has a problem. But the problem isn’t with Emma, it’s with everything else. She needs to tell the truth. But she’s smart enough to know that there’s no such thing. When intoxication feels like the only way to survive the modern world, how can she ever sober up?
The play is a harrowing look at drug and alcohol addiction and recovery. Its writing was prompted by Macmillan's desire to write a leading part for an actress: he has said he “wrote this play believing very strongly that there were a lot of brilliant actresses who just weren't getting parts that would push them and that they could excel in.”
“People, Places and Things” will remain on stage until October 7 at the Art Palace, located at No. 50, Zand-e-Vakil Alley, Razi St., Neauphle le chateau St., Hafez Ave.

Iranian movie, filmmaker participating in 39th Herceg Novi Film Festival
TEHRAN – An Iranian film and a filmmaker are attending the 39th Herceg Novi Film Festival, which kicked off on Saturday in Montenegro.
The documentary “Nazul,” written, directed, and produced by Yousef Ghanati is competing for the Golden Mimosa award in the main competition section of the festival, IRNA reported.
A 2026 production, the 27-minute film, which is Ghanati’s debut film, depicts Sepehr, a village boy gifted with a beautiful voice and a great passion for singing, who attempts to apply for a talent show, facing numerous obstacles along the way.
The two-time Oscar winner, Iranian director and screenwriter Asghar Farhadi, is also a guest at the 39th Herceg Novi Film Festival. Farhadi will attend the screening of his latest film, “Parallel Tales,” which will take place on Sunday at Forte Mare Fortress.
Farhadi will also hold a special masterclass on Tuesday as part of the Montenegro Film Rendezvous industry program, organized by the Film Centre of Montenegro. The masterclass will take place at Park Hall, with Vuk Perović serving as moderator.
The film “Parallel Tales” was produced by the French production company Memento Production in 2026 and has a runtime of 139 minutes. The film was screened at this year’s Cannes Film Festival.
Asghar Farhadi, 54, began making films as a teenager, joining the Isfahan Young Cinema Society in 1986, where he made short films on 8mm and 16mm. He graduated in Dramatic Arts from the University of Tehran in 1998 and, several years later, earned a master’s degree in Theatre Direction, with a thesis devoted to Harold Pinter and the significance of silence and pauses in his dramatic writing.
He made his directorial debut with “Dancing in the Dust” (2002), and gained international recognition with “About Elly” (2009), for which he received the Silver Bear for Best Director at the Berlinale. This was followed by “A Separation” (2011), which received more than seventy awards, including the Academy Award and César Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
He shot “The Past” (2013) in France, with Bérénice Bejo winning the Best Actress award at Cannes for her performance. With “The Salesman” (2016), he won the awards for Best Screenplay and Best Actor at Cannes, as well as his second Academy Award, while “A Hero” (2021) received the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival.
The Herceg Novi Film Festival is the most significant film festival in Montenegro, running for over three decades. The festival has been accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (Fédération Internationale des Associations de Producteurs de Films – FIAPF), becoming part of the global network of the world most prestigious international film festivals.
The primary aim of the festival is to promote regional and world cinema, with a particular focus on creating space for female and male filmmakers and films that nurture an authentic artistic sensibility, a courageous approach to social reality, cinematic language and production, with an emphasis on presenting a cross-section of contemporary poetics and forms of expression.
As part of the festival, Montenegro Film Rendezvous is held, organized by the Film Centre of Montenegro — a film industry event dedicated to strengthening ties between the Montenegrin and European film industries, and to supporting the career development of Montenegrin filmmakers and film professionals.
Having launched on August 22, this year’s edition of the festival will run until August 28 in the coastal city of Herceg Novi.

The constants and variables in the political dynamics of West Asia
LONDON — The policy of the West Asia region is drawn based on political dynamics. These are either constants that are not subject to change or variables. This is especially with regard to the political situation in Lebanon and Syria, and the regional or international sponsorship of political directions.

The second constant is the Turkish-Israeli competition over influence in Syria, regulated so that it does not reach an armed conflict. The third constant is that the final decision on Syria’s future rests with Turkey. The fourth constant is the project of the New Middle East and "Greater Israel" that has ended with no return, because it failed on every front.

The second variable is that if this matter is accomplished, Iran and its allies will be recognized, and their presence will be considered legitimate. This includes the Lebanese resistance movement Hezbollah, Yemen’s Ansarullah, and likewise the balancing of the situation in Iraq.
The third variable is that the Turkish-Israeli conflict over Syria has not yet reached a final result. The fourth variable is between the Turkish-Syrian role and the Saudi role in Lebanon, with boundaries that have not yet become clear. The fifth variable is the scope of the Israeli-Turkish conflict over Syrian territory and Lebanon, which has yet to become clear, as the Trump administration has not yet reached a final decision on the matter.
As a result of these constants and variables, we can draw the first conclusion: the relationship between the Lebanese resistance movement and Syria’s Al-Sharaa is largely governed by the Iranian-Turkish relationship. Turkey considers its national security to begin in Beirut and views the Lebanese resistance movement’s existence as a factor that keeps the Israeli occupation entity preoccupied. Secondly, in the Israeli-Lebanese relationship, America will pass whatever is agreed upon by the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, through the framework agreement between the Israeli occupation entity and Lebanon. It is now suspended, but when it is implemented, America will impose on the Israeli occupation entity withdrawal from all of Lebanon regardless of the course of the framework agreement. Thirdly, there will likely be Turkish-Saudi competition in Lebanese internal affairs. Generally, decision-making in Beirut is largely influenced by Saudi Arabia; in the north, particularly Tripoli and Akkar, it is shaped by Turkish-Syrian interests; and in the south, the Lebanese resistance movement holds the decisive influence.

Fifth, the Israeli occupation entity will contract to the boundaries of historic Palestine of 1948, and America will force it to withdraw from Syria. Otherwise, a resistance movement is expected to form in Syria in the face of the Israeli occupation.
Sixth, Iran's control over the Strait of Hormuz will impose all these equations.
Seventh, the Iran will become an urgent necessity for the Persian Gulf states and for all countries whose economies are affected by the Strait of Hormuz.
Eighth, the coming phase is the phase of recognition of Iranian influence in the region, and it is an Iranian phase par excellence.

Iran condemns US plans to announce new sanctions
Iran on Saturday denounced US plans to announce new sanctions that could put further strain on the Islamic Republic's economy and have an impact on its most important trading partners including China.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Monday after threatening "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran.
Bessent has also urged cooperation with Washington by China, which buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Beijing has urged diplomacy.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said on Saturday the imminent U.S. announcement of new economic sanctions was an "assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations."
"Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law," he said in a post on X.
The chief of staff of Iran's armed forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi, promised on Friday that Iran would respond to enemy threats militarily with "crushing, punishing and devastating responses.”
US President Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences against any country that provides "any type of lifeline to Iran," said on Friday that Washington was observing "what happens" in the conflict.
"They would love to make a deal, but they're not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion," Trump said of Iran.
HORMUZ TRAFFIC HALTED

Only four commodity ships sailed along the strait on Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, ship-tracking data showed.

Qalibaf, who did not say which countries he was referring to, accused the U.S. of endangering the security of its allies in the region for the sake of Israel, adding that an independent, "homegrown" regional order would deliver peace and security.
Trump, meanwhile, has yet to achieve objectives he set at the start of the war such as dismantling Iran's nuclear programme - the state of which remains uncertain given that U.N. inspectors have been shut out since 2025 - and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
Thousands have been killed, mainly in Iran, where 168 Iranian school children were killed on the first day of the war. The U.S. has reported more than 750 military personnel wounded and 18 killed.

What follows Kushner’s meetings with al-Hayya and Netanyahu?
TEHRAN – Gaza remains caught between Israeli intransigence and electoral calculations, U.S. pressure, and Palestinian efforts to preserve the agreement. This is keeping the region in a state of neither war nor peace until the outcome of the upcoming elections becomes clear.
Jared Kushner, the U.S. presidential envoy and “Peace Council” member, met with the Palestinian delegation led by Khalil al-Hayya, head of Hamas’s political bureau, in Cairo. He also held a four-hour meeting with Netanyahu in Tel Aviv. The talks focused on advancing the roadmap for the Gaza agreement, a 15-point framework that the Palestinians had accepted, and the Israeli regime had rejected.
Kushner pledged to al-Hayya that he would pressure Netanyahu to give the agreement a chance to succeed, after the Palestinian leader reportedly told him: “Your turn has come. We have negotiated at length; now it is your time to act and pressure the occupying forces.”
Al-Hayya refused to even discuss reopening negotiations or revisiting the agreement’s provisions. Kushner came away with a positive impression of the Palestinian position, but he failed to make any breakthrough with Netanyahu. The reason is clear: the upcoming Israeli elections and the declining prospects of the regime’s coalition government winning, according to public opinion polls.
The agreement and Netanyahu’s electoral calculations
It is clear that Kushner’s visit did not produce a substantive breakthrough. However, it did demonstrate to the United States how difficult it will be to move forward with implementing the agreement at a time when the occupying regime’s commitment is required, while an election campaign is pushing Netanyahu toward greater rigidity and escalation on multiple fronts.
What Netanyahu has accomplished is showcasing his hardline stance that does not yield to American pressure, bolstering his standing among his extreme right-wing base.

The Israelis, however, insist that both light and heavy weapons held by Palestinian resistance forces must be dismantled before any IOF withdrawal or reconstruction of the Palestinian territory can begin.
The gap between the position of the mediators and Palestinians, on the one hand, and the regime’s position, on the other, appears to be widening. Despite recognizing how difficult it would be to achieve a breakthrough in the regime’s position at this stage, no one has an interest in declaring the agreement dead.
The Palestinian side has succeeded in backing Netanyahu into a corner, leaving him looking as though he is taking punches, even if they are soft ones, from one of his closest allies, the United States.
This is in addition to the explicit condemnations from the eight mediating and guarantor states. Those condemnations had largely faded before the last agreement was reached despite relentless IOF violations. Now, international censure of the regime has resumed, and Gaza has once again taken center stage on the global agenda.
Netanyahu, by contrast, is not concerned with the broader picture, including the regime’s growing isolation internationally and the reported decline in its relationship inside the United States, as well as the deteriorating relations between Netanyahu and Trump.
What Netanyahu wants is simple: to win the election, or, at the very least, to prevent the Israeli opposition from being able to form the next government and from reaching the 61 number of seats in the Knesset (Parliament). Either he wins, or he remains as head of a transitional government preparing for new elections, a scenario that appears increasingly likely in the upcoming Israeli political landscape.
The Palestinian position in the face of Israeli intransigence
The Palestinians understand that showing greater flexibility and agreeing to reopen the latest agreement for negotiations would allow Netanyahu to carry out every form of aggression against Gaza without restraint, criticism, or pressure, under the pretext that negotiations are still ongoing.
The Palestinians would then be portrayed as the ones refusing and obstructing progress, while pressure would once again be placed on them to show greater flexibility. For this reason, the Palestinian delegation is likely to remain committed to its position: there will be no renegotiation of what has already been agreed upon.
The Palestinians understand that the Israeli position on weapons and its refusal to begin reconstruction and withdrawal before disarmament means that the regime will neither withdraw from Gaza nor allow reconstruction to begin.
Gaza could therefore remain as it is for many years, with no one knowing when the situation will end. The Netanyahu regime will find sufficient pretexts to exploit the issue of weapons and evade its commitments.
Moreover, Israel’s rejection of the agreement is consistent with its post-October 7 policy, which rejects containment and deterrence strategies and refuses to return to the pre-war rules of engagement.
Instead, it seeks to impose a new reality across all fronts that grants it the right to continue its policies of assassinations, airstrikes, and aggression, as seen in the massacre that killed seven in Gaza port, the targeting of police commanders in Gaza following Kushner’s visit, recent strikes on Syria, and the aggression on Lebanon that resulted in casualties.
The message is clear: the regime will continue what it calls “eliminating threats” and maintaining “freedom of security” operations across the region, whether an agreement exists or not.
Despite the high costs, which the occupying regime is paying diplomatically and economically, the declining sense of security among settlers, the military’s near-permanent state of alert, and the ongoing uncertainty stemming from its failure to achieve absolute victory or any decisive military outcome, Israel believes its current policy is producing only tactical and temporary losses that can eventually be addressed and repaired.
However, various Israeli figures and institutions see the current path itself as a strategic loss, one for which Netanyahu’s government bears responsibility. They argue that the government has failed to translate military achievements into political results. In their view, the regime lost strategically.
Neither agreement nor war
The current situation in Gaza and across the region is unlikely to undergo any meaningful changes before the end of the Israeli elections. There will be neither a genuine de-escalation nor a full-scale war, nor an agreement, nor a formal withdrawal from the agreement.
Although it is difficult to bet on a significant change in the regime’s position even if Netanyahu loses the election, all parties and actors have little choice but to get through the next two months, even if that means maintaining a fragile calm without a final settlement.
Netanyahu, however, wants a fragile escalation, raising the ceiling of his negotiating positions through heightened aggression short of full-scale war.
The question remains: Did Kushner understand Netanyahu’s domestic position and give him the green light to raise the level of escalation ahead of the Israeli elections?
Given the pattern of American positions, they have consistently offered their staunchest ally in West Asia every opportunity, cover, and unlimited support.
However, Trump has his own domestic calculations as well. He is seeking a foreign policy achievement after his massive blunder in Iran, making him more eager to advance the negotiation track, de-escalate, and reach an agreement in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.
The U.S. president has publicly called on Netanyahu to curb IOF attacks on Gaza, while his envoy Tom Barrack denounced the recent IOF assault on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria.
This suggests that, at this stage, U.S. policy in the region is seeking to limit Israeli military escalation, particularly on the Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria fronts. After successfully keeping the regime out of the current confrontation with Iran, where Tehran’s response had been seriously misjudged in Washington.
Yet the escalation of IOF aggression on all three fronts indicates that the United States has failed to impose its policy on the regime there.
Netanyahu may have reached an understanding with Kushner that gives the regime greater room for calculated escalation in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria in exchange for a commitment not to get engaged with Iran.
If so, the region will remain in a state of neither peace nor war, with controlled levels of escalation across all fronts, until the end of this year, when both the Israeli and American election results become clear.

America cannot turn a failed policy into a winning card

From broken promises to open war: The contradictions of Trump’s Iran policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:39:21 UTC
02:39:21 KST

From broken promises to open war: The contradictions of Trump’s Iran policy
Islamabad — There is a rhythm to Donald Trump’s approach toward Iran. A warning is issued. Markets react. Military assets move into position. Diplomats search for an opening. Then, just as confrontation appears inevitable, Washington steps back.
That pattern defined Trump’s first presidency. It followed Iran’s downing of a US surveillance drone over the Strait of Hormuz in 2019 and resurfaced after Iran’s missile strike on Al Asad Air Base in 2020. Trump’s rhetoric repeatedly suggested war was imminent. His decisions usually stopped short of it.
 
 His return to the White House changed the pattern.
 
 Diplomatic deadlines increasingly ended in military operations. Direct American strikes on Iranian territory followed economic pressure. Negotiations gave way to demands for “unconditional surrender,” before diplomacy returned amid an unresolved conflict.
 
 Read across a decade, Trump’s speeches and official statements reveal more than confrontational rhetoric. They trace the changing purpose of American pressure—from leverage, to deterrence, to military coercion, and ultimately direct war.
 
 For Tehran, one question grew harder to ignore: if Washington’s demands kept expanding while pressure never eased, where was diplomacy supposed to lead?
Tearing up the deal
Iran stood at the center of Trump’s foreign-policy vision long before he entered the White House.
 
 Speaking at the AIPAC Policy Conference in March 2016, Trump called the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) “disastrous” and pledged to dismantle it. He accused the Obama administration of empowering Tehran while failing to curb its missile program and regional influence.
 
 By September, the rhetoric had hardened further. Campaigning in Pensacola, Florida, he warned that Iranian vessels harassing US Navy ships “will be shot out of the water.”
 
 Once in office, he acted.
 
 On May 8, 2018, Trump withdrew the United States from the JCPOA and restored sanctions under the “maximum pressure” campaign. Washington argued that unprecedented economic pressure would force Tehran back to negotiations on American terms.
 
 Tehran reached the opposite conclusion.
 
 Iranian officials argued that Washington had abandoned an agreement negotiated over years, endorsed by the UN Security Council and repeatedly verified by the International Atomic Energy Agency. If one US administration could discard a signed agreement, they asked, why should another be trusted to honor a replacement?
 
 That question would shape every subsequent negotiation.
Pressure without war
By 2019, “maximum pressure” was colliding with events on the ground.
 
 Attacks on commercial shipping and a rocket strike near the US Embassy in Baghdad prompted Washington to deploy B-52 bombers, additional fighter aircraft and an aircraft carrier strike group. Trump warned that if Iran chose to “fight,” it would mean “the official end of Iran.”
 
 Weeks later, Iran shot down a US Global Hawk surveillance drone near the Strait of Hormuz.
 
 Trump approved retaliatory strikes, then cancelled them minutes before they were due to begin.
 
 He later explained that advisers had estimated roughly 150 Iranian casualties and that such a response would have been disproportionate to the loss of an unmanned aircraft.
 
 To many in Tehran, the episode exposed a recurring contradiction. Washington threatened force while insisting diplomacy remained its preferred option. Iranian officials argued that negotiations conducted under constant military pressure could never be negotiations between equals.
 
 The pattern resurfaced after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities. Trump declared the United States was “locked and loaded” but again chose reinforcement over retaliation.
 
 The major exception came in January 2020.
 
 Trump authorized the drone strike that martyred Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis near Baghdad International Airport. Washington described the operation as self-defense. Tehran condemned it as state terrorism.
 
 Five days later, Iran struck Al Asad Air Base with ballistic missiles.
 
 Trump again stepped back.
 
 Instead of escalating, he declared Iran “appears to be standing down” and said the United States was “ready to embrace peace with all who seek it.”
 
 Even in his final months in office, restraint remained visible. Reuters later reported that Trump examined military options against Iran’s Natanz enrichment facility before senior advisers argued against action.
 
 By January 2021, Washington had abandoned the nuclear agreement, imposed unprecedented sanctions, assassinated one of Iran’s most senior military commanders and repeatedly threatened military action.
 
 It had still stopped short of direct war.
From restraint to ‘hit the nuclear first’
After leaving office, Trump defended that record.
 
 He argued that his Iran policy had weakened Tehran while keeping America out of another Middle Eastern war. In the Bedminster recording later made public, he portrayed himself as the president who had restrained military advisers pressing for escalation.
 
 Three years later, campaigning for another term, he offered a different message.
 
 Asked whether Israel should strike Iran’s nuclear facilities, he replied:
 
 “Hit the nuclear first, and worry about the rest later.”
 
 For many in Tehran, the remark reinforced a growing belief that Washington’s objectives had moved beyond nuclear restrictions. Pressure itself had become the policy.
 
 The question would soon move from campaign rhetoric to presidential action.
Crossing the Rubicon
Trump’s second presidency began with diplomacy.
 
 In March 2025, he sent a letter to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei proposing negotiations while giving Tehran sixty days to respond. Indirect talks opened in Oman, even as Washington warned there would be “all hell to pay” if diplomacy failed.
 
 Iranian officials insisted that any agreement required guarantees Washington could no longer credibly provide after abandoning the JCPOA.
 
 The negotiations collapsed.
 
 Three days later, Israel launched large-scale strikes against Iranian nuclear and military facilities. Trump called the operation “excellent.”
 
 Soon afterwards came another phrase:“Unconditional surrender.”
 
 In Tehran, those words confirmed suspicions that Washington’s objectives had expanded beyond the nuclear file.
 
 Nine days later, American aircraft entered the war.
 
 Under Operation Midnight Hammer, B-2 bombers struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan. Trump declared Iran’s nuclear program had been “completely and totally obliterated.”
 
 For Tehran, the sequence mattered as much as the strikes.
 
 Washington had withdrawn from one agreement, imposed sweeping sanctions, reopened negotiations, coupled diplomacy with military ultimatums and then joined direct attacks after talks failed.
 
 The comparison with 2019 spoke for itself.
 
 Then, Trump cancelled strikes because casualties were judged disproportionate.
 
 Six years later, he authorized the largest direct American attack ever carried out against Iran’s nuclear infrastructure.
 
 Iran answered with missile strikes on Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar before a ceasefire ended the Twelve-Day War.
 
 The fighting paused.
 
 The policy did not.
 
 The New Objective
 
 The ceasefire created breathing space, not reconciliation.
 
 Regional governments resumed diplomatic efforts, but Washington’s language continued to evolve.
 
 During his first presidency, Trump insisted the United States was “not looking for regime change.” By late 2025, that distinction had blurred. American debate increasingly extended beyond Iran’s nuclear program to the future of the Islamic Republic.
 
 Inside Iran, the debate changed as well.
 
 Officials argued that Washington’s objectives now reached beyond limiting nuclear capabilities to reshaping Iran’s political order.
 
 When fighting resumed in early 2026, the United States and Israel launched a broader campaign. Trump increasingly framed the conflict in political terms, publicly questioning Iran’s leadership.
 
 Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei was martyred alongside senior military and security officials. The conflict widened across the region and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
 
 Even then, diplomacy returned.
 
 Negotiations resumed through regional intermediaries before fighting restarted. Tehran maintained that talks conducted under military coercion could not produce a lasting settlement.
 
 For Iranian policymakers, the pattern had become unmistakable. Each diplomatic initiative arrived under heavier sanctions, stronger military pressure and broader political demands than the one before.
When the rhythm changed
Donald Trump entered American politics promising to tear up a nuclear agreement.
 
 A decade later, he had presided over the first direct American strikes on Iran’s principal nuclear facilities.
 
 His own words trace the evolution.
 
 In 2016, the JCPOA was “disastrous.”
 
 In 2019, he warned of the “official end of Iran” before cancelling planned strikes.
 
 In 2020, he declared the United States was “ready to embrace peace.”
 
 By 2024, he argued that Israel should have “hit the nuclear first.”
 
 Months after returning to office, he demanded Iran’s “unconditional surrender.”
 
 There is a rhythm to Donald Trump’s approach toward Iran.
 
 For years, threats were followed by negotiations, negotiations by sanctions and military deployments, before Washington stepped back.
 
 The rhythm survived.
 
 What changed was the point at which Washington stopped stepping back.
 
 From Tehran’s perspective, the lesson was not simply that American policy became more forceful. It was that the space between diplomacy and coercion steadily disappeared. Every negotiation unfolded under greater sanctions, stronger military pressure and broader political demands than the last.
 
 That, more than any single speech or military operation, remains the defining contradiction of Trump’s Iran policy.
