Mainland Chinese research ship spotted near Taiwan’s largest naval base
The Tong Ji, operated by a Shanghai university, has a range of advanced equipment and can collect data that may have military uses
A mainland Chinese research ship has sailed close to a key Taiwanese naval base, marking its third appearance near the island since May.
The Tong Ji is a 2,000-tonne scientific research vessel operated by Tongji University in Shanghai. It was spotted 28 nautical miles (52km) southwest of Liuqiu, an island also known as Lamay, on Friday morning, according to the Taiwanese authorities.
Liuqiu sits off the southwest coast of Taiwan’s main island, close to the city of Kaohsiung – home to Taiwan’s naval academy and largest naval base.
The Taiwanese coastguard said they sent ships to monitor the Tong Ji’s movements and broadcast warnings ordering it to leave. They said the vessel had sailed away to the southeast.
On Thursday night, it had been spotted about 25 nautical miles northwest of Hua islet in the central Taiwan Strait. A coastguard vessel sent to shadow the mainland ship tried to force it to change course.
Commissioned in 2025, the Tong Ji is an advanced research ship designed for a wide range of scientific and engineering operations, including surveys, environmental monitoring and offshore engineering work, according to its operators.
In particular, the vessel can deploy remotely operated underwater and surface vessels and is equipped with a range of acoustic equipment, including a variety of sonar systems.

Pollard sets out plan for UK to win NATO manufacturing work
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:30:10 BST
18:30:10 KST

The Ministry of Defence is working through a series of NATO mechanisms to secure British industrial benefit from the alliance’s push to expand collective manufacturing capacity, Luke Pollard has told Parliament in a written answer.
The Minister of State for Defence was responding to James Cartlidge, the Conservative MP for South Suffolk, who asked what steps the department is taking to ensure UK defence manufacturers benefit from the new NATO commitment.
Mr Pollard said the department is “leveraging NATO mechanisms, including the Defence Production Action Plan, the NATO Defence Industrial Production Board, and the Innovation Scale-Up Package, to boost an aggregated demand, improve interoperability, strengthen supply chain resilience, and provide clearer long-term demand signals to industry.”
He said the Defence Industrial Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan reinforce that approach by supporting collaborative programmes with allies, listing deep precision strike, air defence, autonomous systems, munitions production, future combat air and anti-submarine warfare.
Those programmes, he said, help British firms “access new export and multinational procurement opportunities and take advantage of the shift to ‘always on production’.”
The phrase points at what has become the central problem of European rearmament, defence manufacturing has historically worked to intermittent orders, with production lines opened for a batch and then closed, an arrangement that keeps peacetime costs down but leaves no capacity to surge when demand rises. The war in Ukraine demonstrated how long it takes to reverse that, particularly in artillery ammunition, where output could not be raised quickly because plants had closed, tooling had been scrapped and specialist suppliers had left the sector.
Aggregated demand is the mechanism NATO is using to address it. If several allies commit to buying the same equipment on a predictable schedule, a manufacturer can justify investing in capacity that no single national order would support, and smaller states gain access to production they could not sustain alone.
The commercial question for British firms is whether they end up as prime contractors on those programmes or as suppliers into consortia led from elsewhere. European Union funding instruments for defence production have generally restricted or discounted participation by non-member states, and Britain’s access to them has been the subject of negotiation since 2024, which is part of why the answer emphasises NATO mechanisms rather than EU ones.
Mr Cartlidge served as Minister for Defence Procurement in the previous government and now shadows the defence brief.

Government still weighing decision on restricting proxy voters, Hong Kong official says
Proposed changes to law on buildings management meant to combat bid-rigging but limits to proxy votes could be too strict, home affairs director says
Hong Kong authorities have yet to decide whether to restrict proxy voters at homeowners’ meetings to relatives or other flat owners of the same estate under proposed law amendments meant to combat bid-rigging, the home affairs director has said, arguing such a move could be overly strict.
Director of Home Affairs Priscilla To Kit-lai said on Saturday the proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance were aimed at enhancing the legitimacy of proxy votes amid concerns that voting results could be manipulated by a minority.
But she said the government had yet to decide whether proxy holders should be limited to the owners’ relatives or other owners in the same estate.
“For example, an elderly person living alone might have a familiar friend in a different housing estate who helps the person – that’s acceptable now,” she said on a television programme.
“But it might not be possible if we add proposed restrictions. We need to see if society feels this is too strict.”
Issues of building management and owner governance came under intense scrutiny during an independent committee hearing looking into the cause of the devastating fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po that killed 168 people last November, with testimonies alleging bid-rigging and proxy vote collection.

Number of electric cars in Belarus up by 15,000 in January-July 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:27:00 UTC
18:27:00 KST

MINSK, 22 August (BelTA) – How the Belarusian nuclear power plant contributes to the development of electric transport was described to journalists by Belarusian Energy Minister Denis Moroz during the electric vehicle rally BelNPP – Clean Energy of Peaceful Atom, BelTA has learned.
The Belarusian nuclear power plant satisfies about 40% of the country’s total demand for electricity. So far it has generated more than 65.5 billion kWh of electricity. This result allows replacing the consumption of natural gas and thereby reducing the foreign currency burden on the Belarusian economy.
The construction of the nuclear power plant became one of the factors that gave momentum to the development of electric transport in the country. “The emergence of a reliable and stable source of electricity allowed working out approaches that stimulate the development of electric transport. Today more than 65,000 electric vehicles drive on the roads of Belarus. Compared to the same period of last year the indicator has almost doubled,” the energy minister said.
At the beginning of 2026 there were about 50,000 electric vehicles in the country. In more than six months their number grew by approximately 15,000.
The energy minister added: “The development of electric transport provides not only additional driving comfort, reduces noise and environmental burden, but also allows increasing the total economic effect: fuel consumption is reduced, which means the foreign currency burden on the economy decreases.”
In his words, Belarus is one of the leaders in the post-Soviet space in terms of the number of electric vehicles per capita. The country is also supposed to increase the fleet of electric vehicles to 300,000 by 2030 or to about 10% of the total number of automobiles.
Charging infrastructure is developing at the same time. “Just a few years ago Belarus had about 1,000 electric vehicle charging stations with a fleet of approximately 10,000-12,000 electric vehicles. Today there are already more than 65,000 electric vehicles, and the number of charging stations exceeds 2,700,” the minister said.
Since the beginning of 2026 the network has increased by approximately 500 stations. By 2030 the total number of electric vehicle charging stations is supposed to rise to 15,000.
“To ensure genuine comfort of traveling by electric vehicles, it is necessary to develop charging infrastructure not only within population centers, but also along motorways. Today charging stations are installed at almost all Belorusneft gas stations. Their number is not sufficient yet. Their workload is particularly high on weekends. However, there are state programs for the development of charging infrastructure, which include attracting additional operators. They will develop charging infrastructure on highways and install fast and super-fast charging stations,” Denis Moroz concluded.
The BelNPP – Clean Energy of the Peaceful Atom event is aimed at promoting Belarus’ achievements in nuclear power engineering, the role of the Belarusian nuclear power plant in developing eco-friendly segments of the economy, including electric vehicles. The event was organized by the Energy Ministry in partnership with the Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom with support from the Minsk City Executive Committee and the Ostrovets District Executive Committee.

U.S. Navy awards second CHAOS contract for cheap missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:26:24 UTC
18:26:24 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its Rusty Dagger cruise missile under the CHAOS program.
- The award follows a $70 million CHAOS contract the Navy gave CoAspire in July for its RAACM-ER maritime missile.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its AGM-188 Rusty Dagger cruise missile under a new program aimed at fielding low-cost precision weapons for the U.S. and its allies.
The award is an Other Transaction Agreement, a contracting mechanism the Pentagon uses to move faster than traditional acquisition rules allow. CMG Networks brokered the deal on behalf of the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium. Under the agreement, Zone 5 will design, build, test, and deliver a CHAOS-specific version of the Rusty Dagger for the Navy’s Coalition Heterogeneous Affordable Offensive Strike program, which is intended to field affordable, scalable precision strike weapons against land targets and moving maritime targets.
“Zone 5 is proud to partner with the Navy on CHAOS and deliver industry-best scalable maritime strike capabilities to the U.S. and our allies,” said Thomas Akers, CEO of Zone 5 Technologies.
Zone 5 is working on the effort with PAE Munitions and its Precision Strike Weapons program office, PMX-201, the company said. Zone 5 said it will draw on its experience fielding precision strike weapons across multiple service branches and international partners to provide a strike capability it described as credible, affordable, and scalable.
The award is the second CHAOS contract the Navy has issued for a low-cost maritime strike missile. In July, the Navy selected CoAspire for a $70 million agreement to develop a ground-launched maritime variant of its Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile-Extended Range, known as RAACM-ER, which has a claimed range of about 1,800 km (1,120 miles).
The Rusty Dagger, designated AGM-188A by the U.S. Air Force, originated as a low-cost cruise missile developed for the Air Force’s Extended Range Attack Munition program, which began in 2024 to address long-range strike requirements tied to Ukraine. The missile falls in the 200 kg (450 pound) weight class, including a roughly 45 kg (100 pound) warhead, and is powered by a single PBS Aerospace TJ80 turbojet engine. Its air-launched range is reported to exceed 930 km (500 nautical miles) at high subsonic speed. The missile is built within the size and weight envelope of a Mk 82 general-purpose bomb, allowing it to be carried by aircraft already equipped to drop that weapon.
The Rusty Dagger has already seen combat use. Zone 5 has said the missile is in production for Ukraine’s Air Force, and reporting on Russian territory has documented missile debris linked to Zone 5 through a recovered guidance antenna. The Air Force has separately selected Rusty Dagger for its Family of Affordable Mass Munitions program, which called for producing more than 1,000 units in its first year of production, according to Zone 5. The Air Force’s proposed fiscal 2027 budget outlined plans to buy nearly 28,000 Family of Affordable Mass Munitions rounds over five years. The Air Force Research Laboratory separately awarded Zone 5 a $12 million contract in June 2026 to develop manufacturing technology intended to scale Rusty Dagger production, with work centered in Miamisburg, Ohio.
Zone 5 Technologies, based in San Luis Obispo, California, was acquired by Norway’s Kongsberg and now operates as a Kongsberg company. The company describes itself as an aerospace engineering and production firm focused on modular, open-architecture counter-UAS interceptors and affordable ground- and air-launched effects. Founded in 2011, Zone 5 employs more than 500 engineers, technicians, and support staff, with manufacturing operations in California, Texas, and Ohio.

The party of jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan filed a contempt petition against the government Saturday after authorities transferred the cricketer-turned-politician to a state-run hospital instead of the private facility ordered by the country’s top court, party officials said.
“The petition seeks action against the prime minister, law minister, information minister” and other government officials, said Naeem Panjutha, a legal adviser to Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party. He said the petition also calls for Khan to receive treatment at the private hospital designated by the court.
Khan, who remains highly popular in Pakistan, has been imprisoned since August 2023 on charges he says are politically motivated. His removal from office followed a fallout with the country’s powerful military. His arrest triggered massive nationwide protests, including attacks on military installations, and the perception that authorities had forcibly returned him to prison could reignite unrest.
A three-judge bench on Tuesday ordered the government to transfer Khan from Adiala Jail to Islamabad’s private Shifa International Hospital within two days for a medical examination.
Officials instead took Khan to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, or PIMS, overnight Friday for a brief checkup before returning him to jail. They did not give him access to his personal physician, which the party also cited as a breach of the court’s orders.
The PTI interprets the order as requiring Khan to remain under medical supervision until at least mid-September.
Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, who attended the examination at PIMS, told reporters that while her brother is physically fit, “Khan told me that he is being repeatedly tortured in prison.” The interior and law ministries, as well as jail authorities, did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters on the allegations of torture.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said Friday that Khan was examined at PIMS because of security risks.
Khan’s supporters had lined the streets of Islamabad overnight, and PTI leaders said the episode would intensify pressure on the government and boost preparations for a planned protest march on Sept. 27.

The United States and Iran traded defiant messages ahead of Monday’s expected announcement of new U.S. economic sanctions targeting Iran and potentially key trading partners such as China.
Nearly six months into the war, the two sides were no longer exchanging fire but had made little progress toward peace talks. Meanwhile, oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have virtually halted as Tehran seeks to preserve its leverage by threatening to strike unauthorized tankers attempting to pass through the strategic waterway.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to hold a news conference at 2:00 p.m. EDT (6:00 p.m. GMT) Monday, when he is expected to unveil what Washington has described as “the toughest sanctions in history” against Iran and urge China to cooperate with the United States.
China buys more than 80% of Iran’s seaborne oil exports, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Beijing has called for diplomacy and a negotiated resolution.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Saturday that the expected U.S. sanctions announcement amounted to an “assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations.”
“Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law,” he said in a post on X.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences for any country that provides “any type of lifeline to Iran,” said Friday that Washington was watching “what happens” in the conflict.
“They would love to make a deal, but they’re not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion,” Trump said of Iran.
While the U.S. has effectively blockaded Iranian vessels in their ports, the Strait of Hormuz remained bottled up, with thousands of seafarers stranded on hundreds of vessels. Only four commodity ships sailed through the strait Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, according to ship-tracking data.
However, Iran has granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported Saturday.
IRNA said obtaining special permission for Iraqi tankers was one of Baghdad’s main requests during Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf’s visit to Iraq.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the U.S. military helped move a seven-day average of 8 million barrels of oil a day through the strait. That is down from more than 20 million barrels a day before the war, or about one of every five barrels consumed worldwide.
U.S. attacks have severely damaged Iran’s economy and devastated its navy and air force, but Tehran maintains enough missile and drone capabilities to impede oil tanker traffic and attack regional rivals.
Trump, meanwhile, has yet to achieve objectives he set at the start of the war, such as dismantling Iran’s nuclear program. The status of the program remains uncertain because U.N. inspectors have been shut out since 2025. Trump has also sought to create conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
Thousands have been killed, including 168 Iranian schoolchildren on the first day of the war. The U.S. has reported more than 750 military personnel wounded and 18 killed.
The chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, promised Friday that Iran would respond to enemy threats militarily with “crushing, punishing and devastating responses.”
Still, President Masoud Pezeshkian called for a diplomatic solution.
“It would be better to end the war today, when we are powerful and have dignity, and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals and infrastructure and is hated in the world,” Pezeshkian said, according to the ISNA news agency.
Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, the country’s main negotiator in mediated talks with the U.S., acknowledged the strain on Iran’s economy in comments to Iranian and Iraqi businesspeople late Thursday.
“No matter how much military power we have, we won’t survive if people are hungry and we don’t have financial turnover, economic growth and national production,” Qalibaf said, according to the official IRNA news agency.

DRC gets 16,520 Ebola vaccine doses amid deadly outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

The Democratic Republic of Congo has received its first shipment of more than 16,000 doses of an Ebola vaccine as authorities race to contain an outbreak that has killed more than 2,500 people and is spreading rapidly across six provinces.
A batch of 16,520 doses of the Ervebo vaccine arrived in Kinshasa late Friday, Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said, with more than 50,000 additional doses expected by Monday.
“These doses would strengthen the government’s response to Ebola and contribute to the protection of populations, with the support of our partners,” Kamba told reporters at Kinshasa airport.
The World Health Organization said Thursday that 70,000 doses of Ervebo would be supplied to Congo from the global Ebola vaccine stockpile. Of those, 20,000 doses will be used in a Phase 3 clinical trial examining whether the vaccine can protect against the strain responsible for the current outbreak, while 50,000 will be administered to frontline and health workers.
The vaccine, developed by Merck and manufactured in Germany, is licensed and recommended for outbreaks caused by the Zaire strain of Ebola. The current outbreak, however, is being driven by the Bundibugyo strain, for which no vaccine or specific treatment has yet been approved.
Scientists do not yet know whether Ervebo provides protection against Bundibugyo. Early evidence, including animal studies, suggests it could offer some cross-protection, prompting WHO experts this month to recommend a large-scale human trial.
Kamba said Ervebo has been used extensively in previous Ebola outbreaks, including during the major epidemic that struck Congo and neighboring countries between 2018 and 2020.
“This vaccine has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak,” he said.
The latest outbreak, Congo’s 17th, was officially declared May 15 but is believed to have been spreading for weeks before that. It has reached 56 health zones across Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo provinces, many of which face severe health care shortages, limited government presence and persistent insecurity involving armed groups.
The Health Ministry’s latest situation update puts the number of confirmed infections at 5,290, including more than 2,500 deaths.
The outbreak is showing no signs of slowing. Julien Harneis, the United Nations’ senior Ebola coordinator, warned Friday that the epidemic is “growing exponentially.”
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, also warned that communities affected by the outbreak are not receiving enough support to contain the virus.
The group said training for health workers and community leaders must be urgently expanded, particularly on detecting suspected cases, referring patients and preventing and controlling infections within communities.
The uncertainty surrounding the Bundibugyo strain has increased the urgency of developing targeted vaccines. Two candidates are already in clinical trials, one developed by U.S.-based Moderna using mRNA technology and another by the University of Oxford in Britain.
A separate vaccine known as rVSV Bundibugyo is also being developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories and has been described by WHO as the most promising candidate specifically targeting the strain.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids and can cause severe fever and other life-threatening symptoms. The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past five decades.

Terrorists kill, kidnap worshippers during Friday prayers in Nigeria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

Terrorists attacked two villages in central Nigeria’s Niger State during Friday prayers, killing and kidnapping an unknown number of people before a rival militant group intervened and triggered a clash that allowed some residents to escape, survivors and a lawmaker told AFP on Saturday.
The attack took place Friday in Dikera village and nearby Binzi in Borgu Local Government Area, an area in western Niger state near Nigeria’s borders with Kebbi and Kwara states and neighboring Benin. The region has faced growing attacks by armed groups operating across the porous borders of Nigeria’s northwestern states and the Sahel.
Jibril Ahmad, a survivor of the attack in Dikera, said hundreds of fighters belonging to the Lakurawa militant group stormed the village shortly after worshippers finished Friday prayers.
“Soon after finishing the normal Friday prayer, the armed group of Lakuwara, in their hundreds, wielding guns, knives and machetes, began to attack us,” Ahmad told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
He said the attackers killed some residents while accusing them of failing to follow what the militants described as the “true teachings.”
Federal lawmaker Jafaru Mohammed, who represents the area, confirmed that Binzi was also attacked. He said numerous people were killed and many others were abducted and taken into surrounding forests, including areas toward Kainji Lake.
The victims reportedly included young men and heads of households. Local accounts also said a chief imam and a village head who had recently been released from captivity were among those abducted.
The exact death toll and number of people taken remained unclear Saturday. Ahmad and Mohammed could not provide a precise figure, while Niger state police said they were aware that worshippers had been kidnapped but had not received reports of deaths at the time of their initial statement.
Police also said difficult terrain and poor roads were complicating efforts to reach the affected communities and mount rescue operations.
The violence took an unexpected turn when fighters from another militant faction, known as Mahmuda or Mamudawa, confronted the Lakurawa attackers.
Ahmad said many residents managed to flee while Lakurawa fighters were occupied fighting their rivals.
Mohammed said Mahmuda members intervened after learning about the assault and clashed with Lakurawa because of differences between the two groups. The confrontation gave some villagers an opportunity to escape, although many others were already being led into nearby forests.
Lakurawa, also spelled Lakuwara or Lukarawa, is a relatively shadowy Terrorist organization that has operated in northwestern Nigeria and across parts of the Sahel. Researchers have linked the group to Daesh Sahel Province, which operates in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
The group first emerged in communities along Nigeria’s northwestern border around 2017 and initially presented itself in some areas as a force against banditry. It has since developed into a militant organization accused of imposing strict religious rules, carrying out attacks, seizing livestock and abducting civilians.
Nigerian authorities designated Lakurawa a terrorist organization in late 2024. Its activities have added another layer to a security crisis already involving Terrorists, criminal gangs and armed groups operating in remote forests.
Mahmuda is another militant faction that has operated in the region. Nigerian authorities claimed in 2025 that they had dismantled Mahmuda and the related Ansaru group following arrests of senior members. Reports of Mahmuda fighters taking part in Friday’s clash, however, suggest that elements of the group remain active or that its networks have survived earlier operations.
The attack highlights the increasingly fragmented nature of Nigeria’s long-running insurgency.
Nigeria has battled Terrorist violence for roughly 17 years, with the conflict initially concentrated in the northeast, where Boko Haram and Daesh West Africa Province have carried out attacks, mass kidnappings and other abuses.
Mass abductions became one of the conflict’s defining tactics, most notoriously in 2014, when Boko Haram kidnapped hundreds of schoolgirls from the northeastern town of Chibok.
The violence has since spread beyond the northeast as Terrorist factions, criminal gangs and Sahel-based militants have exploited weak security, porous borders and vast forested areas where government forces have limited reach.
Niger state and neighboring areas have become increasingly vulnerable as armed groups move through border communities and use remote forests as hideouts. The security situation has also been complicated by instability in the wider Sahel, including the 2023 military coup in neighboring Niger, which disrupted established regional security arrangements.

Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack

Breadcrumb
Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack
Somali pirates hijacked an oil products tanker off Yemen, a Somali maritime security official said, the latest in a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
Six armed pirates hijacked the Eritrean-flagged M.T. Sibu 1 on Thursday about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometers) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen, and took it toward Somalia’s Puntland coast, the official, who has knowledge of the incident, told The Associated Press on Friday.
He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not allowed to discuss the matter publicly.
The Sibu 1, managed by the UAE-based Qatrat Alnada Almasi Ship Management, was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year for allegedly belonging to an Iranian “shadow fleet” used to transport petroleum products seeking to evade U.S. sanctions.
The tanker had 20 crew members aboard: 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi. The nationality of one crew member was not immediately known. The vessel’s previous port of departure and intended destination remained unclear.
The hijacking came three days after pirates seized the Lutuf, a Cameroon-flagged general cargo vessel, off Somalia’s coast. The vessel had 10 crew aboard, including six Indians, a Turkish national, a Georgian national and two Serbian security guards, according to maritime tracking reports.
The Sibu 1 is the sixth commercial vessel hijacked by Somali pirates since April 21, when the Palau-flagged tanker Honor 25 was seized off Somalia. Pirates later seized the Sward on April 26, the Eureka on May 2, the Asana on July 17 and the Lutuf on Aug. 17.
The attacks have occurred increasingly far from Somalia’s coastline, including the hijacking of the Eureka while anchored off Yemen and the Asana about 65 nautical miles (120 kilometers) southwest of al-Mukalla.
The International Maritime Bureau recorded 38 piracy and armed robbery incidents worldwide during the first half of 2026, including five hijackings. Somali pirates accounted for 94% of crew members taken hostage during that period, the bureau said.
Puntland’s Security Ministry said Friday that its investigations indicated that forces beyond Puntland’s control were behind the renewed piracy, but did not identify any group or country. The claim could not be independently verified.
Puntland said it had deployed security forces along its coast and condemned airstrikes that it said struck fishing vessels and property near coastal communities where hijacked ships were being held. It called on the countries involved to explain strikes near Garacad on Aug. 18 and Aug. 20.
The ministry did not identify who carried out the strikes, and the allegations could not be independently confirmed.

Canada orders more RS4 weapon systems for ACSV fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:02:25 UTC
18:02:25 KST

- Kongsberg signed a NOK 1.1 billion, about $118 million, follow-on contract with GDLS-Canada to supply PROTECTOR RS4 weapon systems for Canada's ACSV fleet.
- The RS4 order builds on a roughly NOK 500 million contract from May 2020 and comes as Canada has ordered 190 additional ACSVs in 2026.
Kongsberg has signed a contract worth NOK 1.1 billion, about $118.4 million, to supply additional PROTECTOR RS4 Remote Weapon Systems to General Dynamics Land Systems-Canada for the Canadian Army’s Armoured Combat Support Vehicle program.
The Norwegian defense company said the deal is a follow-on order building on previous RS4 deliveries for the same program. Kongsberg first won a contract worth roughly NOK 500 million in May 2020 to supply PROTECTOR remote weapon stations for the ACSV fleet, according to prior reporting.
“This contract confirms our customer’s confidence in the PROTECTOR systems and further strengthens our long-term partnership with GDLS-Canada,” said Kjetil Reiten Myhra, Executive Vice President, Kongsberg and President of the Defence Systems division.
“We are proud that the RS4 continues to be selected as a key capability for the Canadian Armed Forces’ modern vehicle fleet.”
The RS4 is a remotely operated weapon station that lets a vehicle crew fire from inside the hull rather than exposing a gunner in an open turret. It can be equipped with machine guns, automatic grenade launchers, and, on some configurations, anti-tank guided missiles. The system uses a stabilized, four-axis mount and sensor package designed to let a crew engage targets accurately while the vehicle is moving. Kongsberg said the RS4 is already fielded with defense customers worldwide and can be integrated across a range of vehicle types.
The Armoured Combat Support Vehicle is a family of eight variants built on the LAV 6.0 chassis, including ambulance, command post, and mobile repair versions. The Canadian government approved the 360-vehicle, $2.52 billion program in 2019, and GDLS-Canada has produced the vehicles at its plant in London, Ontario. The Army accepted its first ACSV in December 2020, and the program reached Initial Operational Capability in January 2025 with the delivery of the Troop/Cargo, Ambulance, and Command Post variants. Full Operational Capability is planned for 2028.
Canada donated 39 Troop/Cargo Vehicle variants originally built for its own fleet to Ukraine, with GDLS-Canada replacing those vehicles under the existing contract. As of August 2024, the Army had received 34 of a planned 49 ambulance variants.
Not every ACSV in the fleet carries an RS4. A Canadian Army official told Canadian Army Today in a report published in December 2024 that the service had been able to buy only 178 of the weapon stations due to cost and availability, even though every vehicle in the fleet is built to accept one. Vehicles without an RS4 instead carry a pintle-mounted C6A1 machine gun. The Canadian Department of National Defence told Shephard Media in February 2026 that it expected final deliveries of the existing RWS order that summer.
Canada has also moved to expand the overall ACSV fleet. The Army ordered 190 additional ACSVs this year to replace aging support vehicles and support NATO operations, according to a July 2026 report. Kongsberg’s announcement did not specify how many additional RS4 units are covered under the new NOK 1.1 billion contract or say whether the order is tied to that fleet expansion.

Shipbuilding now two thirds of Scotland’s defence jobs
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:53 BST
18:00:53 KST

Shipbuilding and submarine work accounted for 7,900 of the 12,200 jobs supported by Ministry of Defence spending with industry in Scotland in 2024/25, according to official statistics published on Friday, a rise of nearly 18 per cent on the previous year.
The figure represents close to two thirds of the Scottish total, and the increase of 1,200 jobs from 6,700 accounts for the bulk of the 800 net rise in defence industry employment across Scotland over the same period.
Other construction supported 800 jobs, with weapons and ammunition at 200 and aircraft and spacecraft also at 200.
The National Armaments Director Group attributed the concentration to the two frigate programmes, stating that the Type 26 supports 2,000 jobs at BAE Systems’ Govan and Scotstoun yards on the Clyde, while the Type 31 accounts for 1,250 directly employed at Babcock’s Rosyth yard in Fife.
Those two programmes therefore account for around 3,250 of the 7,900, with the balance spread across submarine support at Faslane, supply chain work and the wider marine engineering base.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “From investing in naval shipbuilding expertise on the Clyde and at Rosyth, to our nuclear deterrent and submarine support at Faslane, to our world-leading strengths in cyber, space, advanced radar and electronic warfare, we are supporting thousands of jobs and opening exciting career pathways for young Scots.”
The department also points to Norway’s £10 billion Type 26 order, which it says will sustain over 2,000 jobs and support more than 100 Scottish businesses including over 50 small and medium-sized enterprises.
A defence industrial base weighted this heavily towards two frigate programmes is exposed to what happens when they finish, a point made forcefully this week at Ferguson Marine, where the Port Glasgow yard opened a voluntary redundancy programme covering up to 70 staff as work on the ferry Glen Rosa winds down and its BAE Systems subcontract work concludes.
Graeme Downie, the MP whose constituency covers Rosyth, has been pressing the department to confirm that the planned Common Combat Vessel will use the Type 31 hull and be built at the Fife yard, an argument about precisely this problem.
Across the United Kingdom, MOD expenditure with industry totalled £31.9 billion in 2024/25, supporting 274,000 jobs.

NASA Cancels Its Rescue Mission for the Aging Swift Telescope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The Swift space observatory has been in operation since 2004. It specializes in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most energetic electromagnetic explosions known in the universe. Its original mission was supposed to last just two years. More than two decades later, it continues to explore some of the most violent phenomena in the cosmos. Now it is nearing the end of its life.
Swift doesn’t have a propulsion system capable of significantly raising its orbit. Although it is hundreds of kilometers above the Earth’s surface, there are still atmospheric particles at that altitude that exert a small but constant drag on the satellite. With each orbit around Earth, it loses a tiny amount of energy and, little by little, altitude as well. If this process continues without intervention it will eventually reenter the atmosphere.
NASA knew that Swift had limited time left. Some models had indicated that the observatory could remain in orbit until the 2030s, but increased solar activity during 2024 changed those projections. Energy from the sun heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Estimates eventually placed its likely reentry before the end of 2026.
Faced with the rapid deterioration of Swift’s orbit, NASA decided to attempt a rescue maneuver straight out of a movie. The plan was simple in concept but astonishingly complex to execute. A robotic mission would catch up to Swift, capture it with mechanical arms, and use its own thrusters to raise the observatory to a safer orbit, where it could continue operating. To do this, NASA turned to the company Katalyst Space Technologies and its LINK spacecraft.
LINK was launched into space on July 3, 2026. However, problems arose soon after. The spacecraft suffered failures in its attitude control system, which is responsible for keeping it properly oriented and stable in space. For weeks, engineers worked to regain control.
On Wednesday, NASA canceled the rescue mission. In a statement, agency administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the decision was due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system. LINK will no longer capture Swift or raise its orbit. The spacecraft will continue to approach the observatory to conduct demonstrations of rendezvous, navigation, and close-proximity operations. The agency hopes to use this attempt to gather information that can be applied to future missions aimed at repairing, relocating, or extending the lifespan of satellites in orbit.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow,” Isaacman said in a press release.
The agency had warned from the outset that this was a high-risk mission. Swift was not built to be captured or repaired in orbit, while LINK was developed and launched against the clock in response to the observatory’s rapid descent.
“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” Isaacman noted.
Without an intervention to raise its orbit, Swift will continue to lose altitude until it reaches the denser layers of the atmosphere. During reentry, much of the observatory will be destroyed by intense heating and aerodynamic forces. It is still too early to determine exactly when and where this will occur.
For now, NASA estimates that Swift will likely reenter the atmosphere before the end of the year.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Supacat opens new UK production facility in Devon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:54:03 UTC
17:54:03 KST

- Supacat opened a new production facility, the Jones II Building, at its Devon headquarters, named for company co-founder Nick Jones.
- The company said the facility will expand production capacity but did not disclose its size, cost, or which vehicle programs will be built there.
Supacat has opened a new production facility at its headquarters in Devon, England, naming the building after company co-founder Nick Jones.
The British vehicle manufacturer said Maj. Gen. Chris King cut the ribbon at the opening, which the company described as marking the launch of a facility expansion. Supacat did not disclose the size of the new building, its construction cost, or a timeline for when full production would begin there.
Supacat said the facility, called the Jones II Building, will expand its production capacity. The company said this is intended to speed up delivery of tactical vehicles to the British Army and other military customers, though it did not specify which vehicle programs would be built at the new site or provide production figures.
Supacat was founded in 1981 by Nick Jones and David Clayton at Dunkeswell Aerodrome in Devon, initially developing high-mobility all-terrain vehicles. The company’s first major program came during the 1982 Falklands War, when the Ministry of Defence issued an urgent requirement for lightweight transport vehicles capable of operating in rugged terrain. Supacat has since built vehicles including the Jackal, a wheeled reconnaissance and fire support platform used by the British Army and RAF Regiment, and the All Terrain Mobility Platform, in service with British airborne forces since 1988. Supacat has operated as part of SC Group since 2015, alongside sister companies SC Innovation, Proteum, and Blackhill Engineering.
Supacat and Babcock International Group opened a separate new production facility, the Raglan Building at Babcock’s Devonport site in Plymouth, in 2024 to build 70 Jackal 3 vehicles for the British Army under a single-source contract. That contract could expand to as many as 240 vehicles if the British Army exercises an option, according to Babcock. Under that arrangement, Babcock builds 62 of the vehicles at Devonport, while Supacat builds the remaining eight at its own facilities. The Jones II Building announced this week is located at Supacat’s headquarters, separate from the Devonport site.
Supacat has faced financial pressure on other parts of its business over the past year and a half. SC Group Chief Executive Nick Ames said in April 2025 that several major banks had declined to provide the company with commercial accounts or loans due to internal policies restricting defense-related lending, which he said made it “almost impossible” to fund investment in British manufacturing. Separately, the company’s existing Jackal support contract with the Ministry of Defence was projected, as of August 2025, to expire in early 2026 without renewal, a lapse that could have put up to 150 jobs at Supacat’s Derbyshire facility at risk. It is not known whether that contract has since been renewed.
Lizzie Jones, Supacat’s Operations Director, said earlier this year that the company had several ongoing projects planned for 2026, including customer-specific vehicle programs and continued development of new vehicle designs, in addition to the new production facility.

Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack

Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack
MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Somali pirates hijacked an oil products tanker off Yemen, a Somali maritime security official said, the latest in a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
Six armed pirates hijacked the Eritrean-flagged M.T. Sibu 1 on Thursday about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometers) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen, and took it toward Somalia’s Puntland coast, the official, who has knowledge of the incident, told The Associated Press on Friday. He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not allowed to discuss the matter publicly.
The Sibu 1, managed by the UAE-based Qatrat Alnada Almasi Ship Management, was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year for allegedly belonging to an Iranian “shadow fleet” used to transport petroleum products seeking to evade U.S. sanctions.
The tanker had 20 crew members aboard: 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi. The nationality of one crew member was not immediately known. The vessel’s previous port of departure and intended destination remained unclear.
The hijacking came three days after pirates seized the Lutuf, a Cameroon-flagged general cargo vessel, off Somalia’s coast. The vessel had 10 crew aboard, including six Indians, a Turkish national, a Georgian national and two Serbian security guards, according to maritime tracking reports.
The Sibu 1 is the sixth commercial vessel hijacked by Somali pirates since April 21, when the Palau-flagged tanker Honor 25 was seized off Somalia. Pirates later seized the Sward on April 26, the Eureka on May 2, the Asana on July 17 and the Lutuf on Aug. 17.
The attacks have occurred increasingly far from Somalia’s coastline, including the hijacking of the Eureka while anchored off Yemen and the Asana about 65 nautical miles (120 kilometers) southwest of al-Mukalla. The International Maritime Bureau recorded 38 piracy and armed robbery incidents worldwide during the first half of 2026, including five hijackings. Somali pirates accounted for 94% of crew members taken hostage during that period, the bureau said.
Puntland’s Security Ministry said Friday that its investigations indicated that forces beyond Puntland’s control were behind the renewed piracy, but did not identify any group or country. The claim could not be independently verified.
Puntland said it had deployed security forces along its coast and condemned airstrikes that it said struck fishing vessels and property near coastal communities where hijacked ships were being held. It called on the countries involved to explain strikes near Garacad on Aug. 18 and Aug. 20.
The ministry did not identify who carried out the strikes, and the allegations could not be independently confirmed.

Why this is end of the line for Trump in Iran war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:49:10 UTC
17:49:10 KST

Donald Trump's declaration of an unprecedented economic war against Iran cannot be seen merely as a sign of the start of new economic pressure. This decision shows, more than anything else, that Washington, after months of military and sanctions pressure, is facing the narrowing of its effective options. Instead of finding new and decisive targets inside Iran, the United States has now shifted the scope of pressure beyond Iran's borders and is targeting countries, banks, and companies that still allow Tehran to trade and maintain financial access. In fact, Trump's new policy can be seen as an attempt to compensate for the failure of previous pressure; a shift from direct pressure on Iran to pressure on the network that allows Iran to circumvent sanctions.
Over the past years, the United States has placed almost all major sectors of Iran's economy on the sanctions list; from oil and petrochemicals to shipping, metals, the automotive industry, the Central Bank, financial networks, and various economic institutions. The Atlantic Council has also emphasized, in its review of sanctions on Iran, that almost all sectors of Iran's economy have been targeted by US sanctions.
Therefore, Washington's problem is no longer finding a sector of Iran's economy that has not been sanctioned; the problem is that each new sanction, compared with previous sanctions, does not necessarily create new and decisive pressure.
This is why Trump now speaks of an unprecedented economic war, but the main arena of this war is no longer only Iran. The United States wants to pressure foreign banks, shipping companies, oil buyers, trade intermediaries, and even governments that cooperate with Tehran.
This policy shift must also be seen in the context of recent military developments. Washington has turned to intensified economic pressure at a time when military pressure has failed to achieve the political goals the United States expected. If military power alone could have forced Tehran to accept Washington's demands, there would have been no need to declare a new "economic war."
It can therefore be said that Trump's new policy is a kind of change of playing field; the United States has not retreated from the military field to the economic field, but it is trying to complement insufficient military pressure with economic pressure.
In the view of Western experts, the problem is that Iran's economy, over several decades of sanctions, has gradually developed mechanisms to cope with these pressures. Informal trade networks, oil sales, financial intermediaries, the use of local currencies, and cooperation with non-Western partners are part of these mechanisms.
The biggest challenge to the new US policy is China. According to data from the company Kpler, cited in a recent Al Jazeera report, more than 80 percent of Iran's oil exports in 2025 have gone to China. A significant portion of this oil also goes to small Chinese refineries, and payments are made through small banks, trading companies in Hong Kong, and settlement in yuan.
This creates a serious problem for Washington. Sanctioning an Iranian company is fundamentally different from sanctioning a major Chinese bank. In the first case, the main cost falls on Iran; but in the second case, the United States enters into direct confrontation with one of the world's largest economies.
For this reason, as Bloomberg has reported, the United States has previously warned two major Chinese banks about the risk of secondary sanctions related to Iran, but has not yet sanctioned them directly.
Here one of the most important contradictions of Washington's sanctions policy becomes apparent. The power of US sanctions stems largely from the dominance of the dollar and broad access to the US financial system. But the extensive use of this very tool has encouraged target countries to find alternative paths.
Chatham House analyses show that the expansion of sanctions has contributed to deepening cooperation among countries such as Iran, China, and Russia and has pushed them toward creating payment and settlement routes that are less dependent on the dollar.
This means sanctions may create pressure in the short term, but in the long term they increase the incentive of target countries to reduce their dependence on the US financial system.
As a result, the tool Washington uses to preserve its economic power can gradually increase the incentive to create rival tools.
The main problem with Trump's new policy lies precisely here. The more the United States expands the scope of secondary sanctions, the greater the likelihood of colliding with the economic interests of major powers. Sanctioning buyers of Iranian oil can affect global oil supply and raise energy prices. Pressure on China can lead to a reaction from Beijing. Targeting foreign companies can also deepen the rift between the United States and its trading partners.
Washington therefore faces a difficult equation: to increase pressure on Iran, it must shift pressure onto other countries; but the larger this circle becomes, the higher the cost of implementing the policy for the United States itself.
The ultimate goal of US sanctions is not merely to reduce Iran's income; the main goal is to change Tehran's political behavior. But the experience of past years has shown that economic pressure does not necessarily lead to a change in political behavior. Iran can pay higher costs, change its trade routes, and expand economic cooperation with countries such as China and Russia. Even Chatham House has warned, in its examination of the consequences of sanctions, that broad pressure can help form parallel financial and trade networks; networks that ultimately reduce the effectiveness of the US sanctions tool. For this reason, the main question for Washington is no longer "what can be sanctioned against Iran?" but rather "how many other countries is the United States willing to enter into conflict with in order to close each of Iran's economic routes?"
If we place Trump's new policy alongside the military developments of recent months, a clearer picture emerges. After the experience of military pressure, the United States has now returned to sanctions; but this time almost all of Iran's economy has already been sanctioned, and to find new targets, Washington is forced to go after Iran's external network. This is the very point at which "maximum pressure" can turn into "costly pressure." The United States can increase economic pressure, but it cannot expand it indefinitely without cost. China stands in the way of this policy, Russia has greater incentive to cooperate with Tehran, and Iran itself has gained considerable experience over the years of sanctions in creating alternative routes.
Ultimately, Trump's new policy is less a sign of the discovery of a new economic weapon against Iran than a sign of the narrowing of Washington's previous options. After military pressure failed to produce the expected result, the United States is now trying to continue the same pressure in the economic arena.
But this time there is one fundamental difference: the target is not only Iran. To isolate Tehran, the United States must also pressure China, financial networks outside the West, oil buyers, and international companies.
And this is precisely where the tables may turn; the sanctions that were supposed to isolate Iran can deepen Iran's cooperation with the East, increase the use of non-dollar currencies, and reduce the dependence of some countries on the US financial system.
Under such conditions, Trump's unprecedented economic war may be less the beginning of a new phase of pressure on Iran than a sign that US sanctions policy has reached the limits of its own power.
MNA

Canada retaliates as trade war with US escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:46:00 UTC
17:46:00 KST

(AFP photo)
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States, after walking away from a "bad deal" on trade in a deepening rift between the longtime allies.
Negotiations between the neighboring countries broke down on Aug. 21 in Washington, putting into force new 50 percent U.S. tariffs impacting about $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States.
Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement.
"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," Carney said.
U.S. President Donald Trump had said Washington "should be able to have a deal with Canada," citing his "good relationship" with Carney.
But on Aug. 22, Canada's prime minister said Trump set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable even though earlier talks had been positive.
"In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said in Ottawa.
"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked."
New Canadian tariffs will notably target the U.S. steel and dairy industries and take effect on Sept. 8. More details would come this week, Carney said.
A senior U.S. official characterized this week's talks in Washington as candid and not acrimonious.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News on Aug. 22 that Washington was "moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation." He also said no new talks were planned with Canadian negotiators.
Canada has been seeking relief from Trump's tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, which have battered the country's economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.
The White House had alleged "discriminatory treatment" by Canada against U.S. alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.
They were originally set to take effect on Aug. 19, before Trump issued a three-day reprieve citing progress in talks.
Carney said one reason the deal collapsed was U.S. negotiators at the 11th hour introducing restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries.
U.S. negotiators also made unacceptable "threats" to the French language and "Quebec culture," he said, referring to the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.
The escalating trade war was met with anger by Democratic lawmakers and governors from border states including Minnesota, New York and Washington, blaming Trump for triggering chaos that will raise costs on US businesses and families.
"Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That's Trump's economic policy in a nutshell," New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.
Beyond the latest tariffs, the U.S. and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew in its current form.
Trump's threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have also antagonized Canadians.
Carney has repeatedly said relations with the U.S. have been forever altered, and that Canada must reduce reliance on its southern neighbor, which currently accounts for roughly 70 percent of Canadian exports.
"We've been under no illusions. We recognized from the start that America has changed," Carney said on Aug. 22. "We recognize that sometimes, its signature was written in pencil."

Turkish and Japanese officials and experts met in Tokyo to examine how artificial intelligence and geopolitical competition are reshaping strategic communication, economic security and global supply chains.
The STRATCOM Roundtable and STRATCOM Public Forum, organized by Türkiye’s Presidential Communications Directorate and its embassy in Tokyo, brought together representatives of public institutions, international organizations, technology companies, think tanks and universities.
The roundtable focused on the effects of emerging technologies on global governance, digital sovereignty, information security and international cooperation. Participants also discussed disinformation, the changing role of public diplomacy and the use of technology in crisis management.
A separate public forum on managing economic security examined critical technologies, reliable supply chains, data security and the transformation of the digital economy.
In a video message, Presidential Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said digital technologies had widened access to information but also created new vulnerabilities through manipulation, polarization and uncertainty.
“Today, we are facing what can be described as a crisis of truth and a crisis of communication,” Duran said.
He called for greater international cooperation, exchanges of experience and the development of common principles, saying no country or institution could address such challenges alone.
Türkiye’s ambassador to Japan, Oğuzhan Ertuğrul, said multiple crises and growing uncertainty were placing further pressure on the international order. He called for stronger cooperation based on diplomacy and multilateralism, alongside reforms to global institutions.
Ertuğrul said Türkiye and Japan possessed complementary strategic capabilities and could work together to support international peace, stability and prosperity.
Deputy Communications Director Ferhat Pirinççi said information security and a reliable information environment were central to economic resilience. Disinformation could directly affect economic stability, the investment climate and public confidence, he said.
Pirinççi added that the two countries could deepen cooperation in technology, innovation, strategic communication and crisis management.
AK Party Deputy Chair Ömer İleri said protectionism, the growing emphasis on domestic production and the increasing importance of AI and data were transforming both geopolitical and technological competition.
Akira Igata of the University of Tokyo’s Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology drew attention to disinformation and influence operations targeting companies involved in critical-mineral supply chains and data-center infrastructure.
He called for closer cooperation between governments and businesses, as well as greater information sharing and education.
Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Public Policy, said interdependence among major powers, particularly the United States and China, continued to shape economic security policies.
Diversifying critical supply chains and reducing strategic vulnerabilities were becoming increasingly important, he said.
Kunihiko Miyake of the Canon Institute for Global Studies said technological tools alone could not ensure effective communication, which also required a clear strategy and messages tailored to their intended audiences.

Central Bank ends physical gold conversion scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:40:15 UTC
17:40:15 KST

The Central Bank has repealed a regulation that allowed physical gold held outside the banking system to be converted into lira-denominated deposit and participation accounts.
The decision, published in the Official Gazette on Aug. 22, entered into force on the same day. The regulation had been in place since March 14, 2022.
New accounts and renewals under the scheme had already been halted on Aug. 23, 2025. Accounts opened before that date remained valid until maturity.
Under the repealed rules, savers could take physical gold to authorized jewelers or bank branches for transfer to gold accounts. At the account holder’s request, the balance was converted into liras at a price set by the Central Bank.
The funds were placed in deposit or participation accounts with maturities of three, six or 12 months, while banks sold the corresponding gold to the Central Bank at the conversion price.
At maturity, account holders received the principal together with interest or a profit share. If the increase in the gold price exceeded that return, the Central Bank covered the difference through the relevant bank.
The scheme also allowed an additional return under rules set by the Central Bank.

U.S. Marine Corps accepts first Ancillary Surface Craft prototype
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:38:42 UTC
17:38:42 KST

- The Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory completed technical acceptance of its first Ancillary Surface Craft prototype, built by Birdon America under a 2024 contract.
- The 150-foot landing craft can carry 46 tons of cargo and 40 Marines and is rated for Sea State 5 operation, surviving up to Sea State 7.
The U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory has completed technical acceptance of the first Ancillary Surface Craft prototype, moving the roughly 150-foot vessel into a new phase of testing at Quantico, Virginia, the laboratory said in a release.
The ASC is a roll-on/roll-off landing craft designed to carry personnel, equipment, and fuel directly onto unimproved shorelines, delivering what the Marine Corps calls the “last tactical mile” of logistics support. The laboratory said the craft can transport up to 46 tons of cargo and 40 combat-loaded Marines. It is rated for full operation in Sea State 5 and designed to survive conditions up to Sea State 7.
The craft is equipped with forward-looking sonar intended to let operators navigate uncharted, shallow littoral waters and assess beach gradients before landing.
The Marine Corps awarded the ASC contract to Birdon America, the U.S. arm of Australian shipbuilder Birdon, in 2024. Birdon partnered with C&C Marine and Repair in Belle Chasse, Louisiana, to build the vessel, with construction beginning in 2025 at C&C’s facility near New Orleans. Birdon has said the ASC design, which it also refers to as the Ancillary Surface Craft-Medium, was built for rapid, automation-driven production intended to shorten the time needed to build each craft.
“Achieving technical acceptance is a crucial first step in our rigorous testing regimen,” said Aaron Hatfield, Maritime Program Manager, Science and Technology Division, U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory.
“This validation assures that the craft’s advanced systems and robust design are ready for MCWL to begin hands-on technical experimentation, ensuring we can meet the extreme operational demands of the Indo-Pacific theater.”
The ASC now enters limited technical assessments, in which Birdon America craft masters and engineers will work alongside Australian Army crewing support under Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory oversight. The laboratory said the craft will initially be operated by a hybrid crew pairing Marines with contracted mariners as the Marine Corps trains its own personnel toward independent operation of small surface craft.
The ASC is intended to complement the Medium Landing Ship, a larger amphibious vessel the Marine Corps and Navy have been developing to move forces between islands. The Medium Landing Ship program has faced repeated delays, and the Marine Corps has described the ASC and similar smaller craft as part of an interim “bridging strategy” to sustain distributed forces in the Pacific while that program continues. Where the Medium Landing Ship moves forces at a larger scale, the ASC is built with a shallow draft meant to reach landing sites beyond the reach of bigger vessels, including shorelines without ports, piers, or causeways.
“To support Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO), our forces must remain highly mobile and sustained without relying on fixed, vulnerable ports,” said Col. Kenny Jones, Science and Technology Division Director at the Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory.
“This prototype allows MCWL to immediately execute hands-on experimentation, test tactical concepts, and put real hardware in the hands of Marines. By exploring the ASC’s traditional bow-first beaching physics alongside other experimental platforms, we are actively reducing programmatic risk and perfecting the requirements for the future naval fleet.”
Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations is the Marine Corps concept for positioning small, mobile units at temporary locations across contested maritime areas, including islands in the Pacific, to support sea denial and fleet sustainment missions. The concept relies on units that can move between locations without depending on fixed infrastructure that would be vulnerable to attack.
The Marine Corps has ordered two ASC prototypes from Birdon under the current contract. Upcoming testing phases will evaluate force protection and self-defense configurations for the craft, whose primary mission remains logistics and maneuver rather than direct combat.

Explainer: What abrupt cut to joint drills means for U.S.-S. Korea alliance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:34:43 CST
17:34:43 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- A major U.S.-South Korea military exercise ended earlier than planned Friday after U.S. President Donald Trump unexpectedly ordered a substantial reduction in its scale, raising fresh questions over the stability of the U.S.-South Korea alliance, Seoul's plans to assume wartime operational control and the reliability of U.S. security commitments to its allies worldwide.
The Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) military exercise, originally scheduled to run through next Thursday, was cut to five days from 11, with both the duration and scope of training significantly reduced.
The move came after Trump called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to scale back the drills in a social media post just hours before the exercise was due to begin. South Korean officials said they had not been informed of the decision in advance.
A SURPRISE THAT SHOOK SEOUL
The abrupt change was unusual because large-scale U.S.-South Korea exercises are normally coordinated months in advance between the two militaries, according to South Korean media. The two countries also scaled back drills in 2019 amid efforts to promote dialogue with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), but that decision was jointly coordinated beforehand.
This time, South Korean officials said they were caught off guard. Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back said Wednesday that they had not been informed beforehand.
The move also came amid broader friction between Washington and Seoul. Trump has repeatedly complained that the United States does too much for South Korea while receiving too little in return, and recently criticized Seoul for refusing to join U.S. efforts related to Iran's "denuclearization."
NEW UNCERTAINTY RAISED OVER COMMAND TRANSFER
According to local media analysis, the shortened exercise is also significant because South Korea has regarded combined drills as an important mechanism for assessing its readiness to assume wartime operational control of its forces.
Seoul has potentially aimed to complete the transfer in 2027. Commander of the U.S. Forces Korea Xavier Brunson, however, has stressed that any transfer must be based on military readiness.
South Korean officials have insisted that the latest reduction will not delay the process. Ahn said the two issues were unrelated, while Cho said the exercise cut should not be used as a reason to postpone the transfer. President Lee Jae Myung has also reaffirmed his intention to pursue the transfer during his term.
Wang Son-Taek, adjunct professor at Sogang University, noted in an interview with Xinhua that the first phase of UFS, which focused primarily on defense operations, had already been conducted. The part that was mainly reduced was the second phase, involving counteroffensive operations after the defense phase.
Still, South Korean defense and geopolitical expert Do Jin-ho warned that reducing combined drills could delay the command-transfer process and affect the frequency of future U.S. strategic asset deployments to the peninsula.
Yoo Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defense Analysis, said the reduction may not put the command-transfer process on hold, but could expose broader coordination challenges within the alliance.
ALLIANCE TRUST UNDER PRESSURE
South Korean analysts have warned that repeated unilateral adjustments by Washington could weaken mutual trust and make the joint defense system less predictable.
Wang said that the episode could deepen unease among South Koreans over whether Washington would reliably uphold its security commitments, potentially putting additional pressure on the South Korean government.
At the same time, Wang cautioned against drawing the conclusion that Seoul should simply reduce its reliance on Washington.
Analysts said the Trump administration has used U.S. security commitments as leverage in dealing with allies. It has pressed Seoul over defense cost-sharing of U.S. troops stationed in South Korea, and pressured NATO allies over military spending. The latest move has renewed concerns about the reliability of the U.S. security umbrella.
Wang said the episode could contribute to a perception in Northeast Asia that trust within alliances was weakening and could reduce public confidence in the United States in South Korea. In the longer term, he said, such a trend could even become self-defeating for Washington's efforts to maintain its dominant position. ■

BJP passes resolution condemning Congress’ decision to sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram
NEW DELHI: BJP on Saturday condemned the Congress' decision to sing only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram at party programmes, saying the move undermines the national song’s legacy and significance.The party passed a 10-point resolution asserting that it would protect the honour, national character and prestige associated with the complete version of Vande Mataram.
"No compromise on honour, legacy of Vande Mataram will be accepted for political convenience or appeasement," the resolution read.
It further "resolved to strongly condemn and unequivocally oppose the Congress Working Committee’s decision of 19th August 2026 to reaffirm its 1937 resolution and restrict Vande Mataram to its first two stanzas at Congress programmes."Further labeling it as "anti-imperialist cry", the BJP further resolved "to recall and disseminate Mahatma Gandhi’s own testimony that Vande Mataram had become an “anti-imperialist cry” and that he associated it with “the purest national spirit”, demonstrating its larger national meaning beyond the literary or religious context of particular stanzas."The BJP also said it would launch a nationwide campaign to highlight the history, meaning and significance of the national song and counter what it described as attempts to diminish its importance.
After the resolution were passed, BJP leader Sambit Patra held a press conference slamming Congress and highlighting significance of the national song. "This is the 150th anniversary of Vande Mataram. On August 15, 2026, the complete Vande Mataram, which has six stanzas, was sung from the Red Fort. But on August 15, an indecent act took place at the Congress office. In the presence of Congress MP Sonia Gandhi and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, when the Tricolour was being hoisted, Sonia Gandhi signalled to stop Vande Mataram after two stanzas," he added.
"On August 19, a proposal came in at the CWC meeting stating that we will sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram. We all know why this decision was taken in 1937," he added.
Earlier, Union home minister Amit Shah had also attacked the Congress Working Committee’s resolution, calling the decision “anti-national” and accusing the party of reviving what he described as its decades-old “politics of appeasement”.
