====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: East China's Anhui eyes on strategic planning to foster future industries
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
22:46:52 CST
23:46:52 KST

* In the first half of 2026, Anhui's high-tech manufacturing added value surged 44.6 percent year on year, with sectors like electronic information and automobiles contributing over 70 percent of industrial growth.
* While supporting private tech companies through the full cycle, Anhui is also accelerating the commercialization of technologies derived from large scientific facilities.
* In Anhui, long-term planning and funding at both provincial and municipal levels ensure differentiated competition, which prevents redundant construction and enables cities to collaborate.
HEFEI, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Along the "Quantum Avenue" in Hefei, provincial capital of Anhui, futuristic glass buildings house companies in quantum technology and digital services. Within the same vicinity sit facilities dedicated to voice recognition and deep-space exploration.
Two decades ago, populous and less-developed Anhui in east China used to be an inland province with large labor outflow, but in the past years it has drawn a growing number of researchers and entrepreneurs who boast cutting-edge technologies.
The province's long-term commitment to advanced technology has turned things around. In the first half of 2026, Anhui's high-tech manufacturing added value surged 44.6 percent year on year, with sectors like electronic information and automobiles contributing over 70 percent of industrial growth.
CULTIVATING FUTURE GROWTH
Early planning and sustained institutional support have advanced pioneering industries.
Lu'an, a small city renowned for its tea production and picturesque mountains, is now home to China's first megawatt-class hydrogen energy demonstration station, which converts electricity into hydrogen and vice versa to regulate grid peaks and troughs. The station is expected to save around 1,091 tonnes of standard coal equivalent and reduce about 1,889 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually.
Mingtian Hydrogen Energy Co., Ltd. is one of such operators. Since its founding in Lu'an in 2017, the company has proactively aligned itself with the provincial and municipal development framework. Backed by long-term policies, the company has partnered with the State Grid to establish the power station.
For Wang Chaoyun, chairman of Mingtian Hydrogen Energy, the decision to set up in Lu'an was based on the city's diverse application scenarios for heavy freight and steel transport. "But what mattered more was that when some local officials mistook hydrogen energy for 'hydrogen bomb energy,' Anhui had already issued a clear hydrogen industry plan and set up dedicated industrial funds," Wang recalled.
Wang and his team overcame numerous technical hurdles, at a time when China lacked a complete hydrogen supply chain. Some key components, such as air compressors, had to be imported at high costs and with lead times of at least four months.
The city government stepped in to connect enterprises with research institutes. A physical sciences institute under the Chinese Academy of Sciences eventually developed a centrifugal air compressor, removing a critical bottleneck for local manufacturers.
To mitigate the financial risks of heavy R&D investment, the city government partnered with insurers to provide partial compensation if the project failed. After the company moved into full-scale production, Lu'an pioneered hydrogen fuel cells in its public bus fleet, with about a quarter of the buses now hydrogen-powered. The move not only helped the company gain operational experience but also served as a strong commercial endorsement.
Today, Mingtian Hydrogen Energy has built a complete industrial chain covering fuel cell manufacturing and hydrogen-electricity storage, and its hydrogen-powered marine systems have obtained certification from the China Classification Society.
"Anhui embraces new thinking, new technologies and new industries. The government here has a long-term vision and the courage to break new ground and take responsibility," said Wang.
FROM LAB TO MARKET
While supporting private tech companies through the full cycle, Anhui is also accelerating the commercialization of technologies derived from large scientific facilities. These spinoffs not only serve the public but also generate economic returns that are reinvested into long-term R&D.
At Hefei Ion Medical Center, a domestically developed superconducting proton therapy system is undergoing clinical preparations and is expected to treat patients this year. It grew directly out of core technologies accumulated during the development of the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST), dubbed China's "artificial sun," which aims to create nuclear fusion like the sun. These technologies include superconducting magnets, radiofrequency systems and ion sources.
Compared with conventional radiotherapy, the proton system precisely targets tumors while significantly reducing radiation damage to surrounding vital organs. This drastically lowers long-term complications and improves patients' quality of life.
This is far from unique. In Hefei, subway passengers pass through terahertz scanners, another innovation derived from the EAST fusion project. The technology outperforms conventional security devices by detecting prohibited objects previously overlooked, such as ceramic knives, liquid hazardous chemicals, and powdered drugs.
For companies seeking business opportunities in big science spinoffs, the Anhui Innovation Hall offers a one-stop hub that showcases more than 2,700 high-level international achievements and provides transaction and matchmaking services.
The Anhui Innovation Hall has trained over 5,100 "technology managers." With expertise in technology, industry and finance, these professionals offer end-to-end services from scouting to deal-making. The service network has facilitated the commercialization of more than 4,000 research results over the past six years.
This incubator is adopting a more proactive approach. "We have regularly stationed our managers on campus at the University of Science and Technology of China to engage with research teams at the earliest stage, connecting their work with provincial funding and applications, turning breakthroughs into tangible outcomes," said Li Wenxin, deputy director of the hall.
INVESTING IN CHAINS
With Hefei's stake in ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's leading memory chipmaker now worth over one trillion yuan (about 140 billion U.S. dollars), Hefei is called China's boldest "venture capital city." But its investment does not aim to bet on individual companies for financial returns, but aims to extend and strengthen industrial chains based on regional strengths.
In 2008, Hefei invested approximately 6 billion yuan in the sixth-generation production line of BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd. The move shored up a shortfall in local home appliance production and created China's first homegrown liquid crystal display supply. In 2020, it injected 7 billion yuan into NIO China, anchoring the electric vehicle maker's headquarters and R&D center locally and expanding its Anhui-based suppliers from about 60 to nearly 150.
Through these anchor companies, Hefei has cultivated national-level strategic emerging industrial clusters in new display technology, integrated circuits and AI. Quantum information, fusion energy and deep-space exploration are now its next frontiers.
Beyond Hefei, cities across Anhui are also nurturing their own signature industries. As of the first quarter of 2026, Anhui's first 10 provincial-level future-industry pilot zones had already generated over 93 billion yuan in total industrial-chain output.
Bengbu City, leveraging its core competencies in integrated circuits and new materials, has achieved a breakthrough in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology. A local hospital can carry out clinical work for both semi-invasive BCI surgeries and non-invasive BCI systems, offering patients with paralysis a path to restored independence in daily living.
"In Anhui, each city builds on its local strengths and supports leading enterprises to drive industrial chain development. Long-term planning and funding at both provincial and municipal levels ensure differentiated competition, which prevents redundant construction and enables cities to collaborate," said Cui Shihua, deputy director of the Bengbu high-tech zone's management committee.
(Video reporter: Qu Yan; video editors: Zhang Yucheng and Liu Xiaorui)■

Chinese customs official calls for more APEC efforts to remove trade barriers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
22:46:50 CST
23:46:50 KST

DALIAN, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- APEC economies should step up efforts to eliminate trade barriers and take more concrete measures to address cross-border trade bottlenecks, so as to make supply chains in the Asia-Pacific region safer, more stable and more efficient, a Chinese customs official said on Saturday.
"Security and facilitation are eternal themes of customs governance," Zhang Baofeng, deputy chief of the General Administration of Customs, said at the ongoing second plenary meeting of the 2026 APEC Sub-Committee on Customs Procedures (SCCP) in Dalian, northeast China's Liaoning Province.
Amid growing fragmentation of global supply chains, adjusting rules and standards and strengthening supply chain resilience have never been more urgent, Zhang noted.
He expressed hope that all parties will take the meeting as an opportunity to deepen alignment of rules and standards, strengthen coordination on risk management and supervision, reduce transaction costs, improve customs clearance efficiency, and provide businesses with a safer, more transparent and more predictable business environment.
The Asia-Pacific region, home to one-third of the world's population, accounts for over 60 percent of the global economy and nearly half of global trade, serving as a key engine of global economic growth.
China's trade with other APEC economies totaled 18 trillion yuan (about 2.65 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first seven months of this year, up 21 percent year on year, outpacing overall growth in China's foreign trade in goods and demonstrating strong potential for regional cooperation.
During the meeting, participants observed smart devices, exchanged experience and ideas, and built consensus. China's customs shared the latest progress of the smart customs partnership program and held an exhibition showcasing achievements in smart customs development.
Zhang also put forward a three-point proposal to further deepen APEC customs cooperation -- upholding true multilateralism and jointly building a new pattern of open and inclusive Asia-Pacific cooperation; riding the wave of the digital era and reshaping new paradigms of customs governance with technological innovation; balancing security and facilitation, and underpinning lasting prosperity in the Asia-Pacific region with a resilient and stable supply chain system.
The meeting also approved an APEC customs cooperation document on promoting technology and innovation for trade security and facilitation.
The APEC SCCP was established in 1994. China's customs holds the SCCP chairmanship for 2026. This meeting, following the first plenary in Guangzhou in February this year, featured in-depth discussions on cutting-edge topics such as artificial intelligence, smart customs and cross-border e-commerce.
Over 100 delegates, including customs representatives from all 21 APEC economies and officials from relevant government departments, international organizations, and business communities, attended the meeting. ■

Maternal stress during pregnancy linked to children’s social communication skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
14:00:01 UTC
23:00:01 KST

Children whose mothers experienced high levels of stress during pregnancy and shortly after birth may face lasting challenges with social communication. A recent analysis indicates that early exposure to maternal hardship predicts poorer communication skills as youth progress from childhood into adolescence. The research was published in the journal Development and Psychopathology.
Social cognition is the broad ability to perceive, interpret, and respond to social information. It encompasses several distinct skills, including the capacity to recognize emotions in others and the ability to engage in reciprocal social communication. Emotion recognition typically emerges early in life and stabilizes during late childhood. In contrast, complex social communication abilities continue to mature well into adolescence.
The time before birth and the first few months of life represent a sensitive window for brain maturation. During this period, the developing nervous system is highly responsive to environmental inputs. Elevated maternal stress can lead to changes in fetal neurodevelopment, potentially by increasing the transfer of stress hormones across the placenta. This biological process can influence the growth of brain regions involved in social and emotional processing, such as the prefrontal cortex and the amygdala.
Past research has linked early adversity to various emotional and behavioral difficulties, but it has remained uncertain exactly how maternal stress affects specific types of social cognition. Theodora Kokosi, Marta Francesconi, and Eirini Flouri at University College London conducted this study to examine whether prenatal adversity influences distinct social skills differently. They specifically wanted to track these skills across multiple developmental stages, from middle childhood through late adolescence.
The researchers analyzed data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. This large study tracks the health and development of youth born in the United Kingdom in the early 1990s. The analytic sample for this investigation included 10,177 participants who had data available for at least one measure of social cognition.
To gauge early adversity, mothers completed established checklists documenting stressful life events they had experienced. These inventories capture a variety of challenging situations, ranging from relationship difficulties to financial strain. The mothers filled out these surveys at 18 weeks of pregnancy and again at eight weeks postpartum. The researchers combined these responses to create a cumulative score of adverse life events spanning the early prenatal period through the first two months of the child’s life.
The first outcome the researchers evaluated was social communication. Parents completed a standardized checklist assessing their child’s social reciprocity and communication behaviors. This assessment occurred at four different time points: when the children were 8, 11, 14, and 17 years old.
The researchers found that higher maternal exposure to stressful life events was associated with poorer offspring social communication. This link held even after adjusting for factors like family socioeconomic status, maternal postpartum depression, and the child’s intelligence scores. The negative association between early adversity and social communication also widened slightly as the children aged from 8 to 17 years old.
The authors suggest that this widening gap might reflect the changing nature of social environments. As teenagers navigate increasingly nuanced social expectations, underlying communication difficulties may become more pronounced. Early disruptions to neural systems involved in social processing could make it harder for youth to keep up with these escalating demands.
The study also examined emotion recognition, which relies on different neurocognitive systems than social communication. At age eight, children completed a task evaluating their ability to identify emotions from static images. They viewed photographs of faces displaying fear, happiness, sadness, or anger, and they were asked to categorize the expression.
Maternal exposure to stressful life events was not related to the children’s performance on this facial emotion recognition test. Early life adversity did not appear to hinder or help a child’s ability to interpret basic facial expressions. The researchers note that static image tests might not always capture subtle changes in emotional processing.
At age 14, the teenagers completed a different type of emotion recognition assessment. This computer-based test required participants to identify emotions based on the movement patterns of abstract geometric shapes. For example, an animated triangle repeatedly jabbing at a circle was intended to convey anger.
In this case, greater maternal exposure to stressful life events from mid-pregnancy to the early postpartum period predicted slightly better performance on the movement-based task. While this result might seem counterintuitive, it aligns with certain developmental theories. Some researchers propose that individuals raised in unpredictable environments develop a heightened sensitivity to dynamic social cues as a way to adapt and survive.
There are a few caveats to consider when interpreting this research. The study relied on parent reports to measure the children’s social communication skills. This method can introduce subjective bias, as parents might interpret their children’s behaviors differently based on their own experiences or stress levels.
The study is also observational, which means it cannot prove that maternal stress directly caused the differences in social cognition. Other unmeasured environmental or genetic factors could contribute to the observed associations. Additionally, some participants dropped out of the longitudinal study over time, and this missing data could influence the statistical estimates of how communication skills change with age.
The measures used in the study also capture only a fraction of the broader concept of social cognition. Social cognition includes other sub-domains, such as the ability to understand different mental states or draw inferences about the causes of actions. It remains unknown if maternal stress influences these other specialized skills in the same way.
Future investigations could benefit from incorporating objective, observer-rated assessments of social communication to supplement parent reports. Researchers might also explore the biological mechanisms linking maternal stress to fetal brain development. Examining specific pathways, such as changes in immune function or stress hormone regulation, could clarify exactly how the early environment shapes lifelong social skills.
The study, “Prenatal exposure to stressful life events and offspring social cognition across childhood and adolescence,” was authored by Theodora Kokosi, Marta Francesconi, and Eirini Flouri.

Multilingual people may have brains up to 13 years younger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
13:12:23 UTC
22:12:23 KST

Multilingual people may have brains up to 13 years younger
- Date:
- August 22, 2026
- Source:
- Federation of European Neuroscience Societies
- Summary:
- People who speak several languages may have brains that age more slowly, with four-language speakers showing brains that appeared about 13 years younger than those of monolinguals. Starting earlier and becoming highly fluent were also linked to a stronger effect.
- Share:
People who speak more than one language may have brains that appear younger than expected for their age, according to research presented at the Federation of European Neuroscience Societies (FENS) Forum 2026.
The brain depends on billions of nerve cells constantly communicating with one another. As people get older, those connections can weaken, contributing to slower thinking and declines in memory.
The new findings suggest that multilingual experience may help offset some of those age-related changes. People who spoke more languages tended to have younger-looking brains, and the effect also appeared stronger among those who learned another language earlier and became more proficient.
Multilingualism and Brain Aging
The research was presented by Dr. Lucia Amoruso of the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language in San Sebastián, Spain. She worked with researchers from the Latin American Brain Health Institute at the Universidad Adolfo Ibañez, Chile, the Cognitive Neuroscience Center at the Universidad de San Andres, Argentina, and the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin, Ireland.
The team had previously published research suggesting that people living in countries where multilingualism is common may age more slowly. For the latest work, they focused on people from the Basque region of Spain who spoke between one and four languages, using different combinations of Spanish, Basque, French and English.
To measure brain aging, the researchers first studied 728 people and created a 'brain aging clock'. They used magnetoencephalography, a method that detects the faint magnetic fields produced when brain cells are active.
Artificial intelligence was then used to analyze patterns of brain activity across people of different ages. This allowed the researchers to estimate what typical brain connectivity looks like at different points in life.
They next applied the clock to a separate group of 144 people to estimate each person's 'brain age'.
Four Languages Linked to a 13 Year Difference
When the researchers compared participants' actual ages with their estimated brain ages, they found a striking pattern.
People who spoke two languages had brains that appeared about six years younger than those of people who spoke only one language. Those who spoke three languages had brains that appeared about seven years younger. Among people who spoke four languages, the difference grew to roughly 13 years.
Dr. Amoruso said: "In simple terms, people who spoke more languages tended to have brains that looked younger than expected for their chronological age. The effect was not only related to the number of languages spoken. Higher language proficiency and earlier acquisition of a second language were also associated with more delayed brain aging. This suggests that multilingual experience matters as a gradient: it is not simply about being bilingual or not, but about the depth and duration of language experience."
The researchers adjusted their analysis for factors including age, sex and education. However, they cautioned that other influences on brain health, including lifestyle and social engagement, could also contribute to the differences they observed.
Could Language Learning Support Brain Resilience?
Dr. Amoruso and her colleagues now want to investigate whether similar patterns appear in people with neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, where brain aging and resilience are particularly important.
They also hope to explore whether speaking two or more closely related languages could produce an even stronger effect. Switching between similar languages may require greater control because speakers must continually manage competing words and language systems.
Professor Christina Dalla of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Greece, chairs the FENS Forum communication committee and was not involved in the research. She said: "We know that many factors can influence our brain health and mental abilities as we age. For example, we know that not smoking, eating well, social and artistic engagement, as well as being active, can help. How we use our brains throughout life can also have an impact, especially if we engage in effortful learning that activates our brain.
"This study suggests that learning a second, third or fourth language could help our brains to stay younger for longer, and the earlier we start, the better. There are many good reasons for learning another language at any age -- social, cultural and for the health of your brain -- so we should support language learning at school and throughout life, even if it's hard."
Funding: National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Institute on Aging (NIA), the Fogarty International Center and the Multi-partner Consortium to Expand Dementia Research in Latin America (ReDLat). Additional support was provided by the Alzheimer's Association, the Global Brain Health Institute, the Davos Alzheimer's Collaborative, Alzheimer's Society UK, FONDECYT and the Ramón y Cajal fellowship through the Spanish State Research Agency.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Federation of European Neuroscience Societies. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

As families retrieve bodies, Gaza is running out of places to bury the dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
13:10:45 UTC
22:10:45 KST

Gaza is running out of places to bury the dead
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has seen thousands of bodies buried in makeshift sites.
Twenty-year-old Omar al-Sawhi has to find a burial place for his father, Mohammad, 40, who was shot dead close to the “Yellow Line”, an Israeli-designated military zone in Gaza.
Mohammad, from the Zeitoun neighbourhood of Gaza City, was working at a small roadside stall selling tea and coffee when a bullet struck him in the neck on June 10, killing him almost instantly.
Omar headed to the Zeitoun Cemetery to bury his father and found the graves tightly packed together, many of them victims of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza.
Many of them are marked with just a stone and a piece of paper attached bearing the name of the deceased, due to a lack of space and the difficult conditions caused by the war.
“I stood in the middle of the cemetery and saw so many graves. There were mountains of sand, with people buried underneath,” Omar told Al Jazeera.
“A grave was just a stone with a piece of paper bearing the name of the martyr, without the grave being built or properly prepared as it was before the war.”
A grave here currently costs about 500 shekels ($167), a sum his family could not afford, so they had to find an alternative.
“There was also no space for a new grave, so we had to bury him in my grandfather’s grave,” he said.
Burying the dead
The complete breakdown of services in Gaza and the dangers from Israeli attacks meant that thousands of dead Palestinians have been counted as “missing” during the war.
Many of them were buried in gardens, or tents, or the grounds of camps for the displaced, schools or hospitals.
After a relative reduction in Israeli violence in Gaza following the United States-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, families began to recover their dead loved ones from the debris of destroyed homes or temporary burial sites.
At least 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire was announced, every one of them needing a space for burial. Authorities in Gaza said the remains of 529 Palestinians were recovered from seven mass graves in the grounds of hospitals.
Taking advantage of the brief lull in Israeli violence, his family excavated Mohammad’s remains and moved them to a cemetery for a final burial.
The shortage of graves is not just due to the more than 73,000 Palestinians killed since the war on Gaza began in October 2023, but also the destruction of burial sites by Israel.
According to Gaza’s Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs, more than 40 cemeteries have been destroyed since the war began.
Israeli forces have also enforced tight restrictions on access to cemeteries in areas under their control, which has further reduced the number of burial spaces available to families.
With hundreds of thousands of Palestinians forced from their homes by Israeli bombing and forced displacement orders, areas previously designated for burial sites have been converted into shelters for the displaced.
Authorities in Gaza say that shortages of materials, such as headstones, mean the cost of burial now ranges between 700 ($235) and 1,000 shekels ($335).
Masonry from destroyed buildings, mud, or corrugated metal sheets are used as temporary grave markers until the money can be found for a proper gravestone.
Ikrami al-Madallal, a media official at the Endowments Ministry, said many of Gaza’s 60 cemeteries were already at full capacity when the war began.
“We need to establish new cemeteries because of the shortage of available burial space,” he told Al Jazeera.
The ministry is searching for new burial grounds, and transferring bodies from temporary places of rest to cemeteries is an ongoing challenge for authorities.
“The transfer of bodies cannot be carried out randomly. It must be coordinated with the Ministry of Endowments, local government and the relevant government authorities,” he said.
Tafesh Abu Hatab, 50, who has worked as a gravedigger for more than 19 years, said the war on Gaza has been the most difficult period of his career.
Khan Younis Cemetery, where he works, had about 60 graves at the beginning of the war. Now it contains 6,000, and at one stage of the war, Tafesh was preparing about 35 graves a day.
“We have never experienced a period of bloodshed this devastating,” he told Al Jazeera. “Not a day passes without dozens of martyrs being buried.”
Many of the dead he handles are women and children, including infants. Sometimes the bodies of whole families enter the cemetery after an Israeli bomb obliterates an entire building, vehicle, or tent.
“They destroy our homes over our heads, and from the rubble of those homes, we build our graves,” he said.

Myanmar airstrike on monastery kills 14 during Buddhist retreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
13:03:25 UTC
22:03:25 KST

A Myanmar military airstrike on a monastery where civilians had gathered for a Buddhist Lent meditation retreat killed 14 people, including 11 men and three women, according to two local opposition fighters who witnessed the aftermath.
The strike hit a monastery hall at about 9:00 a.m. Friday in Myaung township in the central Sagaing region, one of the main areas of resistance to Myanmar’s military government.
Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel who helped recover the bodies, said the victims were between 50 and 70 years old and had been staying at the monastery for a three-month meditation retreat during Buddhist Lent, a period that largely coincides with Myanmar’s rainy season.
“It wasn’t a mistaken target, they intentionally attacked a monastery,” he said.
A second local opposition fighter, who spoke Saturday on condition of anonymity, said five of the dead were from his village and the other nine came from neighboring villages.
He also said the military aircraft returned to the area while rescuers were trying to recover the victims.
“While we were trying to rescue people, the aircraft came to bomb a second time,” he said.
The Myanmar military could not immediately be reached for comment.
Myanmar has been engulfed in civil war since the military seized power in a February 2021 coup, ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and detaining the Nobel Peace Prize laureate.
The coup triggered widespread armed resistance, with the military fighting a patchwork of pro-democracy groups and powerful ethnic minority armed organizations across the country. More than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed in the conflict.
The military has increasingly relied on airstrikes to attack areas held or contested by its opponents. Analysts say its forces use Chinese- and Russian-supplied aircraft to maintain pressure on rebel groups and compensate for difficulties on the ground.
The latest attack came shortly after United Nations investigators accused Myanmar’s military of carrying out “indiscriminate and intentional aerial attacks against civilians.”
The Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, which investigates serious international crimes committed in the country, said in a report published last week that airstrikes had repeatedly hit civilian areas.
Monasteries and schools are among the public buildings frequently reported to have been targeted in air attacks.
Myanmar’s government rejected the findings, describing them as “one-sided allegations” based on what it called unverifiable and inaccurate information about the country’s security forces.
Conflict monitoring group ACLED said in a report last month that the military’s campaign had increasingly focused on civilian infrastructure and public gatherings, including weddings and religious festivals, in an apparent effort to amplify fear and psychological pressure.
The military has continued its campaign even as it sought to portray the country as returning to political normality through elections held around the beginning of 2026.
The vote was widely dismissed by democracy advocates as a sham designed to legitimize military rule. Aung San Suu Kyi remained excluded, her political party was sidelined and opponents of military rule faced imprisonment.
The UN investigative mechanism said it had observed a notable increase in aerial attacks in the months leading up to the elections.
The elections ultimately paved the way for coup leader Min Aung Hlaing to become civilian president in April. He handed over his position as commander in chief of the armed forces to a close ally.
Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has pursued an international diplomatic campaign aimed at ending Myanmar’s isolation and securing greater recognition for his government.
India, China, Laos and Thailand have hosted him, drawing criticism from campaigners who say such engagements provide legitimacy to Myanmar’s military leadership.
This week, Min Aung Hlaing traveled to Russia and Belarus, two of the military government’s most steadfast international allies since the coup.

Saudi dissident released from years-long Bulgaria detention
A Saudi dissident who unsuccessfully sought asylum in Bulgaria was released on Friday after nearly five years in detention in the Balkan nation, his lawyer told news agency AFP.
Abd al-Rahman al-Khalidi's detention was among the longest faced by an asylum seeker in Bulgaria, according to the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee (BHC).
Although freed, Khalidi still faces a deportation order and must now report to a local police station once a week, his lawyer Diana Radoslavova told AFP.
Khalidi was detained after entering Bulgaria from Turkey in 2021 to seek asylum and was subsequently kept in immigration detention as Bulgarian authorities pursued his removal to Saudi Arabia.
"The unprecedentedly long period of de facto administrative detention is over," Radoslavova said.
"His case will forever remain a stain on Bulgaria," she said, adding she feared that the migration system would "increasingly rely on measures like these".
Earlier on Friday, the BHC announced Khalidi's release on Facebook, saying he had been transferred from the closed detention centre in Lyubimets in southern Bulgaria to Sofia to finalise the procedure for his release.
BHC represents Khalidi before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in a pending case challenging the length of his detention.
In 2024, Khalidi told AFP that he had been served with a detention order while still appealing the decision to not grant him asylum.
International human rights organisations have repeatedly urged Bulgaria not to deport Khalidi to Saudi Arabia, warning he could face persecution because of his activism.
In 2011, Khalidi was active during rare demonstrations in eastern Saudi Arabia, where the country's Shia minority is concentrated, following the Middle East's Arab Spring uprisings.

JWST finds early galaxies may be 4 times more massive than thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:36:23 UTC
21:36:23 KST

JWST finds early galaxies may be 4 times more massive than thought
- Date:
- August 22, 2026
- Source:
- Penn State
- Summary:
- Astronomers using JWST have discovered that massive early galaxies contain far more small, faint stars than expected. That hidden population could make some of these galaxies three to four times more massive than previous estimates. The finding makes it even harder to explain how enormous, mature galaxies formed so soon after the Big Bang. It could also suggest that planets around low-mass stars were more common in the early universe than scientists realized.
- Share:
Astronomers have found that some of the largest galaxies in the early universe contained many more small stars than scientists previously realized. That hidden population means these ancient galaxies may have been significantly more massive than earlier estimates indicated.
The discovery, made by an international team that included Penn State researchers, adds to a growing challenge for theories about how the first galaxies formed and evolved. The findings were published in Nature Astronomy.
JWST Uncovers Faint Stars in Ancient Galaxies
Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), researchers examined nine massive, mature galaxies that stopped producing new stars billions of years ago. They combined JWST observations of the distant universe with earlier ground-based data from the Very Large Telescope.
For the first time, the team was able to reliably estimate the relative numbers of small, faint stars and much larger, brighter stars in galaxies at such great distances.
"These galaxies are different," said Joel Leja, the Dr. Keiko Miwa Ross Mid-Career Associate Professor of Astronomy and Astrophysics at Penn State and coauthor of the paper. "They're different in the way that is really challenging to understand, because they are more massive than we expected -- like a lot more massive, they have three or four times more mass than we expected."
Astronomers made the measurements by separating each galaxy's light into a spectrum. Small variations in color within that spectrum can reveal which kinds of stars are present.
The difficulty is that large, luminous stars dominate the light, while smaller stars are far dimmer and much harder to identify. Penn State researchers contributed expertise and guidance for modeling the light detected from the galaxy systems.
Bright Stars Can Hide Vast Stellar Populations
"If a galaxy were a city, the brightest stars would be the skyscrapers that immediately catch your eye from afar," said lead author Chloe Cheng, a recent doctoral graduate of Leiden University. "Our models demonstrate that a far more numerous population of low-mass stars is concealed by those rare, bright stars, like houses hidden between skyscrapers. As a result, this galaxy turns out to be much more massive than previous estimates suggested."
Traditionally, astronomers estimating the mass hidden in small, faint stars have assumed that stars formed in roughly similar proportions throughout the universe. The new findings challenge that long-standing assumption.
The researchers found that the most massive galaxies in the early universe appear to contain a much greater share of low-mass stars than smaller galaxies such as the Milky Way.
One galaxy stood out in particular, according to coauthor Martje Slob, a doctoral candidate at Leiden University. It likely formed less than one and a half billion years after the Big Bang and could be as much as four times more massive than previous calculations suggested.
"Until recently, measurements like these were simply impossible," Slob said. "We needed not only a telescope capable of magnifying very distant galaxies, but also spectra of exceptional quality and new analysis techniques to reliably detect the subtle signatures of faint, low-mass stars hidden within these cosmic titans."
An Even Bigger Early Universe Puzzle
The findings could have major consequences for scientists trying to understand how galaxies developed in the young universe.
Since JWST began observing the cosmos, astronomers have repeatedly identified unexpectedly massive and mature galaxies that existed relatively soon after the Big Bang. Those discoveries have already put pressure on existing models of galaxy formation.
"This discovery has crucial implications for our understanding of the early universe," said Leja, who is also affiliated with The Penn State Institute for Computational and Data Sciences. "Since the launch of JWST, astronomers have found surprisingly massive and mature galaxies that already existed shortly after the Big Bang. These very early galaxies are thought to evolve into the type of galaxies studied in this work; adding up to four times more stars to these massive, early-forming galaxies sharpens these tensions further."
If galaxies like these contained substantially more stars than researchers previously estimated, theories of galaxy formation must account for how such enormous numbers of small stars could have appeared so early in cosmic history.
Hidden Stars Could Also Mean More Early Planets
The implications may extend beyond galaxy formation.
"This result shows that much more mass than previously thought is hidden in low-mass stars," said Mariska Kriek, who led the research and serves as professor of extragalactic astronomy at Leiden Observatory. "That has consequences for many areas of astronomy. For example, as many planets orbit low-mass stars, this could even indicate that more planets formed in the early universe than we had previously assumed."
Over the next several years, the researchers plan to use the same technique to study galaxies from even earlier periods. Their goal is to push observations closer to the time when the universe's first generations of stars and galaxies began to emerge.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Penn State. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chloe M. Cheng, Martje Slob, Mariska Kriek, Aliza G. Beverage, Pieter G. van Dokkum, Rachel Bezanson, Gabriel Brammer, Charlie Conroy, Anna de Graaff, Elham Eftekhari, Robert Feldmann, Wout M. Goesaert, Meng Gu, Joel Leja, Brian Lorenz, Pavel E. Mancera Piña, Ignacio Martín-Navarro, Andrew B. Newman, Sedona H. Price, Alice E. Shapley, Piyush Sharda, Katherine A. Suess, Arjen van der Wel, Daniel R. Weisz. Hidden mass in early galaxies revealed by bottom-heavy initial mass functions. Nature Astronomy, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02932-4

The world’s first IVF female calf of the Lakhimi breed - native to Assam - has been born at the Assam Veterinary and Fishery University.
GUWHATI: Assam has achieved a major milestone in livestock biotechnology with the birth of the world's first IVF-born female calf of the indigenous Lakhimi breed, chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said on Saturday.Taking to social media platform X, Sarma described the development as a historic convergence of Assam's "Sabhyata, Sanskriti and Srijan", saying the achievement could open new avenues for the state's livestock and dairy sector."The world's first IVF female calf of the Lakhimi breed -- native to Assam -- has been born at the Assam Veterinary and Fishery University," the chief minister said.

In the long run, these interventions are expected to strengthen Assam's dairy economy and improve the incomes of livestock farmers."My heartiest congratulations to all the veterinary scientists and professionals behind this historic achievement," the chief minister said, adding that their work had the potential to usher in a new era for Assam's dairy sector.He described the newborn calf as small in size but significant in terms of the scientific milestone it represents for Assam's biotechnology ecosystem.The latest achievement builds on Assam's ongoing efforts to introduce assisted reproductive technologies into livestock development.Earlier this year, scientists at the veterinary college produced Assam's first IVF-born calf, a female Gir calf born in Sonapur, demonstrating the viability of embryo-transfer technology under field conditions.
Scientists have said such technologies can enable faster multiplication of superior genetic stock, potentially improving milk productivity and supporting dairy farmers' incomes.The successful Lakhimi birth therefore combines modern reproductive biotechnology with the conservation of an indigenous cattle breed, giving Assam a new tool to strengthen its livestock sector.Sarma concluded his message by invoking "Gau Mata" and described the achievement as a milestone carrying significance far beyond the birth of a single calf.

European wildfires expose, detonate buried explosives from past wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:35:04 UTC
21:35:04 KST

European wildfires expose, detonate buried bombs and mines from past wars
The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames.
Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg province in 1944.
Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant. But this wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group. The blazes have led to mass evacuations.
The current situation shows that Europe's "climatic luck" is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London's School of Oriental and African Studies.
"Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable," Njeri said.
"You are not sure where the explosives are"
In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Gov. Hervé Jamar said "a few sporadic detonations" were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.
During World War II, booby traps, bombs and mines were scattered throughout the province's dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens, which stretches across Belgium's border with Germany and was the site of key conflicts, including the bloody Battle of the Bulge. Now, a huge blaze is smoldering in the area.
Bernard Collard, a local historian who is authorized to scan the former battlefields with a metal detector, said that in an environment like this, "you are not sure where the explosives are." He said he has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton. His father once detonated a found bomb in a quarry.
"You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn't take it lightly," Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.
He frequently works with the Belgian demining squad. "It's part of our history. We live with it," Collard said.
"The sound of war"
In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be World War II-era ammunition. Around 400 shells and pieces of ammunition were recovered in the village of Le Porge earlier in August. The munitions, both German and French, consist mainly of mortar shells, along with some high-explosive anti-tank shells.
Fire commander Thomas Mimiague said blasts heard during the blaze may have been shells exploding. Mayor Martial Zaninetti told French news outlet France Info the blasts were similar to "the sound of war."
"There were ammunition depots buried in land within our municipality, but we didn't know it, and they exploded," Zaninetti told France Info, adding that one of the munitions "went through a house."
Over 180 homes were destroyed by the fire, local authorities said. Residents returned to the village earlier in August, after the flames were extinguished.
"Reliving the legacies of war"
Finding unexploded ordnance in Europe isn't unusual. A 1,000-pound aerial bomb used by Allied forces during World War II was removed from a construction site in Belgrade, Serbia, in December. In September 2025, researchers found unexploded Nazi bombs sitting at the bottom of a German bay had become a home for marine life.
Sometimes the discoveries, like the fires, spark mass evacuations. Thousands had to leave their homes in Dresden, Germany, after an unexploded bomb was found in the southern city in August 2025. Traffic at France's bustling Gare du Nord train station had to be halted in March 2025 after an unexploded bomb was found near tracks.
Every year across the nation, Belgium's Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars. In Ypres, a town infamous for harrowing trench warfare in World War I, some farmers call the annual tilling of the soil "the iron harvest" because it turns up so many war remnants.
Typically, the bombs are carefully handled and either defused or intentionally, precisely detonated. But wildfire heat can trigger the explosives, removing control from the equation.
Wildfire also isn't the only weather phenomenon revealing old weaponry. Drought has shrunk Europe's rivers and lakes to reveal munitions that were once invisible.
In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest's Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from World War II emerged at its base in receding water. As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a WWII-era bomb.
Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Njeri, wrote an article on Europe's wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said "the legacy of war keeps creeping up" because of climate change.
"It's reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven't had to deal with in a while in certain places," Greene said.

The Berlin Wall separated his family. Its legacy still endures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:31:00 UTC
21:31:00 KST

This feature is the first in a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography.
Erich Guetinger was 18 years old when he first saw his uncle’s family as an adult.
Having last seen them as a small child, Guetinger was both excited and nervous to see his uncle, aunt, and two older cousins after so long.
It was the summer of 1969 – the Beatles were recording Abbey Road, the United States had begun withdrawing troops from Vietnam, and Neil Armstrong was about to become the first person to walk on the moon.
By then, Germany had been divided for two decades. The Federal Republic of Germany, or West Germany, was a capitalist democracy aligned with the US and Western Europe. The German Democratic Republic, or East Germany, was a Soviet-aligned socialist state governed by the Socialist Unity Party. Berlin itself had been divided since 1945, and the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961 had hardened that separation.
The two states differed sharply in size and population. About 51 million people lived in West Germany and about 18 million in East Germany, separated by a nearly 2,000km (1,242 miles) border running from the Baltic Sea to the Czechoslovak border. By 1969, West Germany’s population had grown to about 61 million, while East Germany’s had fallen to roughly 17 million.
With most of his family in their hometown of Babenhausen, Bavaria, and his uncle Hans, aunt Frieda, and cousins Dieter and Guenter in Brieskow-Finkenheerd, a village near Frankfurt an der Oder in East Germany, the Guetingers were directly affected by Germany’s political partition.
A journey that would take just a few hours by car was, back then, a trip requiring visa approval, designated transit corridors, and border guard inspections.
It was the lengths they had to go through that had caused the young Guetinger some unease.
“My dad and I set off for our trip on a Saturday afternoon,” recalled Guetinger, a genial 75-year-old historian, author, and grandfather, who today lives in what would have been West Berlin.
“After a visa process lasting two to three weeks, during which we had to inform GDR officials where we were staying and the purpose of the trip, we set off for one of the three transit corridors that served as official points of entry and exit between the two countries,” he explained.
They travelled by train through a Bavarian border crossing into Probstzella, in the GDR.
“As soon as the train entered GDR territory”, Guetinger said, “we were stopped, and border guards checked our visas and IDs".
The pair stayed in Frankfurt an der Oder for a week, meeting the family’s friends, eating fresh meat and spending quality time at the small family home.
“My uncle was keen to introduce his brother from the West to all his friends,” Guetinger recounts with a smile.
“It was a nice trip, and while we hadn’t seen each other in some time, we got along well.”
They returned home to Bavaria just in time to see Armstrong take his first step on the moon, which they watched with Guetinger’s other uncle, Erich, and some of his friends.
“Even now, I vividly remember the blurred black-and-white pictures appearing on TV. The distance between us wasn’t very far, but making that trip from Bavaria to Frankfurt an der Oder seemed as far as going to the moon and back.”
Germany splits
At least two generations on both Guetinger’s maternal and paternal sides were from Babenhausen, a small Bavarian market town of about 4,000 people in the 1960s. Surrounded by a castle, it was once home to a merchant family said to have been prominent during the Middle Ages.
Guetinger’s father, Ernst, was among five siblings and the youngest of the three boys. Hans was the eldest, followed by another brother, Erich, and there was a four-year age gap between Ernst and Hans. Guetinger said this age difference played a role in his father's and uncle's relationship.
“My dad and uncle Hans didn’t have a very close relationship because they had grown up during wartime,” he said. “When war broke out in 1939, Uncle Hans was obliged to serve as a soldier.”
Soldiers were in short supply, so German boys aged 16 and 17 were drafted as “Flakhelfer” to work with anti-aircraft guns or man the huge lights that tracked enemy aircraft.
“My Uncle Erich was in this age range so served in this role, but my dad, being the youngest, did not have to serve,” he added.
After Nazi Germany’s defeat in 1945, the country was divided into occupation zones and then formally split into two separate countries in 1949.
Hans returned to Babenhausen, Bavaria, after the war and looked for work as a shoemaker. But jobs were scarce, and he had trouble finding work.
Amid their struggles, Hans’s homesick wife encouraged him to try finding work in the GDR, where she was from. They knew they would be welcomed, because the GDR was keen on people willing to buck the trend of those going west - roughly 2.7 million people moved to West Germany between 1949 and 1961 – for better economic and employment opportunities.
In 1958, Hans's family moved east to Brieskow-Finkenheerd, a village near the Polish border, where Hans started working at a power station that also provided their accommodation. He was also able to indulge in his love of hunting as much as he liked.
“He was very happy hunting,” Guetinger remembered fondly. “In West Germany, you could only hunt if you owned land, but since the government owned all the land in the GDR, my uncle was told he could hunt wherever he wanted.”
Hans became so well known for his hunting abilities that when the big cadres wanted to celebrate something and eat some tasty meat like boar or wild swine, they would ask Hans to go hunting.
“The party had its own hunters, but they considered my uncle one of the best,” Guetinger said.
Meanwhile, Hans’s younger brother Ernst, back in Bavaria, became a father to Erich Guetinger in 1951.
In the 1950s, freedom of movement between the two countries remained largely unrestricted, but from the 1960s onwards, tougher measures were instituted. After that, East Germans were generally only allowed to travel to the West for urgent family matters, such as funerals or weddings.
In August 1961 – 65 years ago – the East German government began building the Berlin Wall, a 155km (96 miles) concrete structure surrounding West Berlin that effectively isolated it within GDR territory and severed the capital.
Outside Berlin, efforts to fortify the division led to the installation of new barbed wire fences, detectors, watchtowers, as well as booby-traps and extended powers for border guards to shoot and arrest escapees. Between then and 1989, when the wall came down, an estimated 75,000 people were imprisoned for trying to escape.
Guetinger says that in the early years of the division, there was barely any contact with his uncle and family.
“Eventually, we were able to start sending letters, but we shared very little in these because everybody knew the East German secret police, known as the Stasi, would carefully check the post between families, often reading our letters,” he said.
Like many families in West Germany, the Guetingers would often send Western products to their relatives in the East.
“For Christmas, we made parcels containing things we knew they would like, and which we knew it would be difficult for them to get, such as coffee and blue jeans," Guetinger said.
"Blue jeans were particularly hot property, and my cousins liked this kind of clothing. And even though we would send parcels, there was always a chance that they wouldn’t reach them,” he explained, noting that shipments were closely monitored.
Guetinger says it is still hard to fully assess how the day-to-day disruption caused by the division impacted their family’s sense of safety and unity.
“Even if my parents had a heavy heart back then, they would rarely talk about it, so today, I have to rely on other indicators to try and understand. And one of the indicators is that my dad and his elder brother tried to visit each other as soon as it was possible for both of them.”
Stasi secrets
Yet, even with the 1969 trip being made possible, Guetinger paints a picture of an uneasy time clouded by the fear of Stasi spies.
“We have been sitting here for more than 30 minutes and not once have I looked over my shoulder,” he said. “I’m not afraid of saying something private or political. I don’t care if anyone is listening.”
That was not true back then.
“During that trip, as soon as we entered anywhere, we first had to scan the room to see who was there and how far they were away from us," he said, noting how this determined their topics of conversation.
"Uncle Hans had a lot of friends whom he met regularly outside of his house, and they did this every time they met. It was understood that the secret service was everywhere, and they could make life very difficult for you.”
Meeting his wife
In 1973, Guetinger travelled to meet his friend in Hessen, West Germany, a trip that would see his life take an unexpected turn.
“My friend had a Chinese girlfriend called Hui-Chui Ma, and the plan was that she and her best friend would be joining us upon their return from a trip to Vienna. Her friend, Yan-Yun, was a nurse from China working in Freiburg, around 400km [250 miles] away from Hessen,” he explained.
“When we left, we got the train together, and eventually we went in different directions. But something had hit [Yan-Yun and I] like a lightning bolt.”
Germany’s division had also shaped family stories beyond its borders, with migration patterns evolving on either side depending on the political alignments and economic needs of each nation.
Alignment with countries inside the neighbouring Eastern Bloc, such as Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria, brought links with socially aligned nations on a global level. This led to approximately 70,000 contract workers from Vietnam, more than 20,000 young people from Mozambique, and a small number of engineers from North Korea coming to East Germany during the division. After unification, many of these migrant workers sought to stay on and build families.
West Germany, meanwhile, had friendly links with South Korea, Indonesia and Japan, among others.
Guetinger says that Yan-Yun came to West Germany through a recruitment drive for nurses initiated in Taiwan in the early 1970s.
The pair started to get to know each other, and despite the language barrier, they found that they had something in common.
“The Chiang family shared a common experience... their extended family had been split by the political tensions between mainland China and Taiwan,” he explained.
“Yan-Yun was born in what was then Peking [Beijing today], and at the age of two, her family fled to Taiwan, where she stayed until she came to West Germany. But they had no idea if other family members in mainland China had survived the internal war.”
West Berlin student life
The relationship between the couple developed quickly, and in the summer of 1974, Guetinger moved with Yan-Yun to West Berlin, where he began studying Chinese politics at the Free University. Like many West Berliners, he took advantage of having better freedom of movement, including the ability to travel to and from the GDR.
“For me, as a student, it was interesting to go to East Berlin because the books there were much cheaper, plus the music in East Germany was very good, and you could get cheaper music discs.”
Yet, there were travel rules that West Germans had to obey, such as registering with local police on arrival. They also could not exchange East German Marks back into hard West German Deutsche Marks when leaving. Instead, they were required to deposit the money into an East German bank.
At the end of one trip, Guetinger went to deposit the money but encountered a long queue.
“So I decided to skip the deposit and placed the money in a pouch with my keys,” he said. “We had different currencies, and GDR money was of no value across the border, so it remained there for many months until I went back.”
On his next trip to East Berlin, the casually dressed student watched as border guards sitting at high counters let in West Germans who were carrying big, heavy bags. Travelling empty-handed, he thought his passage would be hassle-free.
But when the border police got to him, they stopped and ordered him to follow them. They took him to a very small room with no window and a neon light, and they asked him to remove everything from his pockets.
“One by one, out came my passport, some money and the pouch. ‘What’s that?’ the guard asked, and I told him it was for my keys. For a few seconds, I hoped that would be enough," he said.
"Then he ordered me to open it, and instead of finding a key, he found GDR money. This was a major offence, what they called ‘offending the rules concerning the transfer of money’.”
Guetinger was questioned about the purpose of his visit and then left alone for what he says was about 90 minutes while the guards decided his fate.
“I sat in that room alone, and I knew I was in some kind of trouble,” he recalled.
Guetinger says he was ultimately allowed to go because the guards were satisfied with who he was meeting – a well-known writer named Jan Koplowitz, a former member of the German Communist Party.
“I could leave because I had an appointment with this particular connection,” he said.
Guetinger later concluded that X-rays had been used at the border, and that was how the guards had established that he was carrying cash into the GDR.
“We didn’t know about this back then,” he added.
Finding families
Despite the division, Guetinger’s family would find ways to meet, and sometimes broke rules to do so.
He recalls one such trip in the mid-1970s when his father came to visit him in West Berlin.
Guetinger says they decided to visit East Berlin and, at the last minute, decided to go on to visit his family in Frankfurt an der Oder.
Since the plan was hatched late in the day, it meant circumventing strict visa rules. A visa for East Berlin – which is all they had – meant they were only permitted to visit East Berlin and nowhere else in the GDR.
Guetinger says the trip quickly turned into a clandestine affair that involved coordination with his cousin and uncle. In East Germany, hardly anyone had a home phone, so they had to rely on public telephones or phones at work.
That constraint helped shape the family’s plan.
“My uncle and his son both worked at the power station, and anyone entering or leaving the power station had to report to the gatekeeper, who had a telephone. The gatekeeper liked eating fresh game, so in exchange for using the phone, my uncle would bring him deer or birds that he had hunted,” he said.
His cousin used the phone to speak with Guetinger and make the arrangements. Then, once in East Berlin, Guetinger and his family took the train as far as Karlshorst, a station about 30 minutes outside the city, where his cousin collected them by car.
“It was easier in a private car as we had less chance of being stopped by border guards than if we were on a train,” he said.
While it would have been possible to arrange to meet the family in East Berlin, they were eager to see where and how their family lived in the GDR. But they knew it was risky.
“If we had been caught, it would have been a problem not only for us but also for our family [in the East], as it would have been seen as a serious offence. We felt a genuine fear, but luckily, we were able to go and return without any trouble.”
West Germany and China
West Germany established diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China in 1972. For Yan-Yun’s family, the new connection between West Berlin, Taiwan and mainland China created a possible channel for renewing contact.
Guetinger said the family used West Berlin as an informal postal hub, passing letters between relatives in Taiwan and relatives in mainland China.
“The reconnection with my wife’s relatives was managed by postal communication, where our family in Taiwan sent us letters to West Berlin, and we could send them on to addresses in China, and vice versa,” Guetinger explained. “We had the names and old addresses, and that was enough.”
In 1988, Guetinger and his wife – they had married in 1977 – were able to visit mainland China, marking Yan-Yun’s first time back in more than four decades.
“It was an important trip,” Guetinger said, noting that they visited his wife’s family home and her birthplace.
“Some years later, we met Yan-Yun’s mother in Taiwan and travelled together with her from Taiwan to the Chinese mainland to meet other family members in Kunming and Nanjing. The family had been apart for 40 years, and reconnecting with them had all started from West Berlin,” he explained.
Lingering legacies of division
Following months of mounting public pressure, the Berlin Wall finally fell on a cold November night in 1989. Guetinger says it was a “surreal” moment – and his family quickly started seeing one another again.
“By then, Uncle Hans had retired, and both he, my aunt and Guenter visited us a few times in West Berlin. My other cousin, however, didn’t come to visit. He was happy to stay in the countryside. From what I can recall, Uncle Hans never got to return to our hometown of Bavaria before he passed away,” he said.
Today, Guetinger remains in contact with his family from the former GDR, and both of his children have met that part of their family, with the sides visiting each other’s respective homes.
Similarly, the family is also close with their wider family in Taiwan and visits often. Guetinger, who in the early 2000s authored Die Geschichte der Chinesen in Deutschland (The History of the Chinese in Germany), and his wife were there again this summer.
German unification continues to be heralded as a celebration – a peaceful revolution for the people, by the people – but there remain strong signs that the seeds of separation sown during the division have in many ways taken root.
For many, the experience of unification was characterised by economic instability, with job losses and the privatisation of East German companies. While less extreme today, economic disparities between the regions persist.
Unification effectively saw the capitalist-dominant West Germany absorb communist East Germany, and in doing so, left behind some of the more progressive elements of GDR society, including closer wage parity between genders and abortion rights.
For many eastern Germans, reunification also came with a sense that their institutions, careers and social arrangements had been swept aside rather than incorporated into a genuinely shared country. The economic shock was especially acute after the privatisation and closure of many East German enterprises.
Around the 30th anniversary of reunification, the Bertelsmann Foundation published a study based on research by the Berlin institute pollytix. It revealed that 84 percent of eastern respondents felt the unified nation should have kept more elements that worked well in the GDR. Researchers noted that Easterners frequently expressed that a true common society was never created, feeling instead that the Western system was simply imposed upon them.
The upheaval coincided with a surge in racist violence. In Rostock-Lichtenhagen in 1992, several hundred far-right rioters attacked the Sunflower House, which included accommodation for Vietnamese contract workers, and threw Molotov cocktails as police failed for days to regain control. This and other xenophobic attacks reflected the wider discontent non-white people faced as Germany sought to unify amid rising economic uncertainty.
Similar anti-immigration debates and economic fears have fuelled the rise of the far-right Alternative for Deutschland party in recent years.
For Guetinger, the enforced separation he has witnessed, first in his own life and then with his wife’s family, has left a legacy not just for his generation, but also for his children, both of whom were born during the division.
“There is a very famous saying – that you tear down the Wall, but there is still the ‘Mauer im Kopf’, or wall in the mind. I think my children’s generation are affected by this but in a very different way. They know there are these frictions.
“Even now, it’s very difficult to see how the division has affected my life. It feels like a daydream. History has taught us that politics does not work well if people are forced to separate. People should be free. Who are the people to say you are not allowed to meet your own family?
“My experiences have shown me that it’s abnormal to keep people separated and divided.”

Islamuddin Sajid
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
The second World Humanoid Robot Games opened in Beijing on Saturday, bringing together 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries for a five-day competition showcasing advances in humanoid robotics, CGTN reported.
The event, held at the National Speed Skating Oval, has expanded significantly from last year’s inaugural games, with the program featuring 51 events and 1,301 competitions across nine competition sessions.
The competition combines sporting events, artistic performances and challenges designed to demonstrate the practical applications of humanoid robots in real-world scenarios.
Of the 51 events, 30 are competitive sports, while another 21 focus on scenario-based challenges, according to the Chinese broadcaster.
The sporting competitions are designed to test robots’ mobility, coordination, balance and ability to perform tasks in environments modeled on human activities.
The five-day games also provide an international platform for companies, research institutions and robotics teams to demonstrate technologies and compete in practical applications.
The second edition represents a major expansion from the inaugural games, which featured only three days and six competition sessions.
Meanwhile, a Chinese humanoid robot developed by Unitree reportedly reached a top speed of 12.66 meters per second (28.32 mph), surpassing Usain Bolt’s 100-meter record pace of 12.42 meters per second (27.78 mph). The achievement highlights rapid advances in humanoid robot mobility and athletic performance.

Column: Washington's fiscal dysfunction is becoming a global risk
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
20:08:38 CST
21:08:38 KST

by Ahmed Sallam
The U.S. national debt topping the 40 trillion-U.S.-dollar mark is no longer simply a staggering figure on the books of the federal government. It is increasingly a symptom of a deeper problem at the heart of the world's largest economy.
The challenge goes well beyond the size of the debt itself, raising fundamental questions about the U.S. political system's capacity to make difficult, long-term fiscal decisions at a time when structural deficits are widening and the cost of servicing the debt is rising at an unprecedented pace.
The significance of the figure lies not only in its sheer magnitude, but also in the fiscal dynamics behind it. The federal deficit is expected to reach approximately 1.9 trillion dollars in 2026, equivalent to 5.8 percent of GDP. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) offers an even more troubling long-term outlook, projecting that the deficit will widen to 3.1 trillion dollars by 2036, while debt held by the public is expected to rise from about 101 percent of GDP today to 120 percent over the next decade.
This points to an increasingly difficult fiscal feedback loop: debt is no longer simply the consequence of persistent budget deficits; rising debt-servicing costs are themselves becoming a major driver of larger deficits.
The CBO expects net federal interest payments to exceed 1 trillion dollars in 2026, up from approximately 970 billion dollars in 2025, and to approach 2.1 trillion dollars by 2036. As a share of the economy, interest payments are projected to rise to 4.6 percent of GDP, from 3.3 percent today. This represents a growing drain on public resources that could otherwise be directed toward long-term investment in infrastructure, education, technology and other productive sectors.
IS THE UNITED STATES FACING IMMINENT DEFAULT?
The United States is not on the verge of being unable to meet its financial obligations in the short term. It issues the currency in which its debt is denominated and benefits from the world's deepest and most liquid market for Treasury securities, as well as the dollar's central role in the global financial system.
The more immediate concern, therefore, is not a technical default, but the steadily rising cost of sustaining the current fiscal trajectory in the absence of meaningful reforms.
At its core, this is as much a crisis of governance and political will as it is an economic challenge. Highly sensitive fiscal issues, including the debt ceiling, tax policy and mandatory spending programs, have increasingly become instruments of political leverage in the bitter partisan struggle between Republicans and Democrats.
Without the political willingness to pursue difficult and potentially unpopular measures -- whether raising taxes or restraining federal spending -- fundamental fiscal problems continue to be postponed, increasing the burden on future generations. Under current policies, debt held by the public is projected to reach 175 percent of GDP by 2056.
WHY SHOULD THE REST OF THE WORLD BE CONCERNED?
The answer lies in the dollar's unique role in the international financial system. It is not simply the currency of the United States; it is the principal reserve currency and a cornerstone of global finance.
Data from the International Monetary Fund show that the dollar continues to account for more than 57 percent of official foreign-exchange reserves worldwide. As a result, any significant shift in U.S. borrowing costs or financial conditions can quickly reverberate across global markets through interest rates, bond yields, exchange rates and capital flows.
Emerging markets and developing economies are particularly vulnerable to these spillover effects. When yields on U.S. Treasury securities and other safe-haven assets rise, the cost of external financing for emerging economies increases. Their currencies may come under sustained depreciation pressure, while the cost of servicing dollar-denominated debt rises.
Governments already facing tight fiscal constraints may consequently be forced to divert scarce resources toward debt servicing rather than investment in infrastructure, healthcare and education.
At the same time, predictions of an imminent collapse of the dollar are largely overstated. Of course, there are undoubtedly growing international efforts to diversify foreign exchange reserves and expand the use of local currencies in bilateral trade. The more plausible scenario, therefore, is not a sudden collapse of the dollar, but a gradual transition toward a more diversified and increasingly multipolar international monetary system.
WHAT LESSONS CAN ARAB AND AFRICAN ECONOMIES DRAW?
While these developments present Washington with a serious fiscal and political test, they also offer an important lesson for Arab and African economies: economic stability cannot depend excessively on a single source of financing or on the assumption that favorable global financial conditions will persist indefinitely.
For these economies, strengthening resilience requires deeper structural reforms, including diversifying external economic and financial partnerships, expanding domestic production, boosting exports, and building stronger fiscal and financial buffers capable of absorbing external shocks stemming from higher interest rates and exchange-rate volatility.
In conclusion, the U.S. debt surpassing 40 trillion dollars is more than a record figure dominating headlines. It is a warning sign of the mounting constraints facing the fiscal management of the world's largest economy.
If Washington continues to postpone difficult structural decisions, the consequences of political gridlock could extend well beyond U.S. borders. The global economy could ultimately bear the cost through greater financial volatility, tighter financing conditions and recurring economic shocks.
Editor's note: Ahmed Sallam is a former undersecretary of Egypt's State Information Service and a member of the Egyptian Council for Foreign Affairs.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.
